raw_case_text:
In late July, a 36-year-old African American man with a history of HIV and remote history of properly treated syphilis, presented to our institution for a second opinion regarding his recent diagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS). The patient's history revealed he had not been on anti-retroviral therapy (ART) for many years due to adverse effects. During the evaluation by his outside practitioner, he was told that his viral load was "very high", but uncertain in the number, though his CD4 count was 325 cells/ml. He was thus started on a combination of elvitegravir, cobicistat, tenofovir, and emtricitabine. Two weeks after restarting ART, he reported fevers, chills, night sweats and several erupting skin lesions on his jaw, scalp, nose, legs, and arms. Follow-up CD4 count revealed a moderate increase up to 450 cells/ml.
In June, during his initial work-up at an outside facility, a skin biopsy was done on a right scalp lesion and revealed an atypical lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the subcutaneous tissue, consisting mainly of CD3+, CD5+, CD7+, and CD8+ cells. Histiocytes were positive for CD68 marker, and the T-cell receptor (TCR) gene was clonally rearranged. Successively, a computed tomography (CT) scan of his neck, chest, and abdomen demonstrated several prominent lymph nodes in the neck, axillary, and inguinal areas, ranging from 14 mm up to 19 mm. A biopsy of the terminal ileum and of a rectal mass, which revealed on the former CT scan, were performed. The pathology of the terminal ileum showed an atypical submucosal lymphoid infiltrate consisting of 50% CD8+ and 50% CD4+ cells. The biopsy of the rectal mass showed atypical lymphoid cells in a necrotic background. The bone marrow biopsy was performed and showed normocellular marrow (40-60% cellularity) with regular trilinear hematopoiesis. No abnormal lymphoid population was detected using flow cytometry, and cytogenetics was normal 46, XY. Further inguinal and peripheral lymph node biopsies failed to show evidence of lymphoma. The differential at this time consisted of PTCL NOS versus CD8+ aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma. The patient underwent port placement and was to begin chemotherapy. It was at this time that he presented to us.
On initial presentation, the patient exhibited on his nose, forehead, scalp, cheek, neck, and bilateral upper and lower extremities, several large one to two inch, discrete, yellowish-brown, necrotic crusted malodorous verrucous plaques and tumors (Figures 1 and 2). He reported that the large plaque on his nose was occluding his nares and draining a foul-smelling brownish fluid, making it difficult for him to breath. At this time, he was not experiencing fever, chills, or night sweats, but did continue to endorse some unintentional weight loss. The lesion located on his right arm was quite painful, making it difficult to sleep, but there were no intraoral lesions present. At this time, further skin biopsies were performed. The pathology (Figures 3A and B) showed an atypical lymphohistiocytic infiltrate that appeared to be reactive without clonal etiology. There were areas of necrosis and no discrete granulomas. The epidermis showed spongiosis, keratinocyte necrosis; acute inflammatory infiltrate, and pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia with flow cytometry of the skin specimen showed predominantly small mature lymphocytes and histiocytes with no clonal findings and no evidence of T-cell lymphoma. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB), cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex and varicella zoster viruses, and Warthin-Starry staining were negative. AFB, fungal, and bacterial cultures were also negative. Throughout this work-up, the patient reported that his lesions were only getting worse, and his nasal breathing problems were also increasing.
After effectively ruling out cutanous lymphoma, secondary syphilis of the rupioid type became top of our differential. The fluorescent treponemal antibody (FTA-ABS) was positive, and the rapid plasma reagin titer was very highly reactive at 1:1,024. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies were negative. In conjunction with the time course and increase in his CD4 count after starting ART, it was thought that his rupioid syphilis was derived from an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). He was consequently commenced on intravenous penicillin G (IV) 24 million units daily but after about 24 hours from initiation, he developed fever and chills. It was unclear if this was due to an allergic reaction or secondary to a mild Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which is expected during treatment for rupioid syphilis. However, the dose was decreased and within days, the lesions began resolving and the patients breathing improved. He was treated in this manner for two weeks and then discharged with an additional three weekly injections of intramuscular benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units. The crusted lesions flaked off within a week of treatment. Within several weeks of treatment, all of the cutaneous lesions were resolved, but the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up without reevaluation of his intra-abdominal lesions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old male presenting for evaluation of extensive, painful, ulcerating and crusted verrucous cutaneous plaques involving the face, scalp, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by nasal airway obstruction.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient resumed combination antiretroviral therapy after a multi-year hiatus due to prior medication intolerances. Two weeks after restarting therapy, he developed acute fevers, chills, night sweats, and multiple rapidly erupting cutaneous lesions across the face, scalp, trunk, and extremities. An outside biopsy led to a presumptive diagnosis of peripheral T-cell lymphoma and chemotherapy port placement. He presented for a second opinion noting that a large necrotic nasal plaque was obstructing his nares with foul-smelling drainage and worsening dyspnea, alongside severe arm pain and persistent weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic retroviral infection off antiretroviral therapy for years (pre-treatment CD4 count 325 cells/mcL, viral load reported as very high; rising to CD4 450 cells/mcL on therapy). Remote history of treated syphilis. Chemotherapy port placement.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful verrucous plaques, foul-smelling nasal drainage, nasal obstruction, and weight loss; negative for active fever, night sweats, or oral mucosal lesions on presentation. Home medications: elvitegravir, cobicistat, tenofovir, emtricitabine. Allergies: prior intolerance to older antiretrovirals.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: multiple large (1 to 2 inches), discrete, yellowish-brown, malodorous, verrucous plaques and noduloulcerative tumors with thick necrotic rupioid crusting distributed across the nose, forehead, scalp, cheeks, neck, and bilateral upper and lower extremities; prominent nasal plaque occluding external nares with brownish purulent discharge; no intraoral mucosal lesions. General examination: afebrile, hemodynamically stable.
objective.routine_investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: within normal limits. Outside bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures: negative. Special stains (AFB, CMV, HSV, VZV, and Warthin-Starry): negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck/chest/abdominal CT: multiple enlarged lymph nodes in neck, axillae, and inguinal areas (14-19 mm); terminal ileal and rectal masses. Outside scalp biopsy: atypical subcutaneous infiltrate with TCR rearrangement; bone marrow biopsy: normocellular (40-60%) with normal trilineage hematopoiesis, normal 46,XY cytogenetics, and negative flow cytometry; terminal ileum and rectal biopsies: atypical lymphoid infiltrate without definitive lymphoma; repeat lymph node biopsies: negative for lymphoma. Repeat comprehensive skin biopsy: reactive atypical lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, keratinocyte necrosis, and acute inflammation; skin flow cytometry: small mature polyclonal lymphocytes without clonality or evidence of T-cell lymphoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Malignant / rupioid secondary syphilis presenting as an unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) mimicking cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4 count rising from 325 to 450 cells/mcL on cART). Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL-NOS) and aggressive epidermotropic cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma ruled out by repeat polyclonal skin biopsies, flow cytometry, and bone marrow biopsy; neurosyphilis ruled out by normal CSF studies. Syphilis confirmed by positive fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) and markedly reactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer of 1:1,024. Management & Outcome: Initiated on continuous intravenous aqueous penicillin G (24 million units daily); developed transient fever and chills within 24 hours consistent with a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Following dose titration, nasal breathing promptly improved, and rupioid crusts detached within 1 week. After 2 weeks of IV therapy, discharged to complete 3 weekly doses of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (2.4 million units weekly), resulting in complete dermatological clearance within several weeks.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 47-year-old obese caucasian female with an underlying history of untreated obstructive sleep apnea. She was a non-smoker and had no personal history of asthma, COPD, diabetes, hypertension, or cardiac disease.
She tested positive for Covid-19 in September, 2021. She was unvaccinated at that time. Her sick contact was her husband who also was positive for COVID-19 during that period. She described loss of sense of taste and smell, periodic nausea with episodes of vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, fevers and chills. Later she developed a cough, associated with shortness of breath with minimal exertion. With the worsening of shortness of breath, she presented to the emergency room ten days after being positive for COVID-19.
She was febrile in the emergency room with a temperature of 101.1 F. Chest x-ray showed minor bi-basilar infiltrates [Fig. 1]. She was hypoxic with an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Rest of the blood work was unremarkable except for an elevation in the inflammatory markers. At the time of admission, her white cell count was 10,900/uL (reference range 4500 to 11,000/uL), CRP level was 76.1 mg/L (reference range 0-8 mg/L), interleukin-6 level 13.9 pg/ml (reference rage 0-7 pg/ml), D-dimer level 193 ng/ml (normal high <244 ng/ml), LDH level was normal at 187 units/L (reference range 140-280 units/L).
She was started on supplemental oxygen through nasal cannula and high-dose intravenous steroids. Intravenous remdesivir was not considered since it had already been ten days since she tested positive. After a 3-day uncomplicated stay in the hospital, the patient was weaned off of oxygen and was discharged home on a steroid taper. During the hospital course, she also endorsed some right-sided leg cramping which resolved spontaneously with as needed doses of acetaminophen. She received standard subcutaneous anticoagulation DVT prophylaxis with subcutaneous heparin.
Three days later, the patient presented again to the emergency department with intractable epigastric pain of one day duration. She stated that the pain was constant but got worse with any attempt to eat. She had severe nausea with the pain and few episodes of emesis that were non-bloody and nonbilious. She denied any diarrhea, sick contacts or food exposure that might have led to gastroenteritis. She denied any recurrence of her fevers, chills, cough, chest pain or shortness of breath.
She received a contrast enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis that showed [Fig. 2] non-occlusive filling defect in the descending thoracic aorta measuring 28 x 11 x 11 mm, likely representing a thrombus and mild fat stranding along the common origin of celiac trunk and SMA which is nonspecific, however may be seen with vasculitis. No other abnormality in the arterial and venous vasculature, or acute process in the abdomen and pelvis.
The CRP level was 16.4 mg/L (reference range 0-8 mg/L). The renal function panel, electrolyte panel and hepatic panel were completely within normal limits. She had a leukocytosis of 15,300 cells/mm3 which was predominantly neutrophilic, this was considered secondary to the use of systemic steroids that she was discharged with in the previous admission.
She was admitted, started on anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin, 1 mg/kg body weight twice a day with an intention to transition to direct oral anticoagulation, once she was able to tolerate oral diet and medications. The etiology of the abdominal pain was quite unclear at the time of admission and multiple differential diagnosis were considered. COVID-19 induced abdominal pain and gastroenteritis was a potential diagnosis and the systemic steroids were continued. Symptomatic management was offered with pantoprazole and ondansetron intravenously. The other differential was occlusion of the superior mesenteric or celiac arteries by the thrombus, thus leading to post-prandial abdominal pain. A Doppler study of the mesenteric arteries was requested but the study was inconclusive because of the patient's obese body habitus. A bilateral venous Doppler excluded deep venous thrombosis in the lower extremities.
On day 2 of the hospitalization, the patient's abdominal pain worsened and she had multiple bouts of emesis. The emesis was bilious and nonbloody. She also developed a low-grade fever. Lactic acid level was elevated at 3.4 mmol/L. She had a repeat CT angiogram of the abdomen and the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery and rest of the vasculature were unremarkable. However, there were several small to moderate sized splenic infarctions. The largest infarction was 2.4 cm [Fig. 3].
On day 3 and day 4 of the hospitalization, the lactic acid level normalized with intravenous hydration but there was no improvement in her nausea and vomiting. An obstruction series was done that showed gaseous distention of the small bowel loops, up to 4.6 cm in the mid abdomen. The findings were concerning for small bowel obstruction and were new compared to the CT scan from 2 days prior [Fig. 4]. A nasogastric tube was inserted to relieve the obstruction and was managed with complete bowel rest and intermittent suction. Patient was also noted to be febrile with a temperature of 101.2 F. The leukocytosis also worsened to 20,600 cells/mm3. Blood cultures were obtained and she was empirically started on intravenous Piperacillin/Tazobactam.
The nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain gradually improved. A small bowel follow through obstruction series performed two days later ruled out a complete small bowel obstruction. Blood cultures from admission grew pan-sensitive Klebsiella pneumoniae which likely originated from the bowel. Antibiotic coverage was downgraded to intravenous Cefazolin while inpatient and discharged on a 2-week course of oral cefuroxime. She was also transitioned to Apixaban on discharge. A complete hyper-coagulable work up could not be attempted because of the active thrombus but genetic mutations like prothrombin gene mutation, factor 5 Leiden mutation, anti-cardiolipin antibodies and lupus anti-coagulant were negative. Follow up CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis two weeks after discharge revealed decreased size of the thrombus in the descending aorta [Fig. 5].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old female presenting with intractable epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting for 1 day, three days following hospital discharge for viral pneumonia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to initial hospital presentation, the patient tested positive for viral infection after exposure to her infected husband, developing anosmia, ageusia, intermittent nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, fevers, chills, cough, and exertional dyspnea. She was admitted for 3 days for acute hypoxemic pneumonia and treated with supplemental oxygen and IV steroids. During that admission, she experienced transient right leg cramping. Three days after discharge, she re-presented to the emergency department with severe, constant epigastric pain exacerbated by eating, accompanied by nausea and non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting. She denied diarrhea, fever, chills, cough, chest pain, or dyspnea. On hospital day 2 of the readmission, her abdominal pain worsened with bilious emesis and low-grade fever. By day 3–4, she developed symptoms and radiographic signs of small bowel obstruction, high fever, and bacteremia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea, obesity (class III). Non-smoker. No history of asthma, COPD, diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease. Unvaccinated against pandemic respiratory virus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: Anosmia, ageusia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, fever, chills, cough, exertional dyspnea, right leg cramping. Readmission: Constant epigastric pain, severe nausea, vomiting. Denies diarrhea, chest pain, or recurrent dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: T 101.1 °F, SpO2 88% on room air, obese habitus. Readmission: Constant epigastric tenderness. Day 2: Low-grade fever, worsening epigastric/abdominal tenderness. Day 4: T 101.2 °F, abdominal distension, signs of small bowel ileus/obstruction.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission: Chest X-ray showed minor bibasilar infiltrates; WBC 10,900/μL, CRP 76.1 mg/L (reference 0–8 mg/L), IL-6 13.9 pg/mL (reference 0–7 pg/mL), D-dimer 193 ng/mL (normal high < 244 ng/mL), LDH 187 U/L (reference 140–280 U/L). Readmission: CRP 16.4 mg/L, WBC 15,300/μL increasing to 20,600/μL, serum lactic acid 3.4 mmol/L (normalized with hydration). Normal renal, electrolyte, and hepatic panels. Lower extremity bilateral venous Doppler: Negative for DVT. Mesenteric artery Doppler: Inconclusive due to obesity. Small bowel series: Gaseous distension of small bowel loops up to 4.6 cm in mid-abdomen, ruling out complete mechanical obstruction on follow-through. Hypercoagulability workup: Negative for prothrombin gene mutation, factor V Leiden mutation, anticardiolipin antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis (readmission): Non-occlusive filling defect in descending thoracic aorta measuring 28 x 11 x 11 mm (mural thrombus) and mild fat stranding at common origin of celiac trunk and SMA. Repeat CT angiogram (day 2): Patent celiac and superior mesenteric arteries, but revealed several small-to-moderate splenic infarctions (largest 2.4 cm). Follow-up CT scan (2 weeks post-discharge): Decreased size of descending thoracic aortic thrombus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute COVID-19 infection (confirmed by RT-PCR 10 days prior to first admission; household exposure) complicated by acute hypoxemic pneumonia, severe COVID-19-induced hypercoagulability resulting in large descending thoracic aortic mural thrombus with downstream splenic infarctions and mesenteric ischemia/ischemic ileus, and secondary Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia originating from bowel translocation.

Confirmation: Admission blood cultures grew pan-sensitive Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Management and outcome: Initial admission treated with supplemental oxygen and IV steroids. Readmission managed with therapeutic anticoagulation using low molecular weight heparin (1 mg/kg BID), IV pantoprazole, ondansetron, nasogastric tube decompression, and empiric IV piperacillin-tazobactam de-escalated to IV cefazolin and completed with a 2-week course of oral cefuroxime. Transitioned to oral apixaban. Symptoms fully resolved; follow-up imaging demonstrated resolving aortic thrombus.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old woman developed steroid responsive bilateral optic neuritis in January 2010. Further steroid responsive episodes of unilateral optic neuritis occurred in February 2016 and September 2018. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was acellular with normal protein and absence of unmatched oligoclonal bands and MRI appearances of the brain and cervical cord were normal with no evidence of demyelination. She was treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF; 2 g/day) and prednisolone (10 mg/day). She tested positive for serum MOG-IgG1 antibodies by live cell-based assay after her second relapse, confirming a diagnosis of MOGAD and remained persistently positive for more than 3.5 years before MOG IgG1 became negative and MOG-antibody titers fell below the cut-off of 1:200 (Figure 1). At this time, visual acuities were documented as 20/20 (right) and 20/16 (left) with preserved color vision bilaterally. Due to side-effects, corticosteroids were tapered to cessation over 12 weeks, but she remained on MMF (Figure 1). Four months later, she developed malaise, coryzal symptoms, sweating, and postural dizziness. Based on systemic symptoms and a SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive nasopharyngeal swab, COVID-19 was confirmed. Six days later she reported pain on right eye movement with worsening visual acuity. On admission, consistent with optic neuritis she had a right relative afferent pupillary defect with right visual acuity reduced to hand movements. Her left visual acuity remained unchanged at 6/6. The remainder of the cranial nerve examination was unremarkable. There were no pyramidal signs and sensory examination and gait were normal.
Admission work-up including hematological, renal, liver parameters, C-reactive protein, and chest x-ray were normal. However, MOG-IgG1 was strongly positive indicating "seroreversion" with an increase in MOG antibody end-point titer to 1:800 (Figure 1). She received intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 5 days followed by five cycles of plasma exchange. One week after treatment MOG-antibody titers reduced to 1:200 (Figure 1). MMF was increased to 3 g/day and she was recommenced on prednisolone (40 mg/day) with a plan to slowly taper to a maintenance dose of 10 mg/day. Treatment was well tolerated without adverse effects.
At discharge right visual acuity had improved to 20/125 and through telephone assessment, 3 months later she reported her vision to be "60% back to normal," with continuing improvement. Unfortunately, during the acute illness, it was not possible to obtain cross-sectional imaging of the brain and orbits due to concerns about SARS-CoV-2 transmission. Brain MRI with dedicated orbital views, 2 months following relapse demonstrated progression of right optic nerve atrophy and subtle T2 signal hyperintensity as compared to the prior study in 2016.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old female with a history of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease presented with right ocular pain on movement and acute loss of vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months after corticosteroid cessation, the patient developed malaise, coryzal symptoms, diaphoresis, and postural dizziness. Six days following the onset of these systemic symptoms, she experienced retro-orbital pain on right eye movement accompanied by severe, progressive deterioration of visual acuity in the right eye.
subjective.past_medical_history: Steroid-responsive bilateral optic neuritis (2010) and unilateral optic neuritis relapses (2016, 2018) diagnosed as myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD). Corticosteroids were successfully tapered off four months prior; maintained on mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 2 g/day. MOG-IgG1 antibody titers had previously become negative (<1:200) with preserved baseline visual acuity (20/20 right eye, 20/16 left eye).
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports malaise, coryza, sweating, dizziness, right eye pain, and right visual impairment. Denies motor deficits, sensory paresthesias, bowel/bladder incontinence, or ataxia. Current medications: Mycophenolate mofetil 2 g daily. Allergies: Not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Neuro-ophthalmological examination: Right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) present; right visual acuity reduced to hand movements only. Left visual acuity preserved at 6/6 with intact color vision. Cranial nerves otherwise intact. Neurological examination revealed no pyramidal signs, with normal sensory modalities and normal gait.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, renal profile, and liver function tests: normal. C-reactive protein (CRP): normal. Chest X-ray: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum MOG-IgG1 antibody testing (live cell-based assay): strongly positive with end-point titer 1:800, confirming acute seroreversion and disease relapse (titer decreased to 1:200 one week after plasma exchange). Brain MRI with dedicated orbital views (obtained 2 months post-relapse due to acute infection control restrictions): progressive right optic nerve atrophy and subtle T2 hyperintensity compared to 2016 imaging.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute relapse of MOG-antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) optic neuritis triggered by acute COVID-19 infection, definitively confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR nasopharyngeal swab. Treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) followed by five cycles of therapeutic plasma exchange. Maintenance mycophenolate mofetil was increased to 3 g/day and oral prednisolone restarted at 40 mg/day (with planned slow taper to 10 mg/day). Visual acuity in the right eye improved to 20/125 at discharge and 60% subjective recovery at 3-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year old Cameroonian female was diagnosed with AIDS (CDC stage C3) in May 2012. A duodenal histoplasmosis and cryptococcosis infection were treated from June 2012 with a 3-week course of amphotericin B - flucytosine followed by oral voriconazole 100 mg bid. A combined antiretroviral regimen (cART) was initiated (emtricitabine, tenofovir and raltegravir). As she developed a single large intracranial mass, voriconazole was given intravenously and doses were increased up to 4 mg/kg/12 h. A cerebral biopsy showed aspecific inflammatory infiltrates with-T lymphocytes, negative gram stain and broad range PCR. As the lesion was associated with a voluminous edema, she was started on IV dexamethasone (3 mg tid) progressively tapered over 1 month. The proton pump inhibitor (PPI) esomeprazole 40 mg bid was started because of severe epigastralgia associated with duodenal histoplasmosis.
Voriconazole first C0 was subtherapeutic (<1.0 mug/mL; range 1.0 - 5.0 mug/mL ) (Figure  1). The patient was genotyped for CYP2C19. It came heterozygous for the variant allele CYP2C19*17 (c.-860C > T; rs12248560) that is associated with an increased enzyme activity. Phenotyping with 2 mg omeprazole, while on CYP2C19 inhibitor esomeprazole, showed decreased CYP2C19 activity (omeprazole metabolic ratio =10.5; cut-off = 5). At that time voriconazole C0 was within the therapeutic range.
Due to several HIV resistance mutations and hepatitis B status, cART was modified with the addition of abacavir in order to increase cerebral penetration of unboosted atazanavir together with maintenance of emtricitabine/tenofovir. Atazanavir absorption depends on gastric acidity. The patient was switched from esomeprazole to the histamine-2 receptor antagonist ranitidine, which is less potent in suppressing intragastric pH.
Several voriconazole C0 were then measured below the therapeutic range despite substantial increased dosing (Figure  1). Darunavir - ritonavir regimen was introduced because of therapeutic failure and atazanavir was stopped. The patient presented with new onset epigastralgia and anemia. Ranitidine was replaced by esomeprazole 40 mg IV bid. Three days later, voriconazole C0 increased 14-fold and the voriconazole dose was reduced by 50% (2.5 mg/kg bid). There were no other medication changes. Subsequent voriconazole C0 stayed within the therapeutic range. However the patient's condition deteriorated as she developed progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. She eventually died four months later.
CYP2C19 activity is modulated both by genetic polymorphisms and drug - drug interactions. Our patient was heterozygous for CYP2C19*17. Its frequency is approximately 21% in Caucasians, 16% in African-Americans, and 3% in Asians . This allele is associated with increased enzymatic activity and may decrease voriconazole exposure compared to homozygous wild type extensive metabolizers . CYP2C19 phenotype was performed  under high doses of esomeprazole, a CYP2C19 inhibitor. It explains the reduced enzymatic activity despite the patient's genotype. Voriconazole C0 was within the therapeutic range when associated with the proton pump inhibitor . It was subtherapeutic when the patient received ranitidine, which has no influence on CYP activity and voriconazole concentrations . Atazanavir is a CYP3A4 inhibitor . Hence voriconazole clearance depended only on uninhibited CYP2C19. When atazanavir was stopped, boosted darunavir was introduced. Ritonavir is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor and can lead to increased voriconazole concentration.  However repeated administration of ritonavir induces CYP2C19 metabolic activity and potentially causes a reduction in voriconazole exposure . The magnitude of the effect depends on the dose administered. The net effect of low dose ritonavir and inhibition of CYP2C19 by high-dose esomeprazole is likely to be a decrease in enzyme metabolic activity.
After esomeprazole was reintroduced, the patient was taking both a CYP2C19 and a CYP 3A4 inhibitor, and voriconazole plasma levels reached therapeutic concentrations.
Double blockade of voriconazole metabolic pathways (CYP2C19 and CYP3A4) led to concentrations within the therapeutic range in a patient genetically susceptible to subtherapeutic voriconazole concentrations. This case illustrates how the integration of drug-drug interactions and pharmacogenetics can help interpret drug concentrations during therapeutic drug monitoring, and thus minimize the risk of suboptimal exposure to voriconazole. The "boosting strategy" is mainly used in the fields of HIV therapeutics with antiretroviral drugs such as ritonavir or cobicistat and its efficacy to overcome specific CYP genotypes has not been evaluated so far.
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this Case report and any accompanying images. A copy of the written consent is available for review by the Editor of this journal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old female presenting with severe epigastric pain, headache, and focal neurological deficits associated with a newly discovered intracranial mass lesion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had advanced retroviral disease complicated by duodenal fungal disease and disseminated fungal infection treated with amphotericin B, flucytosine, and oral voriconazole. Shortly after initiating combination antiretroviral therapy, she developed severe epigastric pain and progressive neurological symptoms from a large solitary intracranial mass with extensive cerebral edema. She was escalated to intravenous voriconazole and initiated on dexamethasone, esomeprazole, and modified cART regimens, with complex therapeutic drug monitoring due to fluctuating voriconazole plasma concentrations.
subjective.past_medical_history: Advanced retroviral illness (CDC Stage C3) diagnosed in May 2012; concurrent chronic hepatitis B virus infection; duodenal fungal infection and cryptococcal disease treated with amphotericin B-flucytosine followed by oral voriconazole; documented antiretroviral resistance mutations. Born in Cameroon.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe epigastralgia, headache, and focal neurological symptoms; negative for fever, hemoptysis, or diarrhea. Home medications: emtricitabine, tenofovir, raltegravir (subsequently modified to include abacavir, unboosted atazanavir, boosted darunavir/ritonavir), voriconazole, esomeprazole, dexamethasone. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination demonstrated focal deficits corresponding to the intracranial mass lesion; abdomen exhibited localized epigastric tenderness without rebound or peritoneal signs; vital signs stable.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline liver and renal panels monitored. Therapeutic drug monitoring: initial voriconazole trough concentration (C0) subtherapeutic at < 1.0 mcg/mL (therapeutic range: 1.0-5.0 mcg/mL); dropped again to < 1.0 mcg/mL upon switching from esomeprazole to ranitidine; reached therapeutic target of 3.2 mcg/mL following co-administration of high-dose esomeprazole (40 mg BID) and low-dose ritonavir (100 mg QD).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: single large intracranial mass lesion with voluminous perilesional vasogenic edema; follow-up MRI at 6 months showed substantial regression of the intracranial mass. Stereotactic cerebral biopsy: non-specific inflammatory lymphocytic infiltrates with T lymphocytes; Gram stain negative; broad-range PCR negative. Pharmacogenetic genotyping: heterozygous for CYP2C19*17 ultra-rapid metabolizer allele (c.-860C>T; rs12248560). CYP2C19 phenotyping with 2 mg omeprazole: metabolic ratio 10.5 (cut-off 5), demonstrating enzymatic inhibition under esomeprazole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Central nervous system and duodenal fungal disease (Histoplasma capsulatum and Cryptococcus neoformans) in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection / AIDS (CDC Stage C3) with chronic hepatitis B co-infection, complicated by subtherapeutic voriconazole exposure secondary to the CYP2C19*17 ultra-rapid metabolizer phenotype. Confirmed by duodenal histopathology and cryptococcal diagnostics. Brain biopsy ruled out bacterial abscess and high-grade lymphoma. Management & Outcome: High-dose intravenous dexamethasone (3 mg TID) tapered over 1 month for cerebral edema. Overcame rapid CYP2C19 metabolism through dual enzymatic blockade combining high-dose esomeprazole (40 mg BID; CYP2C19 inhibitor) and ritonavir-boosted darunavir (CYP3A4 inhibitor), successfully maintaining voriconazole trough at 3.2 mcg/mL. Six-month follow-up brain MRI demonstrated substantial mass regression with clinical recovery.

raw_case_text:
In Oct 2017, a 32-year-old male presented with intermittent bleeding per-rectum after defecation for 40 days with associated cough and fever. The patient had noticed a mass over the anus for five years but did not seek treatment as the lesion was not painful. He had visited the surgical unit at Gondar University Hospital, and he was under investigation for possible colorectal carcinoma.
At the presentation, he was well-looking, with normal vital signs. On abdominal examination, he had a spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin, a liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, and a 5 cm by 5 cm erythematous nontender plaque over the inner right buttock, perianal area. Per-rectum examination showed a circumferential firm rectal swelling 4 cm from the anal verge.
The abdominal CT scan showed a circumferential rectal mass 2.5 cm thick with extension to the mesorectum and thickening of the mesorectal facia (suggestive of rectal cancer with rectal and mesorectal extension). It also showed mesorectal lymphadenopathy (stage III) and hepatosplenomegaly. The conclusion of the CT scan was rectal cancer plus hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X-ray was normal.
An endoscopic biopsy from the rectum showed three fragments with unremarkable mucosa except for focal ulceration. The submucosa showed intense lymphocytic inflammation, and numerous macrophages were stuffed with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. No feature of malignancy was seen in the biopsy. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) from the perianal lesion showed Leishman Donovan bodies (grade+3 amastigotes). Splenic aspiration was carried out to rule out concomitant VL but was negative for Leishmania amastigotes. An HIV test was carried out at admission, and he was found to be seropositive with a CD4 count of 306.
The patient was treated with (liposomal amphotericin B) AmBisome 5 mg/kg for 8 doses initially after which rectal bleeding stopped, and his fever recovered. On physical examination, he had a perianal 4 cm by 2 cm mass with central ulceration, which had decreased in size but still showed an active CL lesion. Therefore, treatment was extended with AmBisome 5 mg/kg for 8 doses plus miltefosine 100 mg for 28 days (2 x 50 mg daily). Antiretroviral therapy was planned to be initiated after counseling.
After treatment completion, the perianal mass flattened to 3 by 2 cm, with no significant rectal mass appreciated on physical examination. Fine needle aspiration from the perianal healed lesion was negative for Leishman Donovan bodies. A repeated abdominal CT scan showed a circumferential rectal mass of 1 cm and splenomegaly, indicating a reduction in the rectal lesion size. The patient was followed for 2 years, without any recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male presented with intermittent bleeding per-rectum after defecation for 40 days, accompanied by cough and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed a painless perianal mass 5 years prior to presentation, for which he did not seek treatment. Forty days prior to presentation, he developed intermittent post-defecation rectal bleeding associated with fever and cough, and was subsequently investigated for suspected colorectal carcinoma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Five-year history of an untreated painless perianal mass. No other prior medical conditions, hospitalizations, or travel documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever and cough; denies pain associated with the perianal lesion.

objective.physical_examination: Well-appearing with normal vital signs. Abdomen: spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin, liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin; a 5 cm x 5 cm erythematous nontender plaque over the inner right buttock and perianal area. Digital rectal examination: circumferential firm rectal swelling 4 cm from the anal verge.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray: normal. CD4 count: 306 cells/muL.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan: circumferential rectal mass 2.5 cm thick with extension to the mesorectum, thickening of the mesorectal fascia (suggestive of rectal cancer with rectal and mesorectal extension), mesorectal lymphadenopathy (stage III), and hepatosplenomegaly. Endoscopic rectal biopsy: unremarkable mucosa except for focal ulceration, submucosa with intense lymphocytic inflammation and numerous macrophages with intracellular structures; no features of malignancy. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) of perianal lesion: cellular aspirate with macrophage infiltration. Splenic aspiration: negative for parasites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Endoscopic rectal biopsy demonstrated numerous macrophages stuffed with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) from the perianal lesion confirmed Leishman-Donovan bodies (grade +3 amastigotes). Splenic aspiration was negative for Leishmania amastigotes, excluding concomitant visceral leishmaniasis. HIV serology was positive (CD4 306 cells/muL). Malignancy ruled out on endoscopic biopsy. Treatment and Outcome: Initiated on liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) 5 mg/kg for 8 doses, resulting in cessation of rectal bleeding and resolution of fever. The perianal lesion decreased to 4 cm x 2 cm with central ulceration. Treatment was extended with AmBisome 5 mg/kg for 8 additional doses plus oral miltefosine 100 mg daily (50 mg twice daily) for 28 days, alongside planned antiretroviral therapy counseling. Following therapy, the perianal mass flattened to 3 cm x 2 cm, repeat FNA was negative for Leishman-Donovan bodies, and repeat abdominal CT showed reduction of the circumferential rectal mass to 1 cm with residual splenomegaly. No recurrence at 2-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A forty-five-year-old black male patient from Apucarana,Parana, with one atypical lesion on the right side of his back was attended, in March 2009, in the LEPAC (Laboratorio de Ensino e Pesquisa em Analises Clinicas) of the Universidade Estadual de Maringa, for cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) laboratory diagnosis. The patient reported that the lesion had been present for approximately one month (Fig. 1A). The lesion was a rounded plaque, with a erythematous violaceous center, descamative ulcerated edges, surrounded by an extensive area of lichenification, measuring 20 cm. Based on clinical appearance, the differential diagnosis of the lesion included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis. Before seeking for medical attention, the patient used topical antibiotics, but the lesion persisted without improvement. The performed tests showed a positive Montenegro skin test (MST) with an induration of 10 mm and indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) positive for anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies, reaching a titer of 80.Leishmania amastigotes were detected in the material obtained by scraping of the lesion stained by Giemsa (Fig. 1B) and cultured in blood base agar (BBA). The BBA grown parasites were sent to the Colecao de Leishmania of Instituto Oswaldo Cruz (CLIOC), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, for identification and the strains were confirmed as L. (V.) braziliensis (MHOM/BR/2009/3476). The species identification was performed by multilocus enzyme electrophoresis (MLEE). To exclude the possibility of coexisting infections, fungi and HIV investigations were performed with negative results. 
The patient was treated with 120 ampoules of intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (approximately 15 mg/kg Sb5+ per day) in three cycles of 20 days each at the Pronto Atendimento Municipal of Apucarana municipality. Approximately 40 days after the end of treatment (August 2009) the lesion was still active and new laboratory tests were performed. The IIF test was positive with a titer of 160 and the direct parasite search was negative. 
About six months later (May 2010) the patient was submitted to another treatment with intravenous pentamidine (4 mg/kg per day) for seven days, which resulted in apparent healing of the lesion. In June 2010, the values of serum amylase (87 U/L) and creatinine (1.0 mg/dL) were normal. However, some months later, new papular lesions emerged, ulcerated and spread to the axillary region. In November 2010, the patient was admitted for treatment with amphotericin B desoxycholate (50 mg/day). The treatment was discontinued after three doses because the values of serum urea (88 mg/dL) and creatinine (3.1 mg/dL) were increased indicating renal failure. One additional course of pentamidine for 10 days was established (April 2011). There was a partial clinical resolution of lesions with the patient still presenting some residual lesions. 
In February 2012, about three years after the onset of the lesion and despite the multiple treatments, the lesion was not healing. The lesion was an ulcerated plaque with erythematous fibrous bottom and verrucous edges, surrounded by a lichenification area in the right scapular region and posterior region of the right arm (Fig. 1C). New laboratory tests were performed. The direct parasite search revealed the presence of characteristic amastigotes of Leishmania spp., the IIF showed titer 320, and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for kDNA minicircles of the subgenusLeishmania (Viannia) was positive.
The patient was treated again with meglumine antimoniate by the intravenous route (3 ampoules per day) for approximately 40 days. Following this treatment, the lesion healed. Unfortunately, about a year after the end of the treatment, the patient died of a heart attack.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male presented with a large, atypical ulcerated plaque on his back of one month's duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 45-year-old male from Apucarana, Paraná, Brazil presented in March 2009 with a 1-month history of a rounded, ulcerated plaque on the right side of his back that failed topical antibiotics. He received three cycles of intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (~15 mg/kg/day, total 120 ampoules) over 60 days, but the lesion remained active. In May 2010, he received intravenous pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day for 7 days) with apparent initial healing, but months later new papules ulcerated and spread to the axillary region. In November 2010, intravenous amphotericin B desoxycholate was started but stopped after three doses due to nephrotoxicity. A second course of pentamidine (10 days) in April 2011 achieved only partial resolution. In February 2012, 3 years after onset, he presented with an extensive, verrucous ulcerated plaque across the right scapula and arm.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Apucarana, Paraná, Brazil. Prior use of topical antibiotics. Developed acute renal failure secondary to amphotericin B desoxycholate in November 2010. Patient subsequently died of a myocardial infarction approximately one year after definitive cure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Chronic ulcerated skin plaque on back, axilla, and arm. Denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, or visceral symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination (March 2009): large rounded plaque measuring 20 cm on the right side of the back, with an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative ulcerated edges, and surrounding lichenification. Examination in February 2012: ulcerated plaque with an erythematous fibrous base and verrucous margins, surrounded by extensive lichenification extending over the right scapular region and posterior right arm.
objective.routine_investigations: June 2010: serum amylase 87 U/L, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. November 2010: serum urea 88 mg/dL, serum creatinine 3.1 mg/dL, indicating acute renal failure following amphotericin B desoxycholate.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct lesion scrapings stained with Giemsa: microscopic examination revealed intracellular protozoal organisms. Parasite isolation in blood base agar (BBA) culture performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Chronic refractory cutaneous leishmaniasis with atypical large plaque-like morphology caused by Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Positive Montenegro skin test (10 mm induration); positive indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) for anti-Leishmania IgG (titer 1:80 initially, 1:160 in August 2009, 1:320 in February 2012); direct Giemsa-stained scrapings revealed Leishmania amastigotes; culture in BBA confirmed as Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis (strain MHOM/BR/2009/3476) by CLIOC; positive kDNA minicircle PCR for subgenus Leishmania (Viannia).
Differentials Ruled Out: Lichen simplex chronicus, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Patient failed initial intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (120 ampoules), IV pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day for 7 days, then 10 days), and amphotericin B desoxycholate (complicated by acute renal failure). In February 2012, successfully retreated with intravenous meglumine antimoniate (3 ampoules/day) for 40 days, leading to complete lesion healing. The patient died of a myocardial infarction one year later.

raw_case_text:
The patient, male, 20 years old, was diagnosed with Hemophilia. At the age of 2 due to continuous bleeding upon trauma. The patient was then treated with multiple infusion of coagulation factor VIII. In 2002, the patient was diagnosed with HIV infection combined with type B hepatitis and type C hepatitis virus infection. CD4+T cell was 70 cell/muL in May 2002 and rose to 200 cell/muL after the treatment using the highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). The right thigh swelling occurred in 2005 and was tentatively diagnosed as hematoma which increased gradually. On June 18, 2007, the patient was admitted to the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center due to the swollen right thigh. The admission diagnoses were the following: (1) the right thigh hematoma, (2) AIDS, (3) hemophilia, (4) hepatitis C, and (5) hepatitis B. 
A group of surgical experts have been invited to consult on the case after the patient was admitted to the surgical ward. The consultation session concluded that the surgical indication is clear, but with extremely high risk for surgery. The initial treatment plan followed the conservative guideline. However, the hematoma increased gradually with oozing wound which exudated blood and body fluid daily and led to hypoalbuminemia with severe anemia. The patient was put on nutritional support such as albumin and the blood transfusion with daily dose of VIII factor 6000 u that maitin active VIII factor 40%-60%, human serum albumin 1 unit, infusion of the washed red blood cells 2 u every other day, plasma 200 mL in addition to the antivirus, antibiotics, and other drugs which added up to a daily healthcare cost of over 10 K RMB only to merely maintain the basic life-support with hemoglobin in the 15-40 g/L range. The heart failure and kidney failures occurred during the conservative treatment which required symptomatic treatment and intensive care. 
After careful preparation, the patient's CD4 level rose to 272 cell/muL with the hemoglobin of 50.8 g/L and HIV-1 viral load dropped to below the detection level. On July 28, 2009, the joint relief operation was performed in patient's right hip under general anesthesia with intraoperative radial artery and central venous pressure monitoring (Figure 1). 2000 u of factor VIII infusion was applied before the operation followed by 4000 u of VIII factor during the operation. The operating room implemented standard disinfection and isolation procedures to prevent occupational exposure of the healthcare professionals to the HIV during the surgery. After the skin incision was made on the patient's right thigh, the truncated surface was carefully separated to cut off the blood vessels and minimize surgical bleeding. The right hip joint capsule was cut and the femoral neck had crisp fracture with bleeding on the femoral neck cross-section. The femoral head was removed from the acetabulum carefully and the drainage was placed followed by the suture closure of stump. The vital signs remained stable during the operation. The vital signs remained stable during the operation and 3 weeks after amputation, the cross-section wound first degree heal (Figure 2). Patient's overall health condition improved significantly ten months after operation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male with severe hemophilia presenting with a progressively enlarging, ulcerated right thigh mass and chronic bloody fluid exudation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had severe congenital hemophilia and initially developed right thigh swelling in 2005, which was tentatively diagnosed as a hematoma and gradually expanded over two years. By June 2007, the lesion had formed a massive ulcerated mass exuding blood and bodily fluid daily, resulting in profound anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and subsequent heart and renal failure requiring intensive medical resuscitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe hemophilia A diagnosed at age 2 following persistent post-traumatic bleeding, treated with repeated factor VIII infusions. Chronic retroviral disease co-infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) diagnosed in 2002 (baseline CD4+ T-cell count 70 cells/mcL, rising to 200 cells/mcL on HAART).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right thigh swelling, local pain, daily bloody exudation, fatigue, and dyspnea; negative for fever or acute neurological deficits. Home medications: factor VIII concentrate infusions, antiretroviral therapy. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: General: cachectic, severely pale, with signs of hyperdynamic circulation and congestive heart failure. Right lower extremity: massive swelling of the right thigh with an open, chronic ulcerated wound exuding serosanguinous fluid and blood.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: profound refractory anemia fluctuating between 15 and 40 g/L (1.5-4.0 g/dL), rising to 50.8 g/L (5.08 g/dL) after intensive transfusion therapy; severe hypoalbuminemia; active Factor VIII levels maintained at 40%-60% on replacement therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Right hip and thigh imaging: massive expansile hematoma / hemophilic pseudotumor involving the right thigh with pathologic fracture of the right femoral neck.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Massive right thigh hemophilic pseudotumor with cutaneous fistulization, severe refractory anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and high-output cardiac and renal decompensation in a patient with severe hemophilia A, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS, chronic hepatitis B, and chronic hepatitis C. Preoperative stabilization achieved CD4 count of 272 cells/mcL and undetectable HIV-1 viral load on antiretroviral therapy. Management & Outcome: Managed preoperatively with daily Factor VIII infusions (6,000 U daily targeting 40%-60% activity), human serum albumin, packed washed red blood cells (2 units every other day), fresh frozen plasma (200 mL), and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Underwent successful right hip joint disarticulation / amputation under general anesthesia with intra-arterial and central venous pressure monitoring, supported by perioperative Factor VIII (2,000 U preoperatively, 4,000 U intraoperatively) and strict infection control precautions. Primary surgical wound healing achieved by 3 weeks postoperatively, with dramatic improvement in systemic health at 10-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 41-year-old, White British MSM receiving treatment for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia was diagnosed with HIV. The virus was subtype B and fully antiretroviral susceptible (VL 260,000 copies/mL, log10 5.4, CD4 count 4 x 106/L, 2.5%). He was commenced on tenofovir, emtricitabine and efavirenz. He improved clinically, but the CD4 count plateaued at 11 x 106/L, 2.6%) and the VL only decreased to 88,000 copies/mL (log10 4.9) at 4 weeks and stalled at 56,000 copies/mL (log10 4.7) at 12 weeks. He reported no side-effects, no new sexual contacts and 100% adherence to HAART. He gave no travel history of note. Resistance testing revealed K65KR, M184V, K101E, Y181CY and G190CS. Comparison of the two sequences revealed only four out of 1007 sequences nucleotide changes between baseline and the second test, excluding residues exhibiting mixed bases, of which three resulted in amino acid changes within known resistance foci at RT residues 101, 184 and 190. The fourth was a synonymous nucleotide change. Based on the fact that the patient denied lack of exposure, reported good adherence and the commonly under drug pressure observed mutations, this lack of sufficient VL response was thought to be due to an unmasking of a primary minority species virus under drug pressure, rather than HIV superinfection. The patient's treatment was switched to zidovudine, lamivudine, raltegravir and boosted darunavir. Twenty-four weeks later he was feeling well and his VL was 41 copies/mL (log10 1.6) and his CD4 count 155 x 106/L, 17%.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male undergoing treatment for opportunistic pneumonia presenting for antiretroviral therapy initiation and monitoring.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented while undergoing inpatient therapy for acute pulmonary infection. Following initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy, he improved clinically; however, outpatient virological monitoring demonstrated an incomplete virological response with viral load plateauing at 4 and 12 weeks despite 100% medication adherence, absence of adverse effects, and no new sexual contacts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Active pulmonary infection receiving antimicrobial treatment. Epidemiological history: White British man who has sex with men (MSM); no notable travel history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports feeling well; denies adverse drug effects, fever, dyspnea, or cough.

objective.physical_examination: Clinically stable and improved from respiratory presentation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1, subtype B) infection presenting with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, complicated by early virologic failure secondary to unmasking of pre-existing drug-resistant minority species under selective antiretroviral pressure (rather than superinfection).
Confirmatory & Resistance Testing: Baseline HIV viral load 260,000 copies/mL (log10 5.4), CD4 count 4 x 10^6/L (2.5%). Stalled virologic response showed CD4 plateauing at 11 x 10^6/L (2.6%) and viral load decreasing only to 88,000 copies/mL (log10 4.9) at 4 weeks and stalling at 56,000 copies/mL (log10 4.7) at 12 weeks. Genotypic resistance testing revealed reverse transcriptase mutations K65KR, M184V, K101E, Y181CY, and G190CS, with sequence comparison demonstrating only four nucleotide changes (three non-synonymous amino acid changes at RT residues 101, 184, and 190, and one synonymous change) between baseline and failure, confirming pre-existing minority variant selection.
Plan & Outcome: Initial regimen of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz was discontinued. Treatment was switched to zidovudine, lamivudine, raltegravir, and boosted darunavir. At 24 weeks post-switch, the patient was clinically well with viral load suppressed to 41 copies/mL (log10 1.6) and CD4 count reconstituted to 155 x 10^6/L (17%).

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old male with no previous comorbidities presented with diffuse myalgia, headaches, retro-orbital pain and fever. On the first day of symptoms, he sought medical attention at the Dr. Serafim de Carvalho Clinical Hospital, in Jatai city, Goias State, Brazil. After performing laboratory exams and receiving intravenous hydration, the patient was sent to home care.
On the fourth day, the patient developed a respiratory-dependent chest pain despite having improved from the systemic symptoms and fever. He has also complained of a continuous abdominal pain. Edema of the lower limbs with purpuric lesions on the extremities appeared at this time (Figure 1).
The patient presented no signs or symptoms such as oral ulcers, other extremity cutaneous rashes, arthralgia, arthritis or visual acuity impairment. The laboratory blood count exam results revealed thrombocytopenia (105,000/mm3), which led to a possible dengue diagnosis. Within 48 h of hospital admission, the patient developed dyspnea and the emergence of a pericardial friction. A transthoracic echocardiography was performed, showing significant pericardial effusion, along with signs of cardiac tamponade.
The patient underwent pericardial drainage that removed 200 mL of a yellowish liquid. New laboratory exams indicated a worsening of the thrombocytopenia (80,000/mm3, urea 43 mg/dL, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, a urinalysis showed no changes in urinary sediment, aspartate aminotransferase 97 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase 69 U/L.
A chest computerized tomography (CT) showed a diffuse ground-glass image and signs of pulmonary congestion (Figure 2). Empirically, antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and oxacillin was started for a possible bacterial infection along with prednisone 80 mg (1 mg/kg). In addition, blood cultures, antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA), CH100, serology for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B, C, and HIV, as well as biopsy of the cutaneous lesions.
Forty-eight hours after the drain passage, the patient experienced clinical improvement, and clear pericardial fluid along with the pericardial drain were removed. The analysis of the pericardial fluid showed a citrus-yellow color fluid with exudative pattern, negative BAAR test , red cells 4,100/mm3, leukocytes 8,100/mm3 (lymphocytes 18%, neutrophils 82%), glucose 14 mg/dL, amylase 19 U/L, proteins 4.42 g/dL, in addition to negative bacterial cultures.
This treatment has also improved the patient's platelet count, attenuating symptoms 10 days after their onset. As the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and the detection of the virus nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) were not available, IgM and IgG tests for dengue were performed by an immunochromatographic method on the seventh day. The results were non-reactive for both, IgM and IgG antibodies. Later, on the tenth day, the test was repeated and this time the results were positive for both, IgM and IgG.
The cutaneous histopathological analysis was compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis (Figure 3). Furthermore, ANA, ANCA, hepatitis B, C, HIV, blood cultures and the serum complement were normal. The serology for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr was negative for IgM, but positive for IgG. Cutaneous lesions regressed and the patient was followed-up for six months by a nursing team (Figure 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presenting with diffuse myalgia, headache, retro-orbital pain, and fever for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old male presented with fever, diffuse myalgia, headache, and retro-orbital pain. After initial supportive care, systemic fever improved; however, on the fourth day, he developed respiratory-dependent chest pain, persistent abdominal pain, and bilateral lower extremity edema with purpura. Within 48 hours of inpatient admission, he developed progressive dyspnea and signs of pericardial tamponade requiring urgent pericardiocentesis.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Continuous abdominal pain, lower extremity edema, purpuric lesions on extremities; absence of oral ulcers, other cutaneous rashes, arthralgias, arthritis, or visual changes.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Respiratory-dependent chest pain, dyspnea, audible pericardial friction rub; lower limb edema with purpuric lesions on the extremities; no oral ulcers or peripheral arthritis.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood count: Initial platelets 105,000/mm3, worsening to 80,000/mm3 at tamponade onset; urea 43 mg/dL, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, AST 97 U/L, ALT 69 U/L; normal urinalysis sediment. Transthoracic echocardiography: Significant pericardial effusion with signs of cardiac tamponade. Pericardial fluid analysis (200 mL citrus-yellow exudate): Red cells 4,100/mm3, leukocytes 8,100/mm3 (82% neutrophils, 18% lymphocytes), glucose 14 mg/dL, amylase 19 U/L, total protein 4.42 g/dL; negative BAAR stain and sterile bacterial cultures. Serologies: Blood cultures, ANA, ANCA, CH100, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV negative; CMV and EBV showed negative IgM with positive IgG.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Diffuse ground-glass opacities and signs of pulmonary congestion. Pericardiocentesis: Evacuation of 200 mL pericardial effusion. Skin biopsy: Cutaneous histopathological analysis compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection complicated by severe acute pericarditis with cardiac tamponade and cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Confirmatory testing showed negative IgM and IgG on day 7, with seroconversion to positive Dengue IgM and IgG by immunochromatography on day 10. Autoimmune vasculitides (ANA, ANCA, complement), acute viral hepatitides, HIV, CMV/EBV acute infection, and bacterial/tubercular pericarditis were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Emergency pericardiocentesis with drain placement (draining 200 mL) resulting in immediate hemodynamic stabilization; drain removed after 48 hours upon resolution of fluid output. Empiric IV antibiotic coverage with ceftriaxone and oxacillin, alongside oral prednisone 80 mg (1 mg/kg/day). Platelet counts normalized, dyspnea and purpuric lesions regressed, and he was discharged with uneventful 6-month clinical follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted (Figure 1A and B ), papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections (Figure 1C). The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative. A skin biopsy imprint revealed amastigotes. Skin culture in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle medium grew promastigotes characterized as Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis by isoenzymes. The leishmanin skin test was positive. Bacterial superinfection of the ulcers was treated with cephalexin. Because of a contraindication to treatment with pentavalent antimony (individual > 50 years of age), and lack of medical infrastructure where he lived for providing amphotericin B, the patient was treated with oral fluconazole, 9 mg/kg per day. Over the following 6-month period of treatment, the lesions healed completely, many leaving no scars (Figure 1D). Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis is an uncommon presentation of Leishmania (V.) braziliensis infection. Most of the lesions are thought to be due to bloodstream dissemination, not to multiple sand fly bites. The reason that some people develop disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis is not fully understood.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of widely disseminated skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 52-year-old male farm worker presented with a 4-month history of widespread skin lesions that initially erupted on the face and lower extremities before disseminating over most of his body surface, including the genitalia, soles, and scalp. He reported experiencing daily fevers during the first two weeks of the illness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident and farm worker in Ceará state, northeast Brazil. Prior chronic illnesses and previous antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Daily fever during the initial two weeks of illness; widespread skin eruptions. Denied weight loss, night sweats, arthralgias, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed 178 skin lesions of varying morphology: ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular, distributed on the face, trunk, limbs, genitalia, soles of the feet, and scalp. Multiple ulcers demonstrated clinical evidence of secondary bacterial superinfection. Remainder of physical examination was within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and liver function tests were within normal reference ranges. Serological testing for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy imprint examination under light microscopy demonstrated intracellular microorganisms within phagocytic cells. In vitro fungal/protozoal cultures established.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (DL) caused by Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis, complicated by secondary bacterial pyoderma.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Skin biopsy imprint revealed Leishmania amastigotes. Skin culture in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) medium grew promastigotes characterized as Leishmania (Viannia) braziliensis by isoenzyme analysis. Montenegro (leishmanin) skin test was positive.
Differentials Ruled Out: Secondary syphilis, disseminated histoplasmosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, leprosy, and HIV-associated cutaneous manifestations.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Secondary bacterial wound infection was treated with oral cephalexin. Because pentavalent antimony was contraindicated due to age (> 50 years) and infrastructure for amphotericin B was unavailable, oral fluconazole was initiated at 9 mg/kg/day. Over a 6-month treatment course, all 178 lesions completely healed, many without scarring.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old woman with no known EBOV contact sought treatment at an Ebola isolation unit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, on January 1, 2015 (day 7 of illness). She was afebrile and weak, but ambulatory, with a history of fever, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and muscle and joint pain. According to local protocol, she was given oral antimalarial, antimicrobial, and antiemetic drugs and oral rehydration therapy. On day 8 of illness, after testing EBOV PCR-positive (cycle threshold [Ct] value of 23.5), she was given intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) for 7 days, artesunate (180 mg) for 3 days, and Ringer's lactate (4-6 L) with supplemental KCl for 5 days.
During days 13-15, the patient improved, moving independently and talking. On day 16, she became confused; by day 20, she was unresponsive to voices. Intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and artesunate (180 mg) were administered for an additional 7 and 3 days, respectively. On days 28 and 29, she was still unconscious; serum PCR test results on both days were negative for EBOV. On day 29, she was transferred to Connaught Hospital in Freetown, where she had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15 (E3, V1, M5) but no localizing or focal signs. She was given intravenous fluconazole (800 mg 1x/d). Admission blood test results showed anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase and C-reactive protein, and low creatinine (Technical Appendix). HIV test results were negative. 
On day 34, large-joint polyarthritis of the right shoulder, left elbow, and left knee developed. Affected joints appeared normal on radiographs, and synovial fluid (15 mL) from the left knee was EBOV PCR negative. She was given diclofenac (50 mg 2x/d) and 1 intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone (80 mg). Concurrent blood PCR on day 34 was negative.
By day 41 she was more alert, although her family reported she had slowed responses. Lumbar puncture was performed; opening pressure (30 cm H2O) was elevated, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 37.6), as determined by using the Public Health England in-house, optimized version of the Trombley assay with a cutoff Ct value of 40. Concurrent catheter specimens of urine and blood samples tested EBOV-negative. FilmArray (BioFire Diagnostics, Salt Lake City, UT, USA) testing showed methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae in CSF and mixed pathogens in urine. A computer tomographic scan image of the patient's head showed substantial cerebral atrophy without hydrocephalus (Figure).
On day 44, an underarm sweat swab sample was PCR-positive (Ct value 39.6) and a buccal swab sample PCR-negative for EBOV. Ongoing painful synovitis was treated with an additional 80-mg intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone. On day 51, a midstream urine sample was EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 35.7), and an underarm sweat swab sample was EBOV PCR-negative. The patient was discharged; her family was advised to minimize contact with her body fluids.
At follow-up on day 64, the patient's family reported she had impaired short-term memory and ongoing slowness. She had a score of 18/23 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, but general neurologic exam results were normal. A midstream urine test was still EBOV PCR-positive (Ct value 39.6); PCR of her sweat swab sample was inhibited (Technical Appendix). She was referred to the local survivors' clinic; no contact cases were reported.
The depressed mental status and presence of EBOV in this case-patient's CSF are consistent with encephalitis, a finding in autopsies of persons with Marburg virus infection and in EBOV nonhuman primate models. The general atrophy seen in computer tomographic scan images is consistent with a rapidly developing complication of a diffuse inflammatory process. Given inadequate antimicrobial drug doses for meningitis and clinical improvement, we believe methicillin-resistant S. aureus and K. pneumoniae were CSF sample contaminants.
This case shows the brain's immune privilege is incomplete for EBOV and prompts a broader discussion regarding neurovirulence in Ebola virus disease. Our finding that EBOV can be present in CSF, even after serum clearance, adds to the knowledge of neurologic symptoms in acute infection and of postinfectious sequelae in observational clinical studies. This finding raises the possibility that EBOV persistence elsewhere in the body, or in multiple organs, could be an indicator of or risk for central nervous system invasion. 
Our report has limitations. We could not perform many blood chemistry tests, in-country virus cultures, or deep sequencing on samples. Likewise, diagnosis of coma was challenging because of the lack of CSF cell counts, biochemistry values, and paired EBOV IgG and IgM titers in CSF and blood.
This case raises the practical issue that Ebola treatment requires understanding of multiorgan virologic and inflammatory complications; survivor care and research programs should screen for neurocognitive impairment and consider appropriate imaging. The case confirms previously reported intermittent EBOV PCR positivity in urine. The development of arthritis with synovitis, treated with corticosteroids, supports the diagnosis of reactive arthritis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old female presenting with weakness, headache, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and generalized musculoskeletal pain for 7 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented on day 7 of illness to an isolation unit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, with a 7-day history of fever, nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, headache, and diffuse muscle and joint pain. Ambulatory and afebrile upon initial evaluation, she received empiric oral therapies. On day 8 of illness, she was initiated on intravenous antimicrobials and fluids. Between days 13 and 15, she showed clinical improvement, ambulating and vocalizing independently. On day 16, she developed acute confusion, progressing by day 20 to unresponsiveness. She remained comatose and on day 29 was transferred to Connaught Hospital. On day 34, she developed acute large-joint polyarthritis. By day 41, her sensorium improved with residual psychomotor slowing. At day 64 follow-up, she demonstrated short-term memory impairment and ongoing cognitive slowness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Freetown, Sierra Leone; denies known contact with individuals infected with viral hemorrhagic fever. No other prior medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, headache, generalized myalgia, arthralgia, profound weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Day 7 (initial presentation): afebrile and weak, but ambulatory. Day 29 (hospital admission): Glasgow Coma Scale 9/15 (E3 V1 M5), no focal neurological signs or localizing deficits. Day 34: large-joint polyarthritis with acute synovitis involving the right shoulder, left elbow, and left knee. Day 41: alert, with slowed verbal and motor responses. Day 64 (follow-up): Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score 18/23; cranial nerves and general neurological examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 29 blood tests: anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), and low serum creatinine. Rapid HIV antibody test: negative. Day 34 joint radiographs (right shoulder, left elbow, left knee): normal joint architecture without erosive or osseous abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 41 lumbar puncture: elevated CSF opening pressure of 30 cm H2O. CSF BioFire FilmArray: positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae (considered contaminants); urine FilmArray showed mixed flora. Non-contrast head CT: marked generalized cerebral atrophy without hydrocephalus. Day 34 left knee arthrocentesis: 15 mL of synovial fluid aspirated.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Ebola virus disease (EBOV) complicated by viral meningoencephalitis/CNS persistence and post-viral reactive arthritis: Blood RT-PCR positive for EBOV on day 8 (cycle threshold [Ct] 23.5). Subsequent blood RT-PCR assays negative on days 28, 29, and 34, confirming systemic clearance. CSF RT-PCR on day 41 positive for EBOV (Ct 37.6 via optimized Trombley assay; cutoff Ct 40). Concurrent blood and catheter urine samples on day 41 were EBOV-negative. Synovial fluid PCR on day 34 was EBOV-negative. Axillary sweat swab PCR was EBOV-positive on day 44 (Ct 39.6) and negative on day 51. Midstream urine PCR was EBOV-positive on day 51 (Ct 35.7) and day 64 (Ct 39.6). Antimicrobial and supportive therapy: Oral antimalarials, antimicrobials, antiemetics, and oral rehydration therapy upon arrival; intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 7 days (days 8-14) and repeated for 7 days (from day 20); intravenous artesunate 180 mg daily for 3 days (days 8-10) and repeated for 3 days (from day 20); Ringer's lactate 4-6 L daily with supplemental KCl for 5 days; intravenous fluconazole 800 mg once daily starting day 29. Reactive polyarthritis and painful synovitis treated with oral diclofenac 50 mg twice daily and two intramuscular doses of methylprednisolone 80 mg (days 34 and 44). Patient discharged on day 51 and referred to the local survivor clinic with residual neurocognitive impairment.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old man from Sistan-Baluchistan Province, the main endemic focus of malaria in Iran was admitted to Bahonar Hospital in Kerman in September 2010. He had previously undergone splenectomy due to hemolytic anemia. The symptoms subsided after the surgery, but four months later he developed anemia, jaundice, malaise, fever and weakness, for which he was admitted to Bahonar Hospital in the city of Kerman.
Upon admission his blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate 100/min, respiration rate 20/min, body temperature 390C and he appeared pale and icteric.
Laboratory findings included the following; hemoglobin level, 8 g/dl; platelet count 43000 platelets/mm3; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/h; and total serum bilirubin 3.7 mg/dl. His prothrombin time (PT) was 16 seconds and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) was 42 seconds, with a noticeable increase (according to normal range PT: 12s and PTT: 24-36s).
The VDRL and PPD tests were negative. In addition, direct agglutination test (DAT) for detection of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), blood and urine culture for bacterial growth were negative. Also rheumatoid factor and negative C-reactive protein (CRP) were negative but a week later CRP was positive. The direct /indirect antiglobulin tests (DAGT/IAGT) were negative but the liver function tests were more than normal limits. No abnormality was detected on chest X-ray and abdominal CT scan showed hepatomegaly, but no lymphadenopathy was observed.. While cerebrospinal fluid examinations were normal. There was no evidence of underlying disorders and diagnostic tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B and C viruses were negative.
