objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.7 °C. Lymphatics: cervical lymphadenopathy. Abdomen: hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular: grade 2/6 diastolic aortic murmur (new finding). Developed clinical signs of decompensated heart failure during admission.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC: hematocrit 24% (anemic), WBC 3,200/muL (leukopenic). Inflammatory markers: ESR 102 mm/h. Renal function: serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, BUN 92 mg/dL (acute renal failure, which gradually resolved). Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): vegetations present on a bicuspid aortic valve.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE): confirmed active vegetations, severe aortic regurgitation, and rupture of the noncoronary aortic valve leaflet. Emergency cardiothoracic surgery: aortic valve replacement surgery on day 24 of hospitalization.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapsed brucellar native bicuspid aortic valve endocarditis complicated by leaflet rupture, severe aortic regurgitation, decompensated heart failure, and acute renal failure.
Confirmation: Wright standard tube agglutination test positive at a titer of 1:1600; blood cultures positive for Brucella spp., subsequently identified as Brucella melitensis.
Differentials ruled out: Non-brucellar infective endocarditis and non-infectious acute aortic insufficiency ruled out by blood culture isolation of B. melitensis and echocardiography.
Treatment & Outcome: Triple antibiotic regimen initiated with oral rifampicin (900 mg daily), oral doxycycline (200 mg daily), and renal-adjusted streptomycin. On day 21, streptomycin was switched to cotrimoxazole. On day 24, successful surgical aortic valve replacement was performed. The patient recovered without surgical complications, completed a 6-month course of antibiotic therapy, and remained healthy on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old African American male with no significant past medical history presented to an emergency department in Baltimore, Maryland in late November 2010 complaining of 4 days of progressive generalized muscle pain, fever, and shaking chills. He also reported abdominal pain, diarrhea, tea-colored urine, jaundice, decreased urinary output, headache, and drowsiness. He denied smoking, alcohol, or illicit drugs. He was sexually active with one female partner. Hepatitis and HIV panel had tested negative a few months before. He denied sick contacts, recent travel, or exposure to pets, birds, new drugs, or toxins but admitted that he was a trash collector and rat trapper in streets and alleys in Baltimore and that this exposed him to a wide variety of hazards. However, he did not recall any specific recent injury such as a needle stick, animal bite, or skin laceration.
His temperature was 39.3, blood pressure was 102/67 mm Hg, pulse rate was 125 beats per minute. He was a well developed, well nourished, but ill looking African American male with rigors. He was drowsy but arousable. Sclera were icteric. Conjunctival suffusion was present. No nuchal rigidity was noted. Lungs were clear. Heart was tachycardic without murmurs. Abdomen was mildly tender in right upper quadrant without organomegaly. Both arm and calf muscles were tender to touch, pressure, and pinch. No rash was seen on the skin but a small necrotic eschar was noted on his left shin (Fig. 1). Neurologically he had no focal findings.
Significant initial lab values were: WBC: 10.3 K/UL, PMN 85.8%, and bands 13%; HgB: 12.1 g/dL; platelet count: 90 K/UL; BUN: 49 mg/dL; creatinine 4.23 mg/dL; Alkp: 134 u/L; AST: 207 u/L; ALT: 81 u/L; total bilirubin: 10.1 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 9.6 mg/dL. The CPK was 4,290 u/L, amylase 210 u/L, and lipase 2,323 u/L. No schistocytes were seen in the peripheral blood smear. Autoimmune hepatitis panel was negative. Initial microbiology included blood and urine cultures, viral hepatitis panel, HIV serology, serology for leptospira and rickettsial pox.
The patient was stabilized and started on empiric antibiotic therapy with pipercillin/tazobactam and doxycycline with suspicion for leptospirosis or other ricketsial diseases. In the first 48 hours, he became afebrile but remained aneuric. He was started on renal replacement therapy on day 4. All cultures and serology tests came back negative but serum creatinine, liver function tests, bilirubin, and lipase remained elevated despite the patient's clinical improvement (Fig. 2). Renal ultrasound, liver ultrasound, abdominal CT, MRI, and MRCP were all normal. Renal biopsy showed acute interstitial nephritis and tubular necrosis (Fig. 3). The abnormal labs peaked in the third week and returned to baseline by the fourth week.
Due to high clinical suspicion for leptospirosis, serology testing by indirect hemagglutination was repeated 10 days after the first sample. This was positive at 1:400 titer, confirmatory for the diagnosis.
He completed the 14-day course of antibiotic treatment. He remained on hemodialysis for a total of 16 days. In the first outpatient visit within a week after discharge, his serum creatinine was at baseline off dialysis. He experienced a full recovery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of fever, shaking chills, progressive muscle pain, jaundice, and tea-colored urine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 4 days prior to presentation with progressive generalized muscle pain, high fever, and shaking chills with rigors. He subsequently developed abdominal pain, diarrhea, tea-colored urine, jaundice, oliguria, headache, and drowsiness. Within 48 hours of admission he became afebrile but developed anuria requiring initiation of hemodialysis on hospital day 4.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history. Denied cigarette smoking, alcohol, or illicit drug use. Sexually active with one partner; routine hepatitis and HIV panel negative several months prior. Occupation and epidemiological exposure: trash collector and rat trapper in the alleys and streets of Baltimore, Maryland. Denied recent travel, pets, or remembered animal bites or lacerations.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for rigors, drowsiness, headache, generalized muscle aches, abdominal pain, diarrhea, jaundice, tea-colored urine, and marked oliguria. Denied new medications or toxin exposures.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.3 °C; blood pressure: 102/67 mmHg; pulse: 125 beats/min. Well-developed, ill-appearing male with rigors, drowsy but easily arousable. Ocular: icteric sclerae and prominent conjunctival suffusion. Neck: supple, no nuchal rigidity. Pulmonary: lungs clear to auscultation. Cardiovascular: tachycardic, no murmurs. Abdomen: mild right upper quadrant tenderness without organomegaly. Extremities: marked muscle tenderness of both arms and calves to touch, pressure, and pinch. Skin: no generalized rash, but a small necrotic eschar was present on the left shin. Neurologic: non-focal.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 10.3 x 10^3/muL (85.8% PMNs, 13% bands); hemoglobin: 12.1 g/dL; platelets: 90 x 10^3/muL; BUN: 49 mg/dL; creatinine: 4.23 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase: 134 U/L; AST: 207 U/L; ALT: 81 U/L; total bilirubin: 10.1 mg/dL (direct bilirubin: 9.6 mg/dL); CPK: 4,290 U/L; amylase: 210 U/L; lipase: 2,323 U/L. Peripheral blood smear: no schistocytes. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Viral hepatitis panel, HIV serology, autoimmune hepatitis panel, and rickettsialpox serology were negative. Renal and liver ultrasound examinations were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT, abdominal MRI, and MRCP were all normal. Renal biopsy: histopathology demonstrated acute interstitial nephritis and acute tubular necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with anuric acute renal failure secondary to acute interstitial nephritis and tubular necrosis, severe hepatic dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, and pancreatitis. Diagnosis was confirmed by repeat serology 10 days after the initial sample showing indirect hemagglutination (IHA) positive at 1:400 titer. Rickettsialpox, viral hepatitis, HIV, autoimmune liver disease, and thrombotic microangiopathy were excluded. Treatment & Outcome: Empirically started on intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam and oral/intravenous doxycycline for a 14-day course. Managed with hemodialysis for a total of 16 days. Laboratory parameters peaked in week 3 and normalized by week 4, resulting in complete clinical recovery with baseline serum creatinine off dialysis at outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text: The 57-year-old was an African male, originally from Rwanda, from where he initially immigrated to Russia. He lived in Russia for 20 years (1984-2004) before he eventually immigrated to Canada in 2004. He started to experience right shoulder pain and stiffness in 2010. There was no history of trauma to the joint and morning stiffness nor involvement of other joints. The right shoulder pain and stiffness progressed in severity over the ensuing three years and became debilitating, limiting his ability to work in construction. He had undergone multiple courses of physiotherapy and had been prescribed high doses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications without a meaningful response. For the six months prior to presentation, he had been experiencing night sweats without accompanying fever, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. He did give a history of exposure to MTb while living in Russia as one of his workmates developed pulmonary Tb; however, our patient was not investigated at that time. Examination of the right shoulder revealed minimal swelling and that erythema and warmth were absent, but there was a decreased range of motion. Due to the worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness, a plain radiograph of the chest and shoulder was performed, revealing only an old clavicular injury and that the acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints were intact. Neither acute nor chronic parenchymal lung, bone, or joint space abnormalities were observed. An X-ray (Figure 1) and MRI (Figure 2) of the right shoulder were therefore performed, demonstrating intra-articular effusion and erosions of articular margins, compatible with a septic joint. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 68, and HIV test result was negative. Operative drainage and debridement were undertaken, and the thick purulent joint fluid subsequently yielded MTb by direct smear examination with Ziehl-Neelsen staining and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), the Xpert MTB/RIF test, establishing the diagnosis of osteoarticular Tb. Antituberculosis therapy was therefore initiated with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) in addition to pyridoxine. The subsequent Tb culture revealed no resistance to the standard first-line regimen RIPE. He was treated with RIPE for 2 months followed by rifampin and isoniazid for 10 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male presented with debilitating right shoulder pain and stiffness progressing over 3 years and night sweats for 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 57-year-old male noticed insidious right shoulder pain and stiffness that progressively worsened over 3 years, eventually limiting his ability to work in construction. He had completed multiple courses of physiotherapy and high-dose NSAIDs without symptomatic benefit. Over the 6 months prior to evaluation, he experienced recurrent night sweats without fever, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. He had an occupational exposure to a coworker with active pulmonary tuberculosis while living in Russia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immigrated from Rwanda to Russia (resided 1984-2004), then to Canada in 2004. Known occupational exposure to pulmonary tuberculosis in Russia (uninvestigated). Old clavicular trauma. Multiple courses of physiotherapy and high-dose NSAIDs without relief.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right shoulder pain, severe stiffness, and night sweats for 6 months. Negative for fever, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, morning stiffness, or symptoms in other joints. Home medications: high-dose NSAIDs. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right shoulder: minimal swelling, decreased active and passive range of motion; erythema and warmth absent. Clavicular deformity consistent with remote fracture. Remainder of physical examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: ESR 68 mm/h. HIV serology negative. Initial plain radiographs of chest and shoulder: remote clavicular fracture; acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints intact without acute parenchymal lung, bone, or joint abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat dedicated right shoulder radiograph and MRI: glenohumeral intra-articular effusion with erosions of articular margins compatible with a septic joint. Operative arthrotomy with drainage and debridement performed, yielding thick purulent joint fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Monoarticular tuberculous arthritis of the right glenohumeral joint (osteoarticular tuberculosis), confirmed by operative drainage yielding purulent joint fluid positive on Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli, positive nucleic acid amplification testing (GeneXpert MTB/RIF), and culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis with documented pan-susceptibility to first-line agents. Management & Outcome: Treated with operative drainage and debridement, followed by antituberculosis therapy with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE), and pyridoxine for 2 months, followed by rifampin and isoniazid for 10 months (total duration 12 months). Demonstrated excellent clinical recovery with restoration of shoulder function.

raw_case_text:
A 7-day-old girl was admitted to our NICU because of a 30-hour intermittent fever with a peak temperature of 38.5 C. Her parents noted that she had a stuffy nose with clear rhinorrhea and choked when feeding over the past two days. She coughed occasionally but had sputum in her throat. Her appetite was unchanged without increasing work of breathing, vomiting, and diarrhea. Her caregivers had confirmed infection of SARS-CoV-2 several days ago. Her mother was healthy during pregnancy but detected fetal hydronephrosis with the right duplex kidney in the third trimester. The baby was born through an uneventful C-section delivery at a gestational age of 40w+6. The baby looked well after birth, and there was no evidence of early-onset sepsis. On physical examination, she had a temperature of 38.6 C and mild tachypnea of a respiratory rate of 50 breaths/min without retraction. Her lungs demonstrated coarse breath sounds without crackles and wheezes. The lab investigations showed that CRP was increased to 19.8 mg/L(0-10 mg/L) (see Table 1).
WBC, blood gas analysis, transaminase level, and bilirubin levels were all in the normal range. The blood culture for bacteria was negative. Chest x-rays suggested increased and blurred bilateral lung markings in both lung fields (see Figure 1). Cardiac ultrasound demonstrated a left-to-right shunt of 2.6 mm through a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Abdominal ultrasound showed mild bilateral hydronephrosis and calculus in the right kidney (3.1 mm x 2.7 mm), and there were no abnormalities in the liver, gallbladder, and spleen structures. PCR and quick antigen tests for SARS-CoV-2 from the throat swab were positive. There was no evidence of infection from other viruses [RSV, EBV, TORCH, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), influenza A/B, adenovirus, mycoplasma, chlamydia, HIV, Human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and hepatitis B/C virus]. Normal saline helped to clean the airway, and nasal drops were used to relieve nasal congestion. Moreover, superficial skin cooling was given when the baby was febrile, and piperacillin/tazobactam was administered for pneumonia.
The baby's body temperature declined to normal on the 2nd day after admission. The respiratory symptom alleviated over the following days. On the 6th day, the laboratory tests showed that the transaminase level increased significantly without abnormality of bilirubin and albumin (see Table 2 and Figure 2). Then, the hepatoprotective treatment of glycyrrhizin and bicyclol was administered.
ALT decreased by half on the 11th day. Given that the baby had recovered from fever and respiratory symptoms, she was discharged home with oral drugs of glycyrrhizin and bicyclol and was continued to be followed up in the outpatient department. Two weeks later, lab tests suggested that ALT and AST decreased to the normal range.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-day-old female neonate presenting with a 30-hour history of intermittent fever up to 38.5 °C, nasal congestion, and choking during feeding.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 7-day-old girl presented with a 30-hour history of intermittent fever peaking at 38.5 °C. Over the preceding two days, her parents noted nasal congestion with clear rhinorrhea, choking during feeding, and an occasional cough with pharyngeal sputum. Appetite was preserved, and there was no vomiting, diarrhea, or respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born via uneventful cesarean delivery at 40 weeks and 6 days gestation; third-trimester prenatal ultrasound showed fetal hydronephrosis with a right duplex kidney. No early-onset neonatal sepsis. Epidemiological exposure: caregivers had a confirmed respiratory viral infection several days prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, choking with feeds, and occasional cough. Negative for vomiting, diarrhea, or appetite changes. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.6 °C, respiratory rate: 50 breaths/min (mild tachypnea without retraction). Lungs: coarse breath sounds bilaterally without crackles or wheezes.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: CRP: 19.8 mg/L (reference: 0–10 mg/L); WBC, arterial blood gas, transaminases, and total bilirubin were within normal ranges. Blood culture: negative for bacterial growth. Day 6 labs: significant elevation of transaminases (ALT/AST) with normal bilirubin and albumin; ALT decreased by 50% on hospital day 11 and normalized by 2 weeks post-discharge. Chest X-ray: increased and blurred bilateral lung markings in both lung fields. Cardiac ultrasound: 2.6 mm left-to-right shunt across a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Abdominal ultrasound: mild bilateral hydronephrosis and right renal calculus (3.1 mm x 2.7 mm); normal liver, gallbladder, and spleen morphology. Infectious workup: negative for RSV, EBV, TORCH agents, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), influenza A/B, adenovirus, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, HIV, human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and hepatitis B/C viruses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Neonatal COVID-19 pneumonia complicated by acute viral hepatitis/elevated transaminases, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR and rapid antigen tests from a throat swab. Concomitant right duplex kidney, nephrolithiasis, and patent foramen ovale. Differential workup excluded bacterial sepsis (negative blood cultures) and alternative viral/atypical respiratory pathogens. Management & Outcome: Managed with airway clearance via saline lavage, decongestant nasal drops, antipyretic superficial cooling, and intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam. Following the onset of transaminitis on day 6, oral glycyrrhizin and bicyclol were administered. Temperature normalized on day 2, respiratory symptoms resolved, and transaminases completely normalized within two weeks after discharge.

raw_case_text:
An 8-year-old Kachchi breed of dromedary camel was presented with abortion after the 9th month of gestation during her 2nd pregnancy. This camel belonged to a herd comprised of 350 dromedary camels in the Thar desert of Rajasthan, India. The herd is maintained in a semi-intensive husbandry system, mostly in outdoor facilities, and fed with a mix of pellet feed, hay, and ad libitum water. A history of sporadic occurrence of TB has been reported in this herd. Clinically, the aborted she-camel appeared healthy with a good body condition score and normal appetite and did not show any respiratory symptoms and fever at the time of the abortion. The she-camel was tested negative for brucellosis on Rose Bengal Plate Test. However, she tested positive in a single intradermal tuberculin test performed a day after abortion, showing marked swelling and a 2-fold increase in skin thickness at the injection site.
After the abortion, the placenta and aborted fetus were examined for gross lesions. The expelled placenta was thickened, edematous, and multifocal to coalescing ecchymotic hemorrhages on the allantoic surface (Figure 1A). The fetus showed generalized subcutaneous edema, congestion, and a moderate amount of sero-hemorrhagic fluid in the abdominal and thoracic cavity along with generalized congestion of all internal organs, which is likely due to autolysis and hemoglobin imbibition. The striking finding in the fetus was the presence of multiple, white-yellow, solid nodules scattered over the lung, the pleura, and the liver which measured from 2 to 15 mm in diameter (Figure 1B). The lung was collapsed, severely congested, and had multiple small white-yellow tubercle nodules scattered on all lobes. These nodules were also found attached to the pleura and inner surface of the rib cage. The liver was found enlarged considerably, congested, and had multiple tubercle nodules (Figure 1C). The other organs viz., the heart, the spleen, the kidney, and the intestines showed severe generalized congestion without any evidence of tuberculous lesions.
The tissue samples suspected to have TB lesions, such as the lung, the liver, and the placenta, were collected in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for histopathology, as well as in sterile vials for DNA extraction. For histopathology, tissues after fixation were embedded in paraffin, cut into 4-mum-thick sections and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Selected sections were also subjected to Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) staining. On histology, the lung and liver sections showed typical granulomatous lesions characterized by a central area of caseous necrosis and mineralization surrounded by scattered lymphocytes, macrophages, and/or occasional giant cells, and concentric layers of fibrosis (Figures 2A,B, 3A). Scarce acid-fast bacilli were observed on ZN-stained sections of the lung and the liver (Figure 3B). Histopathology of the placenta showed normal physiologic and/or autolytic changes of mineralization of the chorionic epithelium, necrosis of villous stroma, and hyperemic blood vessels. However, granulomatous inflammation and acid-fast bacilli were not observed.
Tissues (placenta, fetal lung, and liver) were processed for DNA extraction using the PureLink  Genomic DNA Mini Kit (Invitrogen). The DNA was subjected to PCR amplification of a 245bp region of IS6110 sequence specific for the MTBC, using primer pairs INS1 (5'-CGTGAGGGCATCGAGGTGGC-3') and INS2 (5'-GCGTAGGCGTCGGTGACAAA-3'). Briefly, a 25 mul reaction was prepared using 12.5 mul Gotaq  green master mix (Promega), 1 mul each primer (10 picomoles), 5 mul of DNA, and 5.5 mul of nuclease-free water. The cycling conditions used were initial denaturation at 94 C for 5 min, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 94 C for 1 min, annealing at 65 C for 1 min, and extension at 72 C for 1 min. This was followed by a final extension step of 72 C for 10 min. The PCR-amplified products were visualized in 2% agarose gel and the purified PCR products were subjected to nucleotide sequencing for the IS6110 gene using Sanger sequencing based on the chain-terminating dideoxynucleosides method (Eurofins, India). These sequences were deposited in NCBI GenBank (accession numbers: MW393780 and OL436218) and aligned with the published sequences for phylogenetic analysis using the ClustalW tool and the Maximum Composite Likelihood method. This analysis involved 30 nucleotide sequences, and the evolutionary analyses were conducted in MEGA X. The DNA extracted from the lung and the liver showed amplification of the IS6110 region of MTBC by PCR (Supplementary Figure 1). The sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that sequences in this study clustered with M. tuberculosis.
On a managemental aspect, this she-camel was isolated and maintained away from the herd after abortion. After 1 year of isolation, the she-camel exhibited the clinical signs of chronic infection, including poor appetite, weakness, and progressive emaciation. Eventually, this she-camel died after 7 months of exhibiting symptoms. Considering the clinical history and the safety of the personnel, neither necropsy nor tissue evaluation was performed on this she-camel. Instead, the carcass was immediately disposed of by deep burying.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old pregnant dromedary camel presented following abortion at nine months of gestation during her second pregnancy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 8-year-old female dromedary camel (Kachchi breed) from a herd of 350 camels in Rajasthan, India, presented after aborting at 9 months of gestation during her second pregnancy. Sporadic cases of herd infection had been previously reported.
subjective.past_medical_history: Second pregnancy; herd maintained in semi-intensive outdoor husbandry with pellet feed, hay, and ad libitum water; history of sporadic herd tuberculosis. Brucellosis Rose Bengal Plate Test negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Late-term abortion; denies fever, anorexia, respiratory distress, or systemic signs at time of abortion.

objective.physical_examination: Good body condition score, normal appetite, clinically healthy appearance without fever or respiratory symptoms at time of abortion. Expelled placenta: thickened, edematous, with multifocal to coalescing ecchymotic hemorrhages on allantoic surface. Fetal necropsy: generalized subcutaneous edema, sero-hemorrhagic thoracic/abdominal effusions; multiple white-yellow nodules (2-15 mm) scattered over lung, pleura, and liver; collapsed, congested lungs with tubercle nodules; congested hepatomegaly with nodules. Intradermal tuberculin test: marked swelling with a two-fold increase in skin thickness at injection site.
objective.routine_investigations: Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) for Brucella: negative. Single intradermal tuberculin skin test: positive (marked swelling and 2-fold skin thickness increase).
objective.advanced_workup: Fetal and placental histopathology: lung and liver sections showed granulomas with central caseous necrosis, mineralization, lymphocytes, macrophages, occasional giant cells, and concentric fibrosis; placenta showed chorionic mineralization, villous stromal necrosis, hyperemic vessels without granulomas.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Congenital tuberculosis causing late-gestation abortion in a dromedary camel, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Confirmation: Ziehl-Neelsen staining of fetal lung and liver demonstrated acid-fast bacilli; PCR amplification of a 245-bp region of IS6110 sequence specific for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) using INS1/INS2 primers from fetal lung and liver DNA; Sanger sequencing of IS6110 (GenBank accession numbers MW393780 and OL436218) with phylogenetic analysis clustered 100% with Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Differentials ruled out: Brucellosis (negative Rose Bengal Plate Test), other infectious causes of camelid abortion.
Treatment & Outcome: The she-camel was isolated from the herd; no antimicrobial therapy was administered. After 1 year of isolation, she developed chronic progressive emaciation, weakness, and anorexia, dying 7 months later. Carcass was disposed of by deep burial without necropsy for personnel biosecurity.

raw_case_text:
On September 6, 2003, a 46-year-old physician sought care from the Department of Infectology, ("Baranya County Hospital" Pecs, Hungary); he reported a 4-day history of fever, headache, malaise, maculopapular rash, and pharyngitis. He had recently returned from a trip to Thailand and recalled having been bitten by a mosquito at Bangkok airport 11 days earlier. The patient had no history of illnesses before he left Hungary to go to Thailand. On examination, laboratory results indicated leukopenia (3,300 leukocytes/mm3) and mild thrombocytopenia (119,000 platelets/mm3). Leukopenia is characteristic of dengue virus and has been associated with suppression of bone marrow production. We conducted additional tests because thrombocytopenia could have been the first sign of a more severe form of dengue infection, dengue hemorrhagic fever, which is associated with hemorrhagic diathesis and shock. Lymphocytosis and monocytosis with 26% atypical lymphocytes and a high-normal level of alanine aminotransferase (56 U/L) were found. The C-reactive protein level and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal. Blood smears for malarial parasites were negative.
Examination of the patient showed a maculopapular rash, pharyngitis, and conjunctivitis. Dengue fever was the clinical diagnosis based on the patient's history of a mosquito bite in a dengue-endemic country, the patient's symptoms, and the laboratory results. The patient's general condition was relatively good, so we treated him on an outpatient basis and recommended that he return for daily examinations.
On September 7, while collecting a blood sample from the patient, the patient's sister, also a physician, accidentally stuck her finger with the needle, which was contaminated with the patient's blood. Seven days later she became ill, with fever, headache, diffuse maculopapular rash, myalgia, cervical lymphadenopathy, and malaise. Her laboratory tests showed leukopenia with a normal thrombocyte level, C-reactive protein level, liver function tests, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. On physical examination, painfully enlarged cervical lymph nodes and conjunctivitis were found. No complications were observed and the disease resolved within 10 days after onset in both patients. The female patient had never traveled to a dengue-endemic region.
Serologic and virologic evidence confirmed the clinical diagnosis. Acute-phase serum samples from each patient were tested for immunoglobulin (Ig) M and IgG antibodies to dengue viruses by using a commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kit. IgM, but not IgG, antibodies to dengue viruses were detected in the serum sample from the male patient 7 days after the onset of his illness; a convalescent-phase serum sample was not available for further testing. The first serum sample was obtained from the female patient 6 days after onset of her illness. IgM and IgG antibodies were not found in that sample. In the serum sample obtained from the female patient 12 days after onset, IgM, but not IgG, antibodies to dengue viruses were found. Both IgM and IgG antibodies were found in serum samples from this patient 3 weeks after onset of her illness.
Diagnosis was also confirmed by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction assays of early serum samples of both patients by using universal flavivirus primers. Amplification products were directly sequenced (GenBank accession no. AY538627 and AY538628). The nucleotide sequences were identified with a BLAST search (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST/) using the GenBank database. Highest similarity was with dengue virus type 2 strain ThNH76/93, which had been isolated from a patient in northeast Thailand during the epidemic season of 1993. The virus- specific nucleotide sequences detected in the Hungarian patients showed 98% nucleotide identity with the corresponding sequences of the Thai strain.
Viremia and simultaneous antibody production has been observed in several studies of dengue (,,). Virus isolation is possible in dengue infections early in the illness, and in our experience, virus RNA was detected during the early febrile period. The male patient still had fever when the needle accident occurred, and the needle was contaminated.
Infectious disease specialists and other physicians should recognize that vector-borne diseases, such as dengue and malaria, are potentially life threatening. Therefore, they should consider these diseases in the differential diagnosis of febrile patients returning from tropical countries. In most patients, dengue fever resolves without hemoconcentration, an indication of dengue hemorrhagic fever. Nosocomial transmission of dengue viruses is not a common event, however, physicians must consider these diseases.
These unique cases demonstrate the possible introduction and transmission of exotic tropical viruses in a country within temperate zones; all that is needed are competent vectors. Whereas A. aegypti is not endemic in Europe, it could be introduced. The A. albopictus mosquitoes, an invader from Asia, already exists there, albeit in isolated areas. Patients returning from distant regions should be treated with increased attention and care. Although dengue viruses are rarely transmitted person to person, this incident emphasizes the importance of having reliable and rapid diagnostic methods available for early detection of imported infections with exotic viral agents.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of fever, headache, malaise, sore throat, and a maculopapular rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-day history of acute fever, headache, constitutional malaise, pharyngitis, and a maculopapular cutaneous eruption following return from a trip to Southeast Asia. He recalled sustaining a mosquito bite at Bangkok airport 11 days prior to symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent international travel to Thailand with mosquito bite exposure at Bangkok airport 11 days prior. No prior illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, headache, malaise, sore throat, and skin rash. Denied ocular pain, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or spontaneous bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination demonstrated an acute maculopapular rash, prominent pharyngeal erythema (pharyngitis), and bilateral conjunctival injection (conjunctivitis). Patient appeared in stable general condition without hemodynamic compromise or petechiae.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Leukocyte count 3,300/mm3 (leukopenia), platelet count 119,000/mm3 (mild thrombocytopenia), with lymphocytosis and monocytosis demonstrating 26% atypical lymphocytes.
Biochemistry & inflammatory markers: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 56 U/L (high-normal); C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were both within normal limits.
Microbiology: Thick and thin blood smears for malarial parasites were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever confirmed by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) with direct sequencing showing 98% nucleotide homology to Dengue virus type 2 (strain ThNH76/93), along with positive acute-phase dengue IgM and IgG antibodies. Malaria was excluded by negative blood smears.
Treatment and outcome: Managed conservatively on an outpatient basis with supportive therapy and close daily clinical observation. The illness followed a self-limiting course and resolved completely within 10 days of onset without complications.

raw_case_text: We report a case of a 22-year-oldfemale patient, diagnosed to have HIV infection 8 years back. She was on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the last 8 years. The patient had not been taking ART regularly for the last 2 years. Her CD4 count had gradually fallen to 238/mm3 from 520/mm3 over 2 years. She presented to us with complaints of headache and altered behavior for a week and focal fits for 2 days. She had holocranial, throbbing headache associated with episodes of vomiting. She was irritable and showed no interest in her surroundings. The mother found her muttering to herself for the last few days. She was scared and believed that someone wanted to kill her. Later, she had multiple fits in the form of right-sided facial twitching and clonic jerky movements of the right upper limb. There was no history of fever, neck pain, or loss of consciousness. Neurological examination was unremarkable. Her routine blood investigations were normal. CD4 count was 238/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed total cell count of 30/mm3 with lymphocytic predominance. CSF protein was 68 mg/dl, while sugar was 72 mg/dl. On further testing, EBV was detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test. While tuberculosis PCR, virology (including herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, cytomegalovirus, and JC virus), syphilis, toxoplasma serology, cryptococcal antigen, bacterial, and fungal cultures were negative in blood and CSF. The quantitative viral assay showed a high level of EBV in CSF (42,864 copies/ml). Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities involving the left frontal cortex left thalamus and right medial temporal cortex [Figures 1 and 2]. The patient was started on antiviral therapy with valganciclovir considering the diagnosis of EBV encephalitis. The patient completely recovered over the next few weeks. She was discharged on antiepileptic and ART.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old female presenting with a 1-week history of throbbing headache, behavioral changes, and focal motor seizures for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-week history of holocranial, throbbing headache associated with vomiting, severe irritability, apathy, and persecutory delusions. Over the preceding two days, she developed repeated focal seizures characterized by right-sided facial twitching and clonic jerking of the right upper extremity. Denied history of fever, neck pain, or loss of consciousness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 8 years earlier, receiving combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) with reported irregular adherence over the preceding two years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Holocranial headache, vomiting, paranoid delusions, irritability, and focal motor seizures; denies fevers, neck stiffness, photophobia, or visual changes.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination was unremarkable without focal motor deficits, meningeal signs, or cranial neuropathies at the time of clinician evaluation; vital signs were stable.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and routine biochemical panels: Normal. Blood and CSF serology/cultures: Negative for Treponema pallidum (syphilis), Toxoplasma gondii, cryptococcal antigen, and routine bacterial and fungal cultures.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis: Total nucleated cell count 30/mm3 with lymphocytic predominance, CSF protein 68 mg/dL, CSF glucose 72 mg/dL; negative CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, and JC virus. Brain MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals involving the left frontal cortex, left thalamus, and right medial temporal cortex.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) encephalitis and focal status epilepticus in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4+ T-cell count 238/mm3). Diagnostic confirmation: High viral load of Epstein-Barr virus DNA detected in CSF by quantitative PCR assay (42,864 copies/mL), with exclusion of alternative viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic central nervous system pathogens. Plan & Outcome: Treated with antiviral therapy using oral valganciclovir, along with antiepileptic medications and resumption of combination antiretroviral therapy. The patient achieved complete neurocognitive and motor recovery over several weeks and was discharged home on maintenance antiepileptics and regular ART.

raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Caucasian man was admitted to the University Hospital of Patras, Western Greece, with fatigue, fever up to 39 C, and retrosternal pain. He denied anorexia, night sweats, and generalized malaise. No significant past medical history was reported. There were no risk factors for HIV infection, no recent travel outside Greece, and no exposure to animals. The patient denied smoking and drinking, and also no allergies were noted.
On physical examination, the temperature was 39.0 C, the heart rate was 90 bpm with sinus rhythm, and the blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg. The patient was respiratory stable (respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air). No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was identified. There were no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and the lungs were clear on auscultation and percussion. The abdomen was nondistended, with normal active bowel sounds and mildly tender in the midepigastrium but without rebound or guarding. No liver or spleen enlargement was noted. No abnormalities like clubbing, cyanosis, or edema were found on all extremities. The rest of the examination was unremarkable.
Electocardiography (ECG) revealed a sinus rhythm with ST elevation (ST 2 mm in I, II, aVL, and V4-V6) (Figure 1). Furthermore, laboratory tests showed a low platelet count 134.000 (normal range 150.000-400.000 Kappa/mul), raised aspartate aminotransferase (193 U/L, upper normal limit (UNL) 40 U/L) and alaninoaminotranferase (42 U/L 40 U/L), high CPK levels (2166 mg/dl, upper normal limit 190 mg/dl) with CPK-MuBeta lower than 10% of total CPK (112 mg/dl), troponine (TaunI) 48.51 ng/ml, and CRP 4.60 mg/dl. The hemogram was normal (Table 1). Chest X-ray image did not reveal any abnormalities. Blood and urine cultures were taken on admission. The transthoracic echocardiography Doppler showed wall motion abnormalities and absence of pericardial effusion. Accordingly, a cardiac MRI using delayed enhancement was performed (Figures 2 and 3) revealing recent myocardial damage with edema and fibrosis in the middle and upper left and right lower wall and increased left ventricular dimensions with normal systolic function.  In addition, cardiac MRI revealed overriding of the right ventricle with normal systolic function
Serology for Influenza A and B, parvovirus B19, EBV, and CMV, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus, HSV, VSV, and adenovirus, Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydia, Leptospira spp., and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were negative. On day 3 of hospitalization, Brucella melitensis was isolated from two consecutive blood cultures. The Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) was positive >1/1280, so a diagnosis of Brucella-related myocarditis was made. Treatment with oral rifampicin (900 mg once daily) and doxycycline (100 mg twice daily) along with intravenous gentamycin (320 mg once daily) was immediately commenced. Gentamycin was administered for ten days. The patient recalled that he had consumed unpasteurized goat cheese a month ago. After five days of treatment, the patient was clinically improved, asymptomatic, and fever was regressed. No signs of cardiac arrythmias or other ECG abnormalities on serial ECGs, during hospitalization, were noted. On discharge day, all laboratory tests were normal (Table 2). Patient had a total antibiotic course with Doxycycline and rifampicin for 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old male presented with acute retrosternal chest pain, fever up to 39 °C, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute retrosternal chest pain, high fever reaching 39 °C, and fatigue. He denied anorexia, night sweats, or generalized malaise.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history. Denied alcohol use, tobacco smoking, or high-risk behaviors for HIV. No recent travel outside Greece; denied animal contact. Epidemiological exposure: recalled consuming unpasteurized goat cheese one month prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Retrosternal chest pain, fever, fatigue. Denied anorexia, night sweats, or generalized malaise. Home medications: none. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.0 °C, heart rate: 90 beats/min (sinus rhythm), blood pressure: 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate: 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation: 98% on room air. Cardiovascular: no cardiac murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Respiratory: clear to auscultation and percussion. Abdomen: soft, mildly tender in the midepigastrium without rebound or guarding; no hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities: no clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema. Lymph nodes: no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count 134,000/microL, AST 193 U/L, ALT 42 U/L, total CPK 2,166 mg/dL, CPK-MB 112 mg/dL, cardiac troponin I 48.51 ng/mL, CRP 4.60 mg/dL. Hemogram normal (Table 1). Electrocardiogram (ECG): sinus rhythm with 2 mm ST-segment elevations in leads I, II, aVL, and V4-V6. Chest X-ray: normal. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE): left ventricular wall motion abnormalities without pericardial effusion. Infectious serologies negative: Influenza A and B, Parvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, Echovirus, Coxsackievirus, HSV, VZV, Adenovirus, Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydia, Leptospira spp., and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
objective.advanced_workup: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (delayed enhancement): recent myocardial damage with myocardial edema and fibrosis in the middle and upper left and right lower ventricular wall, increased left ventricular dimensions with normal systolic function, and overriding of the right ventricle with preserved systolic function.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Brucella-induced myocarditis. Confirmed by 2 consecutive blood cultures isolating Brucella melitensis on day 3 of hospitalization and Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) positive at >1/1280. Viral and atypical causes of myocarditis (Coxsackie, Influenza, Parvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, ECHO, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Mycoplasma) were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on triple therapy with IV gentamicin (320 mg once daily for 10 days), oral rifampicin (900 mg once daily), and oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily). Within 5 days, fever regressed, symptoms resolved, and repeat serial ECGs showed no arrhythmias. Discharged with normalized cardiac biomarkers and liver enzymes to complete a 6-month course of oral doxycycline and rifampicin.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old woman started antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 2007 with zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC) and efavirenz. Her baseline human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) viral load and cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4) cell count results were not available. In September 2009, she experienced virological failure (this HIV viral load result is not available), and a genotypic antiretroviral resistance test showed a thymidine analogue mutation (TAM, K219KE [i.e. mixed population of mutant and wild type at that codon]), M184M/V and three non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) mutations (A98G, E138A and K238T) (see Table 1).
Based on this genotype, her regimen was changed to tenofovir (TDF), emtricitabine (FTC) and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir. She then transitioned from HIV care in the private sector to the public sector where she was changed to abacavir (ABC), 3TC and ritonavir-boosted lopinavir. When she returned to private sector care in May 2017, she reported severe diarrhoea, resulting in poor adherence to ART. Her medication was switched to ABC, 3TC and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir and the diarrhoea settled.
In June 2017, she was diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB) and was started on a rifampicin-based TB treatment. Her HIV viral load at this time was 345 406 copies/mL. As she already had significant diarrhoea on standard dose ritonavir-boosted lopinavir, it was felt that double-dose ritonavir-boosted lopinavir during TB treatment would not be tolerated. Given that AZT was still fully susceptible at the time of first-line failure, it was thought that AZT would still be susceptible and therefore providing one active nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) to accompany dolutegravir (DTG). The patient was therefore switched to AZT, 3TC and DTG 50 mg 12-hourly. The patient informed her doctor in July 2017 that she was experiencing insomnia on this regimen. She was reassured and advised to continue until she had completed TB treatment.
There were regular pharmacy claims for treatment from June 2017 until November 2017 when her viral load was 2800 copies/mL. A resistance test was performed in February 2018, and the following mutations were observed: three integrase mutations (T66TI, G118R and E138EK) resulting in high-level resistance to raltegravir and elvitegravir and intermediate resistance to DTG (based on the Stanford score), M184V and two NNRTI mutations (A98G and E138A). A sample was also collected for phenotypic testing at monogram and the results showed that there was a 21-fold reduction in DTG susceptibility. Furthermore, all the other available integrase inhibitors had reduced susceptibility (3.92; 32- and 24-fold reduction to bictegravir, elvitegravir and raltegravir, respectively).
She then admitted to only taking DTG 50 mg in the morning because she had experienced insomnia with twice daily dosing, which resolved if she skipped the evening dose. Based on the resistance test result, her ART regimen was changed to TDF, FTC and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir in February 2018 with rifabutin replacing rifampicin for the remaining months of TB treatment. An HIV viral load performed 3 months after the change was 230 copies/mL, and subsequent viral loads have been below 20 copies/mL for about 12 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old female receiving treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis and undergoing antiretroviral therapy modification presenting with treatment-emergent insomnia and virological failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 38-year-old female on long-term antiretroviral therapy developed active tuberculosis in June 2017 and was initiated on a rifampicin-based antitubercular regimen. Due to anticipated drug interactions and intolerance to ritonavir-boosted lopinavir, she was switched to twice-daily dolutegravir with zidovudine and lamivudine. In July 2017, she reported severe insomnia, leading to unprescribed self-reduction of dolutegravir to once-daily morning dosing, resulting in suboptimal drug exposure and secondary virological failure by November 2017.
subjective.past_medical_history: Active tuberculosis (TB) diagnosed in June 2017 receiving rifampicin-based antitubercular therapy; history of medication-induced diarrhea on lopinavir/ritonavir; long-term antiretroviral therapy initiated in 2007 with sequential regimens (AZT/3TC/EFV from 2007 to 2009; TDF/FTC/ATV/r; ABC/3TC/LPV/r; ABC/3TC/ATV/r; and AZT/3TC/DTG).
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe insomnia associated with evening medication doses, resolved upon skipping evening dose; resolution of prior chronic diarrhea; denies active cough, hemoptysis, or systemic fever.

objective.advanced_workup: Genotypic and Phenotypic Resistance Testing (February 2018): HIV reverse transcriptase mutations M184V, A98G, and E138A; integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) mutations T66TI, G118R, and E138EK conferring high-level resistance to raltegravir and elvitegravir and intermediate resistance to dolutegravir; Monogram phenotypic assay demonstrated a 21-fold reduction in dolutegravir susceptibility, 3.92-fold reduction to bictegravir, 32-fold reduction to elvitegravir, and 24-fold reduction to raltegravir. Historical 2009 genotypic resistance: TAM K219KE, M184M/V, and NNRTI mutations A98G, E138A, and K238T.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection with emergent high-level integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) resistance and virological rebound (viral load 345,406 copies/mL in June 2017, 2,800 copies/mL in November 2017) precipitated by subtherapeutic once-daily dolutegravir dosing in the setting of concurrent rifampicin-based tuberculosis therapy.
Treatment & Outcome: Antiretroviral regimen was switched in February 2018 to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), emtricitabine (FTC), and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir (ATV/r). Rifabutin was substituted for rifampicin to complete antitubercular therapy. Plasma HIV viral load declined to 230 copies/mL at 3 months, with sustained virologic suppression (< 20 copies/mL) documented for over 12 months.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old male with a past medical history of liver cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (in remission), chronic back pain, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and chronic psychiatric illnesses presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of cough and fever. He was admitted following a diagnosis of COVID-19, confirmed by a positive SARS-CoV PCR test from a nasopharyngeal swab.
His condition remained stable until day 13 of admission, when he became increasingly breathless and required supplemental oxygen. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed severe hypoxaemia, and he was admitted to the ICU for high-flow oxygen support and closer monitoring.
A computed tomography angiography of pulmonary arteries revealed bilateral patchy airspace consolidation with ground glass changes, suggestive of infection. There was no evidence of pulmonary embolism or intrapulmonary vascular malformation. He had a normal transthoracic echocardiogram, which did not reveal any intracardiac shunt. His liver function test was abnormal, but this did not differ much from his pre-infection findings.
Hypoxaemia resolved with a lateral/prone positioning regime and high-flow oxygen support. He was transferred to the general ward after staying for 8 days in the ICU.
Physiotherapy was initiated on the first day out of the ICU (day 26 from symptom onset). A supine SpO2 of 96% was noted whilst the patient was receiving 4 l/min of oxygen provided via nasal cannula. When he was stood and walked, SpO2 decreased to 88%, whilst on 4 l/min of oxygen delivered via nasal cannula. He was immediately rested, reclined and instructed to carry out deep controlled breathing. This restored his SpO2. A subsequent physiotherapy session was conducted 2 days later. Once again, his SpO2 decreased from 96-99% to 92-93% as he sat up from a lying position (whilst on 3 l/min of oxygen via nasal cannula). This was associated with tachypnoea and dyspnoea. There was a concomitant increase in heart rate (from 95 to 114 beats/min on verticalization), with no significant change in blood pressure. An increase in intranasal oxygen to 4 l/min improved his SpO2 to 95-97%, with relief of dyspnoea. This strategy was sufficient to allow for standing and ambulation training. The degree of oxygen supplementation was tuned downwards after the therapy sessions. During exertional activities, his SpO2 occasionally dropped to 88%, but this resolved with activity pacing and deep breathing. Caution was taken with oxygen supplementation for this patient in view of his background of COPD.
The patient experienced 22 days of POS, followed by complete resolution. He did not require supplemental oxygen on discharge, and was independent in ambulation and performing self-care tasks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of fever and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-day history of cough and fever. His clinical condition remained stable until hospital day 13, when he developed acute progressive dyspnea and rapidly escalating oxygen requirements.
subjective.past_medical_history: Liver cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (in remission), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic back pain, and chronic psychiatric illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Denies chest pain, abdominal pain, or neurological deficits. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Hospital day 13: acute respiratory distress and severe hypoxemia. Day 26 evaluation: supine SpO2 of 96% on 4 L/min nasal cannula, dropping to 88% upon standing and ambulating. Day 28 evaluation: supine SpO2 96-99% on 3 L/min dropping to 92-93% upon sitting upright, accompanied by tachypnea, dyspnea, and heart rate acceleration from 95 to 114 beats/min without blood pressure change (platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome).
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas analysis on hospital day 13 revealed severe hypoxemia. Liver function tests were abnormal, consistent with pre-existing cirrhotic baseline. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal, demonstrating no intracardiac shunt.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA): bilateral patchy airspace consolidation with ground-glass opacities, without pulmonary embolism or intrapulmonary vascular malformation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab, complicated by platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) in a patient with COPD and cirrhosis. Treated in the ICU for 8 days with high-flow oxygen support and prone/lateral positioning therapy. Rehabilitation utilized controlled breathing exercises, activity pacing, and position-directed oxygen titration (up to 4 L/min nasal cannula). POS completely resolved after 22 days. The patient was discharged home on room air, fully independent in ambulation and activities of daily living.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old Caucasian man went to a hospital emergency department 15 days after returning from a house-boating trip to New Melones Reservoir in the Sierra Nevada foothills of northern California. He reported a 4-day history of headache, fatigue, low back pain, myalgia especially of the calves, vomiting, and fever as high as 40.6 C. Signs included erythema of the left flank, with scattered tiny red macules on the legs. Initial laboratory studies showed proteinuria, a creatinine level that peaked at 1.7 mg/dL, and mild transaminasemia, with ALT 182 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 370 U/L. His leukocyte count was within normal range at 9.0 K/muL.
Other serologic tests, including for hepatitis A, B, and C, rickettsia, brucella, and ehrlichia, were all negative. He took doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days and made a complete recovery. MAT and IgM-ELISA for leptospirosis were processed at CDC; titers from serum taken 21 days and 36 days after the houseboat trip were most strongly positive with serovars from L. interrogans serogroup Mini (Table 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of high fever up to 40.6 °C, severe calf myalgias, headache, low back pain, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 11 days after a house-boating trip (4 days prior to emergency department evaluation) with high fever peaking at 40.6 °C, severe myalgias especially prominent in the calves, headache, fatigue, low back pain, and repeated episodes of vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: house-boating excursion to New Melones Reservoir in the Sierra Nevada foothills of northern California 15 days prior to admission, with exposure to muddied freshwater creeks. Past medical conditions, chronic medications, and allergies are unmentioned.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, headache, fatigue, low back pain, prominent calf myalgias, and vomiting. Home medications and allergies are unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: high fever peaking at 40.6 °C. Dermatologic examination revealed erythema of the left flank and scattered tiny red macules on the lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 9.0 x 10^3/muL (normal range). Renal panel: serum creatinine peaked at 1.7 mg/dL. Urinalysis: proteinuria. Hepatic panel: ALT: 182 U/L; alkaline phosphatase: 370 U/L. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, Rickettsia, Brucella, and Ehrlichia were all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis presenting with high fever, calf myalgias, macular rash, acute kidney injury, and transaminasemia. Confirmed by CDC serology: IgM-ELISA and microscopic agglutination test (MAT) on sera obtained 21 and 36 days post-exposure demonstrated strongly positive titers against Leptospira interrogans serogroup Mini. Serologies for viral hepatitis A, B, C, Rickettsia, Brucella, and Ehrlichia were negative. Treatment & Outcome: Successfully treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days, resulting in rapid symptom resolution and complete clinical recovery.

raw_case_text:
During October 2012, A previously healthy, 31-year-old Canadian-born man sought treatment at a hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, after 3 days of fever and severe headaches. He had returned 10 days earlier from a 10-day work trip to South Sudan. He did not use malaria chemoprophylaxis while there but did sleep under an insecticide-treated net. During initial assessment, a blood smear showed Plasmodium falciparum malaria with parasitemia of 22% (1,100,000 parasites/muL) and the following levels: bilirubin, 88 (reference range 5-17) mumol/L; aminotransferase, 105 (reference range 10-38) U/L; creatinine, 130 (reference range 80-115) mumol/L; hemoglobin, 144 (reference range 140-160) g/L, and a platelet count of 17 x 109/L (reference range 150-450 x 109/L). In the emergency department, he was given 1 dose each of doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, and artemether/lumefantrine; within an hour of ingestion of these drugs, he vomited. He was transferred to a tertiary level hospital for admission to the intensive care unit and exchange transfusion. Intravenous artesunate was administered (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h), then a 3-day course of oral atovaquone/proguanil was ordered. On admission, his chest radiograph showed no abnormalities, and blood cultures were negative; his hemoglobin level was 125 g/L; no treatment was initiated for decreased hemoglobin. Parasitemia was undetectable within 36 hours of admission to the intensive care unit. The patient was discharged 5 days later.
Four days after discharge, the patient returned to the tertiary level hospital seeking treatment. He reported that beginning 2 days after discharge, he had fever and "merlot-colored" urine. On admission, he was noted to be jaundiced. Laboratory values included levels of bilirubin of 89 mumol/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 1,976 (reference 120-240) U/L, hemoglobin of 81 g/L and marked hemoglobinuria. Multiple thick and thin blood smears were negative for Plasmodium spp. 
During the course of his second admission, he required 8 blood transfusions to maintain his hemoglobin level above 75 g/L. He continued to have unexplained hemolysis and hemoglobinuria: laboratory results showed a nadir of hemoglobin at 68 g/L and an LDH peak of 3,429 U/L and a low haptoglobin level (<0.12 g/L [reference 0.3-2.0 g/L]). His glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level was within reference range. Supportive therapy was continued, and hemolysis ceased spontaneously 10 days after onset. When seen during a follow-up visit 6 weeks later, he was asymptomatic and his hemoglobin level was 135 g/L. Pre- and post-transfusion and follow-up testing did not show evidence of red blood cell alloantibodies, making the possibility of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction unlikely. Serologic tests showed that the he was also positive for causative organisms for schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, and Q-fever. These diagnoses were consistent with past infections and were not considered to be contributory to the current severe hemolytic event.
In all previous case reports of delayed hemolysis, patients received World Health Organization-prequalified, but not GMP-certified, artesunate. In this report, the parenteral drug used was GMP certified and produced by the US Army Medical Materiel Development Activity. A diagnosis of artesunate-associated hemolysis was made in this case based on the temporal relationship with therapy and the absence of other identified causes of intravascular hemolysis. His time course of hemolysis after treatment corresponds with recent case series in Europe: his hemoglobin level reached a nadir at approximately day 15. The outcome of this case corresponds with a proposed case definition by Rolling and colleagues to distinguish artesunate-related hemolysis from that attributable to malaria infection alone. 
We suggest a case definition whereby a decrease in hemoglobin combined with an increase in LDH between week 2 and 3 is characteristic of delayed hemolysis associated with artesunate. Because treatment for severe malaria is not given as monotherapy, we cannot exclude a potential contributory role of the other antimalarial agents he received. However, severe intravascular hemolysis has rarely been reported in relationship to these agents. Additionally, we cannot exclude a potential role for drug-induced immune hemolysis. Nonetheless, given the severity of the hemolysis and the delayed onset, health care workers should be cognizant of this late, potentially life-threatening complication of artemisinin-based therapy. All patients treated with artesunate for severe malaria should be monitored for 4 weeks and evaluated for hemolytic anemia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presenting with high fever and severe headaches 10 days after returning from South Sudan, followed days after discharge by gross dark ('merlot-colored') urine and severe anemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high fever and severe headaches 10 days after returning from a 10-day work trip to South Sudan. Upon emergency presentation, severe thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, and renal impairment were noted. He received initial oral antimalarials but vomited within 1 hour, prompting transfer to a tertiary intensive care unit for intravenous therapy. After rapid clinical stabilization and discharge, he represented 4 days later with recurrent fever, jaundice, profound asthenia, and merlot-colored urine, found to have severe Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Canadian-born, previously healthy. Traveled to South Sudan for 10 days without chemoprophylaxis; slept under an insecticide-treated net. Positive serologies for past schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, and Q-fever.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe headaches, vomiting, jaundice, dark red urine, and fatigue. Medications: initial doses of doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, and artemether/lumefantrine vomited in ED. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile on initial presentation. Jaundiced on second admission; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were otherwise normal. No organomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial presentation labs: Total bilirubin: 88 mumol/L (reference: 5-17 mumol/L), aminotransferase: 105 U/L (reference: 10-38 U/L), serum creatinine: 130 mumol/L (reference: 80-115 mumol/L), hemoglobin: 144 g/L (reference: 140-160 g/L), platelet count: 17 x 10^9/L (reference: 150-450 x 10^9/L). Chest X-ray: Normal. Bacterial blood cultures: Negative. Readmission labs (day 9): Hemoglobin: 81 g/L falling to a nadir of 68 g/L, serum bilirubin: 89 mumol/L, serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 1,976 U/L peaking at 3,429 U/L (reference: 120-240 U/L), serum haptoglobin: <0.12 g/L (reference: 0.3-2.0 g/L). Urinalysis: Marked hemoglobinuria. G6PD level: Within reference range. Pre- and post-transfusion red blood cell antibody screening: Negative for alloantibodies. Follow-up hemoglobin at 6 weeks: 135 g/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hyperparasitemic severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (22% parasitemia) successfully cleared, complicated by post-artemisinin delayed hemolysis (PADH) manifesting as severe non-immune intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, and transfusion-dependent anemia.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial peripheral blood film demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum with 22% parasitemia (1,100,000 parasites/muL); parasites were completely cleared (<0.001%) within 36 hours of intravenous artesunate. Readmission thick and thin blood smears were repeatedly negative for Plasmodium spp. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction, G6PD deficiency, and active secondary infections were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with GMP-certified intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours), followed by a 3-day course of oral atovaquone/proguanil. Delayed hemolysis on readmission was managed supportively with 8 units of packed red blood cell transfusions maintaining Hb >75 g/L. Hemolysis ceased spontaneously 10 days after onset; patient made a complete recovery with Hb of 135 g/L at 6-week follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old gravida III woman presented to our hospital at 39.5 weeks of gestation with no significant medical history. During her pregnancy period, she did not regularly follow the consultant schedule nor fulfill prenatal tests. At 39 weeks of gestation, the parturient woman was reported to have polyhydramnios by ultrasound and then admitted to a provincial hospital for observation. Unfortunately, we could not obtain the images confirming her polyhydramnios state.
On her fourth inpatient day in the provincial hospital, she suddenly had a continuous high-grade fever (39 C) associated with myalgia and arthralgia. The first complete blood count result showed a platelet count of 69.000/mm 3 and hematocrit of 38.8%. The patient was suspected to have Dengue and received symptomatic and supportive treatment with acetaminophen and intravenous fluids for 3 days. Vital signs and bleeding manifestations were also closely monitored. On the seventh inpatient day, the body temperature declined and then remained stable at 37 C. In the same day, the patient noted small petechiae sized 1-2 mm in diameter, around her arms and forearms. The platelet count at this time was 50.000/mm 3 and hematocrit was 40.8%. One day later, the patient abruptly experienced an intermittent hypogastric pain and had vaginal bleeding. She was transferred to our tertiary obstetric hospital where she was confirmed to have Dengue with warning signs.
On the day of admission, the patient was alert and the vital signs were unremarkable (blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, temperature of 37 C, pulse of 100 beats/min and respiration rate of 20 breaths/min). On obstetric examination, the clinician recorded a 33 cm fundal height, fetal heart rate of 142 beats/min. The cervix was 2 cm dilated and 60% effaced. Regarding laboratory analysis, the rapid test for Dengue diagnosis revealed the following results: NS1 antigen (+), IgM Dengue (+) and IgG Dengue (-). Hematocrit increased to 45.2% and the platelet count showed a continuously downward trend to 32.000/mm 3. Liver and renal function tests as well as coagulation workup revealed no abnormalities. In the delivery room, the patient was administered 2 units of packed platelet concentrate in around 30 minutes before giving birth. The patient successfully delivered a healthy female infant weighing 3.500 grams by vaginal route with APGAR score of 8 and 9 after 1 and 5 minute(s), respectively. A uterine atony and a first-degree vaginal tear were recorded, leading to the loss of about 200 ml of blood. The third stage of labor was actively managed, then the perineal laceration was sutured and the retained products of conception were excluded. After that, the uterus was well contracted and a blood pressure of 120/72 mmHg and pulse of 86 beats/min were noted. The mother and newborn were transferred to the waiting room for observation. After 10 hours, the uterine contractions decreased suddenly and became boggy; the total amount of blood loss was about 1000 ml. The patient was diagnosed with postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony. Intravenous fluid resuscitation with 500 ml of 0.9% NaCl in two hours and a half was implemented. 20 IU of oxytocin diluted with 500 ml of Lactated Ringer's solution was also administered intravenously with the infusion rate of 3 ml/min. In addition, the patient was given a dose of 200 mcg Methylergometrine by intramuscular injection. After 2 hours of intensive treatment, there was no further bleeding episodes and the normal range of vital signs were recorded. Repeated tests after childbirth showed moderate thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 47000/mm 3 but no abnormal coagulation was detected. After bleeding was well-controlled with oxytocin, the clinicians decided to transfuse one more unit of platelets in order to increase the patient's platelet concentration to a safe range. The platelet count and hematocrit were 52.900/mm 3 and 35.9% respectively, after transfusion. The patient was transferred to the department of postpartum care. The patient gradually recovered without any abnormality. The laboratory findings of the newborn were unremarkable, especially the negative serological test for detecting Dengue infection. Consequently, the patient and her neonate were discharged in a stable state after 7 inpatient days in our hospital. The one-week follow-up also did not show any abnormal conditions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old gravida 3 female at 39.5 weeks of gestation presenting with intermittent hypogastric pain and vaginal bleeding following fever, arthralgia, and petechiae.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At 39 weeks of gestation, the patient was hospitalized for ultrasound-diagnosed polyhydramnios. On inpatient day 4, she developed continuous high fever (39 C) with myalgias, arthralgias, and thrombocytopenia. On day 7, fever resolved to 37 C and petechiae appeared on her forearms. On day 8, she developed acute intermittent lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, prompting transfer to a tertiary obstetric hospital in labor. Ten hours postpartum following normal vaginal delivery, she developed severe secondary postpartum hemorrhage from acute uterine atony.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida 3, para 2 woman at 39.5 weeks gestation. Irregular antenatal visits; no prior chronic medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, myalgia, arthralgia, petechiae, hypogastric pain, and vaginal bleeding. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Alert, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, temperature 37 C, pulse 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Skin: 1-2 mm petechiae on arms and forearms. Obstetric exam: Fundal height 33 cm, fetal heart rate 142 beats/min; cervix 2 cm dilated, 60% effaced. Postpartum exam: At 10 hours after birth, uterine contractions ceased and uterus became boggy, with ~1,000 mL blood loss.
objective.routine_investigations: Provincial hospital labs: Initial platelets 69,000/mm3, hematocrit 38.8%; day 7 platelets 50,000/mm3, hematocrit 40.8%. Tertiary hospital admission labs: Platelet count 32,000/mm3, hematocrit 45.2% (hemoconcentration). Liver and renal function tests and coagulation profile: Normal. Postpartum labs: Platelets 47,000/mm3; post-transfusion platelets 52,900/mm3, hematocrit 35.9%; normal coagulation. Antenatal ultrasound: Polyhydramnios. Neonatal labs: Normal; negative dengue serology.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue infection with warning signs (plasma leakage and severe thrombocytopenia) during late third-trimester pregnancy and labor, complicated by peripartum uterine atony and severe secondary postpartum hemorrhage (total blood loss ~1,200 mL). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive rapid dengue diagnostic test with positive NS1 antigen, positive dengue IgM, and negative IgG, confirming acute primary dengue. Vertical transmission excluded by negative dengue serology in the neonate.
Plan & Outcome: Transfused 2 units of packed platelet concentrates before vaginal delivery. Successfully delivered a healthy female infant (3,500 g, APGAR 8/9); repaired 1st-degree perineal tear (200 mL blood loss). At 10 hours postpartum, developed severe atonic postpartum hemorrhage (1,000 mL blood loss); successfully managed with active fluid resuscitation (500 mL normal saline), intensive uterotonic therapy (IV oxytocin 20 IU in 500 mL Ringer's lactate at 3 mL/min, IM methylergometrine 200 mcg), and 1 additional unit of platelet concentrate. Hemostasis was secured, maternal vitals and hematocrit stabilized, and mother and infant were discharged in good health on postpartum day 7 with normal 1-week follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 9-year-old male child was admitted to the hospital with fever and headache for 12 days associated with polyarthralgia. He had autoimmune hepatitis treated with prednisone, azathioprine, and vitamin D. He was pale with hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice. On day 2, the patient was diagnosed with VL by means of an immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen and hemophagocytic syndrome and lipossomal amphotericin was started. The child also presented increased ferritin, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. Because of the febrile neutropenia in an immunosuppressed patient, cefepime was started on day 5. On day 8, lipossomal amphotericin was completed. Due to clinical and laboratory improvement, the antibiotic was finished and the child was discharged on day 11.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old male presented with a 12-day history of fever, headache, and polyarthralgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high fever and severe headache 12 days prior to admission, accompanied by diffuse polyarthralgia, progressively developing pallor and jaundice.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of autoimmune hepatitis treated with chronic maintenance prednisone, azathioprine, and vitamin D supplementation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache and polyarthralgia.

objective.physical_examination: Marked cutaneous and mucosal pallor, jaundice, and palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation revealed febrile neutropenia, markedly elevated serum ferritin, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) triggering secondary hemophagocytic syndrome (HLH) in an immunosuppressed child: on hospital day 2, immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania. The patient was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (initiated day 2, completed day 8) and intravenous cefepime (commenced day 5 for febrile neutropenia). Following substantial clinical and laboratory improvement, antimicrobial therapy was finalized and the patient was successfully discharged on hospital day 11.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 56-year-old Ethiopian immigrant who moved to Italy in 1974. Symptoms started 17 days after returning from a 6-week holiday trip to Cote d'Ivoire (June 28-August 8, 2004). The patient had stayed both in rural and urban areas. She had not taken any malaria chemoprophylaxis during the trip.
