Three days after onset of fever with recurrent vomiting episodes she referred to the family doctor and she was treated with antibiotic; malaria was not clinically suspected. On arrival on August 25, the patient was dehydrated and pyrexial with a temperature of 37.8 C. Initial laboratory studies showed high creatinine level (2.42 mg/dL; reference range 0.50-1.10), uremia (urea 192 mg/dL; reference range 18-48), hyperglycaemia (glucose 794 mg/dL; reference range 70-110), lactic acidosis (lactic acid 3.1 mmoli/L; reference range 0.60-1.80), hypocalcemia (calcium 6.56 mg/dL; reference range 8.50-10.50), hyponatraemia (sodium 129 mmoli/L; reference range 132-143), anaemia (haemoglobin 7.9 g/dL; reference range 12.0-16.0), thrombocytopenia (platelet count 6 x 109/L; low-normal 140 x 109/L), and high levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) (CRP 13.4 mg/dL; reference range = 0.0-0.5 mg/dL). The results of the rest of the routine blood tests were within normal limits. A blood smear detected a P. falciparum, with a density of 40% of parasitized red blood cells (RBCs). A chest X-ray performed showed right middle lobe pneumonia and moderate bilateral pleural effusion. The patient was screened for Human immunodeficiency virus, Parvovirus B19, Hepatitis B virus, Hepatitis C virus, Coxsackie B 1-6, Cytomegalovirus; Herpes Simplex Virus 1 and 2, Epstein-Barr virus, and enteric fever. The patient was admitted to intensive care unit (ICU) and she was treated for 7 days with intravenous quinine 10 mg/kg every 8 hours after an initial loading dose of 20 mg/kg, for 7 days with doxycycline 100 mg.iv. every 12 hours and for 14 days with ceftriaxone 2 gr once a day. Hyperglycemia was controlled by applying an intensive insulin protocol with a target glycemia of 150 mg/dL. During the acute phase the patient was described with angina pectoris with normal troponin T levels; ECG showed T-wave alterations and echocardiography a global left ventricular hypokinesia; a supportive care with dopamine and nitrates was necessary. On followup, ECG and echocardiography had normalized. From August 25 to August 29, 2004 she was transfused with 6 units of compatible packed red cells (PRC), 3 unit random platelet concentrates (RPCs), and 4 units of fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) obtained by apheresis.
24 hours after starting quinine the parasitemia decreased by 50% and less insulin was needed to achieve glucose control. Thick and thin smears obtained 72 hours after therapy were negative for parasites. 
The insulin was injected subcutaneously according to blood glucose control since September 2. She did not need insulin since September 3. Her fasting blood sugar was in the normal range when discharged on September 9, 2004.

Serum creatinine: 2.42 mg/dL (reference: 0.50-1.10 mg/dL), serum urea: 192 mg/dL (reference: 18-48 mg/dL), blood glucose: 794 mg/dL (reference: 70-110 mg/dL), serum lactic acid: 3.1 mmol/L (reference: 0.60-1.80 mmol/L), serum calcium: 6.56 mg/dL (reference: 8.50-10.50 mg/dL), serum sodium: 129 mmol/L (reference: 132-143 mmol/L), C-reactive protein (CRP): 13.4 mg/dL (reference: 0.0-0.5 mg/dL). assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hyperparasitemic severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (40% parasitemia) complicated by severe lactic acidosis, profound thrombocytopenia (6 x 10^9/L), acute kidney injury, new-onset severe stress hyperglycemia / diabetic ketoacidosis-like state, right middle lobe pneumonia, and transient stress cardiomyopathy (angina with global LV hypokinesia).
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitemia density of 40% parasitized red blood cells. Parasitemia decreased by 50% within 24 hours of quinine therapy and cleared completely by 72 hours (thick and thin films negative). Multiple acute viral and enteric pathogens were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to ICU. Treated with intravenous quinine (20 mg/kg loading dose, then 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7 days), intravenous doxycycline (100 mg every 12 hours for 7 days), and intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g once daily for 14 days). Resuscitation included transfusions of 6 units of packed red cells, 3 units of platelet concentrates, and 4 units of fresh frozen plasma. Glycemia was controlled using an intensive intravenous insulin protocol; insulin was discontinued on September 3 with normal fasting glucose. Cardiac ischemia/dysfunction was treated with dopamine and nitroglycerin with complete echocardiographic and ECG normalization. The patient made a full recovery and was discharged on September 9, 2004.

raw_case_text:
The 38-year-old female patient, who had no known systemic disease other than lumbar disc herniation and cervical disc herniation, sought medical care at a state hospital in the Eastern Black Sea region of Turkey with complaints of weakness, widespread muscle pain, unmeasured fever, night sweats, loss of appetite, and redness in the face and neck region for about a week. The laboratory examinations revealed that the patient had elevated acute phase reactants and renal function tests. The patient was then referred to the Giresun University Training and Research Hospital with a preliminary diagnosis of vasculitis. The patient's vital signs measured in the hospital's emergency department were as follows: arterial blood pressure: 100/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation (sO2): 95%, pulse in sinus rhythm: 100/min, and temperature: 36.7  C. The physical examination found that her general condition was moderate, and she was conscious, cooperative, and oriented. There was a V-shaped erythematous rash accompanied by increased temperature in the neck and the buccal region of the face bilaterally. The patient's lung sounds were normal. No tenderness or defense-rebound positivity was observed with palpation of the abdomen. There was also no bilateral pretibial edema.
The patient's lab parameters at the time of admission are shown in Table 1. These findings revealed a mild metabolic acidosis along with mild neutrophil leukocytosis, normocytic anemia, severely increased acute phase reactants such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and ferritin, moderately increased creatinine, and decreased B12 levels. Other lab test results were within normal range, such as INR, TSH, urinalysis, liver enzymes, electrolytes, and ELISA tests.
The posteroanterior chest X-ray and non-contrast abdominal tomography performed in the emergency department did not indicate any pathological finding that could explain the patient's clinical presentation. The patient was then hospitalized for differential diagnosis and treatment in the internal medicine service. The patient was prescribed isotonic fluid therapy for the possible prerenal cause of renal damage and 2 g/day IV ceftriaxone therapy for the potential bacterial infection. Infectious disease consultation revealed a recommendation for rheumatology consultation, suggesting that the possible underlying cause was considered rheumatologic rather than infectious. However, the rheumatological workup revealed no sign of vasculitic or auto-inflammatory disease (Table 1).
A more comprehensive anamnesis found that the patient who lives in the district center visited the village frequently and interacted with animals. The patient informed us that she had contact with chickens, cats, and dogs a week before the symptoms started. Serological tests for possible hantavirus infection and MAT test for possible Leptospira infection were requested for the patient under the coordination of Giresun Provincial Health Directorate. The results of the serological tests for hantavirus were negative. On the other hand, the leptospira MAT test performed at the Spirochet Diseases Diagnosis Laboratory of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, Veterinary Control Central Research Institute revealed antibodies against L. interrogans serovar Bratislava type strain Jez Bratislava at 1/800 titer in the patient (Figure 1). Thus, a definitive diagnosis of leptospirosis was made. MAT was negative for other Leptospira serovars (Figure 1). Since ceftriaxone is one of the treatment choices in leptospirosis, and the patient's clinical findings were improving with the help of supportive treatments, no additional therapy was applied. The patient was discharged on the fifth day of hospitalization.

General: moderate general condition, conscious, cooperative, and oriented. Skin: V-shaped erythematous rash with localized warmth over the neck and bilateral buccal facial regions. Lungs: normal breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no defense or rebound tenderness. Extremities: no pretibial edema bilaterally.

Acute phase reactants markedly elevated: severely increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and ferritin. assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis presenting with acute febrile illness, V-shaped erythematous facial and neck rash mimicking systemic vasculitis, acute renal impairment, and marked systemic inflammation. Confirmed by Leptospira microscopic agglutination test (MAT) showing diagnostic antibody titer of 1/800 against Leptospira interrogans serovar Bratislava (type strain Jez Bratislava); MAT negative for other Leptospira serovars. Differential diagnoses ruled out: hantavirus serologies negative; autoimmune and vasculitic serologic workup negative.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous isotonic crystalloid fluid hydration for prerenal azotemia and intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g/day for targeted antibacterial therapy; supportive care.
Outcome: Clinical symptoms and inflammatory markers rapidly improved; renal function normalized; discharged home in improved condition on hospital day 5.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old woman, 26 weeks pregnant, was admitted to a hospital in Recife-PE, in April 2020, with persistent headache associated with respiratory symptoms, which progressed with a drop in oxygen saturation and the need for orotracheal intubation after 5 days of admission.
As the patient was in a critical condition, pregnancy termination was carried out, with subsequent fetal death. Her condition worsened in the intensive care unit, with hyperactive delirium and focal seizure, characterized by blink and left upper limb clonic movement with progression to generalization. Neurological examination revealed left hyperreflexia and left homonymous hemianopsia.
During the investigation, the presence of SARS-COV-2 in the nasal swab was confirmed and analyzed using real-time polymerase chain reaction. Serum analysis revealed an increase in D-dimer (3,504 mug/L) levels, leukopenia (2,850 K/microL), mild anemia (10.6 g/dL), hematocrit of 31.5%, and thrombocytopenia (136,000/mm3). High C-reactive protein (26.68 mg/dL) levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (45 mm/h). Normal levels of serum iron, ferritin, troponin, total creatine kinase and creatine kinase MB levels. 
Chest computed tomography with contrast showed an interstitial pattern in ground-glass opacity in both lungs. Transthoracic echocardiography showed moderate reduction in left ventricular systolic function, suggesting myocarditis. 
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed signal hyperintensity on T2 FLAIR at the right frontoparietal lobes, related to ischemic arterial vascular event (Figure 1. A-C); while the magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) without venous contrast revealed asymmetry of the middle cerebral arteries, with subtle changes to the right (Figure 1. D). 
Additionally, we noticed a posterior rounded lesion in the cingulate gyrus, with spontaneous hypersignal on T1 (Figure 2. A) and hypersignal with a hypointense halo on T2* (Figure 2. B), which was related to a parenchymal hematoma (Figure 2. A-C).
Hypercoagulable studies were normal, including antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-dsDNA, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmicantibody levels.
The patient received oral anticoagulants and oxcarbazepine to control the seizures. She was discharged after 45 days, with good clinical recovery and a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 29 points.
This study was approved by the ethics committee of Oswaldo Cruz University Hospital, Certificate of Presentation for Ethical Consideration (CAAE) number 34779420.1.0000.5192, and consent letter from Unimed I Hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old pregnant female presenting with persistent headache and respiratory symptoms.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was a 34-year-old female at 26 weeks of gestation who presented in April 2020 with persistent headache and progressive respiratory symptoms. Five days after admission, she developed acute respiratory failure with desaturation requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Due to critical maternal condition, pregnancy was terminated resulting in fetal demise. In the intensive care unit, she developed hyperactive delirium and focal clonic seizures involving the left upper extremity and eyelid with secondary generalization.

objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, hematocrit 31.5%, white blood cell count 2,850/microL, platelet count 136,000/mm3, D-dimer 3,504 microg/L, C-reactive protein 26.68 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/h. Normal levels of serum iron, ferritin, troponin, total creatine kinase, and CK-MB. assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (severe COVID-19) confirmed by nasal swab RT-PCR, complicated by severe ARDS, acute myocarditis, acute right frontoparietal ischemic stroke, intracranial intraparenchymal hematoma in the cingulate gyrus, and secondary focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with invasive mechanical ventilation, emergency termination of pregnancy, oral anticoagulation for cerebrovascular thromboembolism, and oxcarbazepine for seizure control. Following a 45-day hospital stay, the patient achieved marked clinical and neurological recovery, attaining a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 29 points at discharge.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 39-year-old Mozambican citizen who had been residing in Johannesburg. He reported multiple visits to Mozambique bi-annually, usually 3-4 weeks at a time. He had no known comorbidities and was previously well. He reported multiple previous episodes of malarial infection, the last of which was 2 years prior, treated with oral medication.
He had been in Mozambique for the last 3 weeks, where he developed fever and vomiting, which lasted 10 days, followed by non-bloody diarrhoea. He presented at a local clinic in Mozambique, where he was diagnosed with malaria and received outpatient treatment. He received four tablets twice a day for 3 days - which is in keeping with our presumption of artemether and lumefantrine ('Coartem'). He returned to Johannesburg during his last day of treatment. On previous occasions, he would improve within days; however, after the completion of the treatment, he experienced worsening dyspnoea, fever, jaundice and macroscopic haematuria for 5 days. Thereafter, he presented to Helen Joseph Hospital Casualty.
On examination, the patient was pale, the blood pressure was 168/98 mmHg, the pulse rate was 121 beats per minute, the temperature was 37.8  C and the respiratory rate was 36 breaths per minute using accessory muscles, indicating significant respiratory distress. This is in association with an oxygen saturation of 85% on ambient air, which did not improve on face mask oxygen at a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 60%. On systemic examination, the liver was enlarged (2 cm), with a smooth surface, and was non-pulsatile. On inspection of the urine sample, there was macroscopic haematuria confirmed as blood on the urine dipstick.
Laboratory investigations showed haemolysis evidenced by a haemoglobin decrease from 10 g/dL on admission to 4 g/dL (after 3 days), with a macrocytosis of 104 fL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 2425 U/L (normal range 15-40), an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (total bilirubin 35 micromol/L and conjugated bilirubin 17 micromol/L) and a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of > 3500 U/L (normal range 100-190) (see Table 1).
During the first 3 days of admission, the patient developed temperature spikes between 38.4  C and 38.8  C. The patient was in respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 24-36 breaths per minute. There were no obvious respiratory signs on clinical examination or abnormalities on the chest X-ray, as seen in Figure 1. The patient was admitted to the high care unit and was initiated on intermittent haemodialysis.
The first arterial blood gas determination demonstrated a discrepancy between the reading of the pulse oximeter (85%) and the blood gas co-oximeter, which showed an oxygen saturation of 99.6%. The difference in the saturations can be explained by the methaemoglobin level of 12.4% demonstrating that this patient has methaemoglobinaemia, as seen in Table 2.
On day 2 of hospitalisation, an urgent blood smear was done, showing significant blister cells and Heinz bodies. In association with the haemolysis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency was suspected (see Figure 2 and Figure 3). The smear was negative for malaria and confirmed on a pan-malarial polymerase chain reaction.
A septic screen was done as part of the initial workup, including blood, urine and stool cultures. On day 6 of admission, the stool culture was positive for Salmonella typhi, as seen in Figure 4 (colonies are colourless and transparent with black centres as seen by black arrow), Figure 5 (colonies are red with black centres as seen by blue arrow) and Figure 6 (colonies are grey as seen by green arrow).
Supportive management, including intermittent haemodialysis, supplementary oxygen, fluids, blood products and targeted antibiotic (ceftriaxone), was the mainstay of treatment. Specific treatments for methaemoglobinaemia, such as methylene blue and high-dose ascorbic acid, were both relatively contraindicated because of the ongoing haemolysis and renal dysfunction in this clinical case. The patient subsequently improved and was discharged with full recovery. The patient was counselled on precautionary measures for G6PD deficiency, such as avoiding fava beans, mothballs and the use of aspirin. He was also counselled to let healthcare workers know if seeking medical advice that he has a G6PD deficiency.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of worsening dyspnea, persistent fever, jaundice, and macroscopic hematuria following a febrile diarrheal illness in Mozambique.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: While in Mozambique for 3 weeks, the patient developed fever and vomiting lasting 10 days, followed by non-bloody diarrhea. He attended a local clinic where he was empirically treated for malaria with oral artemether/lumefantrine (four tablets twice daily for 3 days), returning to Johannesburg on the final treatment day. Following completion of antimalarial therapy, he developed progressive dyspnea, persistent fever spiking between 38.4 °C and 38.8 °C, jaundice, and gross hematuria over 5 days, prompting emergency presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Mozambican citizen residing in Johannesburg, with bi-annual visits to Mozambique for 3-4 weeks. No prior chronic medical illnesses. Reported multiple previous episodes of malaria, most recently 2 years prior, treated with oral medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Worsening dyspnea, fever, jaundice, gross hematuria, nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Pale, in significant respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. Blood pressure 168/98 mmHg, pulse rate 121 bpm, temperature 37.8 °C (spiking to 38.4-38.8 °C during early admission), respiratory rate 36 bpm (ranging 24-36 bpm), oxygen saturation 85% on ambient air refractory to 60% FiO2 via face mask. Abdomen: liver enlarged 2 cm below costal margin, smooth surface, non-pulsatile. Inspection of urine showed macroscopic hematuria. Respiratory examination revealed no focal chest signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Urine dipstick confirmed macroscopic hematuria. Hemoglobin decreased precipitously from 10 g/dL on admission to 4 g/dL over 3 days, with macrocytosis (MCV 104 fL). AST 2425 U/L (reference range 15-40), unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with total bilirubin 35 micromol/L and conjugated bilirubin 17 micromol/L, LDH >3500 U/L (100-190). Arterial blood gas revealed pulse oximetry saturation of 85% discordant with co-oximeter arterial oxygen saturation of 99.6%, with methemoglobin fraction of 12.4% (methemoglobinemia). Urgent peripheral blood smear on day 2 showed prominent blister cells and Heinz bodies, suggestive of G6PD deficiency. Peripheral blood smear and pan-malarial PCR were negative for Plasmodium species. Chest X-ray showed no focal pulmonary abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella typhi infection (typhoid fever) confirmed by positive stool culture on day 6 of admission (demonstrating characteristic colourless colonies with black centres, red colonies with black centres, and grey colonies); complicated by acute intravascular hemolysis, severe hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia (12.4%), and acute renal failure secondary to underlying glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency triggered by typhoid infection and/or artemether-lumefantrine exposure. Acute malaria was ruled out by negative blood smear and pan-malarial PCR. Methylene blue and high-dose ascorbic acid were contraindicated due to G6PD deficiency and ongoing hemolysis/renal failure.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to the high care unit and managed with intermittent hemodialysis, supplemental oxygen, IV fluids, packed red blood cell transfusions, and targeted antibiotic therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement, recovery of renal and hematological function, and was discharged in full recovery. Counselled regarding lifelong G6PD deficiency precautions (avoidance of fava beans, mothballs, aspirin, and oxidative medications).

raw_case_text: A 64-year-old woman weighing 67 kg who had undergone breast cancer surgery over 10 years earlier presented with mental abnormalities 3 months before coming to the hospital for sudden-onset limb weakness. On January 14, 2021, the patient was admitted to Huizhou Third People's Hospital due to sudden weakness in her left arm and leg that lasted for 3 h. Physical examination revealed drowsiness, rightward gaze, aphasia, left facial palsy, and left-sided hemiplegia. Her initial National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 13. Head and neck computed tomography(CT) angiography did not show any signs of cerebral hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion (Figure 1I). Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with acute IS of undetermined cause and received intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) 40 mg (0.6 mg/kg) in the emergency room. Following thrombolysis, there was improvement in the patient's neurological function such that her NIHSS score improved to 8. Brain magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) performed 24 h after thrombolysis showed infarction only in the right temporal lobe and posterior horn of the ventricle (Figure 1II). However, the patient developed a high fever 10 h after being transferred to the stroke unit. The patient's mental function also deteriorated significantly. Lumbar puncture results showed elevated total protein levels (374 mg/dL) and a high nucleated cell count (2.58 x 106/L), along with a decreased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)/blood glucose ratio. This led us to suspect that the patient had developed IS complicated by an intracranial infection. To treat the infection, we immediately administered ceftriaxone(2 g, q12h), while continuing clopidogrel (CYP2C19 genotype *1/*1) and atorvastatin for secondary prevention. However, even after three days of ceftriaxone treatment, the patient's fever persisted and the cause of the infection remained unknown. Consequently, on the third day after admission, we discontinued ceftriaxone and transitioned to meropenem (2g q8h) for continued anti-infective therapy. On the 7th day after admission, metagenome next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF and venous blood cultures confirmed infection with Brucella melitensis. The new treatment plan comprised intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h), oral doxycycline (100 mg, bid), and oral rifampicin (0.6 g, qd). Notably, brain MRI conducted on the 20th day after admission revealed a new IS (Figure 1III). Subsequently, the patient's condition worsened. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 11 as of 44 days after admission. A brain CT scan indicated a HS of approximately 66 mL, which required an urgent craniotomy (Figure 1IV). Immunohistochemical analysis of the hematoma sample collected during the operation revealed CD4+ and C8+ T lymphocytes surrounding the blood vessels (Figure 2). Upon discharge, the patient was prescribed a 3-month regimen of atorvastatin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. The patient attended follow-up appointments at our hospital's outpatient clinic on the 7th day and 1 month after being discharged. During both visits, normal liver and kidney functions were observed. The blood routine results showed a slightly higher proportion of lymphocytes and monocytes, along with a slightly lower proportion of neutrophils and neutrophil count. Subsequent follow-up calls will occur every 3 months or semi-annually until the end of the follow-up period in February 2023. The patient had regained the ability to walk and had a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 2, although she still experienced incoherent speech (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old female presented with sudden weakness in her left arm and leg lasting for 3 hours, preceded by mental abnormalities for 3 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 64-year-old woman presented with acute left hemiparesis for 3 hours, preceded by a 3-month history of behavioral/mental changes. In the emergency department, she was diagnosed with acute ischemic stroke of undetermined etiology and received intravenous thrombolysis with rt-PA 40 mg (0.6 mg/kg), which improved her NIHSS score from 13 to 8. Ten hours after transfer to the stroke unit, she developed high fever and severe cognitive deterioration. Secondary stroke prevention with clopidogrel and atorvastatin was maintained, while empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h) was initiated, escalated to IV meropenem (2 g q8h) on day 3 due to persistent fever. On day 20, she suffered a recurrent ischemic stroke. On day 44, neurological decline (GCS 11) prompted imaging that revealed a 66-mL intracerebral hemorrhage requiring emergency craniotomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of surgical resection for breast cancer over 10 years earlier. Mental abnormalities present for 3 months prior to presentation. Epidemiological exposure to livestock or unpasteurized dairy not documented. Home medications and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Preceding 3-month history of mental/behavioral changes; acute left hemiparesis, drowsiness, aphasia, high fever, and incoherent speech. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 67 kg. Neurological: drowsy, rightward gaze, aphasia, left facial palsy, and left-sided hemiplegia. Initial NIHSS score: 13 (improved to 8 post-thrombolysis). Subsequent course marked by high fever, severe mental function deterioration, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score declining to 11 on day 44.
objective.routine_investigations: Pharmacogenomics: CYP2C19 genotype *1/*1. Follow-up laboratory evaluation: normal liver and kidney functions; blood routine showed slightly higher proportion of lymphocytes and monocytes, along with slightly lower proportion of neutrophils and neutrophil count.
objective.advanced_workup: Head and neck CT angiography: no signs of cerebral hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion. Brain MRI (24 h post-thrombolysis): infarction in right temporal lobe and posterior horn of the ventricle. Brain MRI (day 20): new acute ischemic stroke. Brain CT (day 44): hemorrhagic stroke / intracerebral hematoma of approximately 66 mL. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: total protein 374 mg/dL, nucleated cell count 2.58 x 106/L, and decreased CSF/blood glucose ratio. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of evacuated hematoma: CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes surrounding cerebral blood vessels, consistent with cerebral vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (Brucella melitensis CNS infection / cerebral vasculitis) complicated by recurrent ischemic strokes and catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage requiring surgical evacuation.
Confirmation: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF and venous blood cultures confirming Brucella melitensis on day 7 post-admission.
Differentials ruled out: Large vessel atherothrombotic stroke (CTA negative for large vessel occlusion), cardiogenic embolism, routine pyogenic bacterial meningitis (fever refractory to ceftriaxone and meropenem).
Treatment & Outcome: Received acute rt-PA thrombolysis, followed by clopidogrel and atorvastatin. Following mNGS confirmation of Brucella melitensis, targeted antimicrobial therapy was initiated with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h), oral doxycycline (100 mg, bid), and oral rifampicin (0.6 g, qd). Following secondary hemorrhagic transformation (~66 mL hematoma) on day 44, she underwent emergency craniotomy and hematoma evacuation. Discharged on a 3-month oral regimen of atorvastatin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. At long-term follow-up through February 2023, she regained unassisted ambulation with a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 2, with residual incoherent speech.

raw_case_text: In 2009, a 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on her nose, which started as a papule, referred to Sedighe Tahereh Clinic, Isfahan, Iran. The lesion had existed for a period of 14 months and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. The diagnosis of leishmaniasis was confirmed with a positive smear of the lesion showing leishmania bodies about 1 year before. All five members of her family had had a history of proven leishmaniasis. In the past medical history, the patient was a renal failure case since 11 years before and received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure. She was also suffering from hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She was receiving oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Her skin type was determined as IV in the skin examination. No actinic keratosis was present. A 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose (Figure 1). Her therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injection (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week, intralesional injection). After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant. Therefore, surgical excision was advised and performed under local anesthesia. The histopathology was that of a BCC.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old female renal transplant recipient presented with a persistent, enlarging 3 cm x 3 cm ulcerated plaque on the tip of her nose of 14 months duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a slowly enlarging nasal lesion that began as a small papule 14 months prior and expanded into an indurated plaque with ulceration. One year prior to presentation, a lesion smear was reported positive for protozoa. She underwent a course of 20 weekly intralesional injections without clinical resolution.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease diagnosed 11 years prior; underwent deceased/living donor renal transplantation 7 years prior. Comorbid hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current immunosuppressive medications: oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Epidemiological history: resident of Isfahan, Iran; all five household family members had a history of proven leishmaniasis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports a painless enlarging nasal plaque; denies systemic complaints, fevers, or constitutional symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Fitzpatrick skin type IV. Dermatologic examination revealed a 3 cm x 3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated rolled borders on the tip of the nose. No actinic keratoses were noted.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional surgical biopsy of nasal tip lesion: histological sections revealed nodular aggregates of atypical basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, confirming basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis previously documented on direct smear showing Leishmania amastigotes 1 year prior; following 20 sessions of weekly intralesional meglumine antimonate (Glucantime, ~1 mL of 1.5 g vial/week) without improvement, the lesion was deemed antimonial-refractory. Surgical excision histopathology confirmed secondary basal cell carcinoma (BCC) arising within the chronic leishmanial ulcer/scar in an immunosuppressed transplant patient. Management and Outcome: Complete surgical excision under local anesthesia was performed, successfully removing the malignant neoplasm.

raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old Asian male presented to Ibrahim Bin Hamad Obaidallah Hospital, Ras Al Khaimah, United Arab Emirates, on 24th March 2022 with abdominal pain and multiple watery diarrhea episodes for the last 24 hours. The patient had nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting and denied blood in stools or any drug or antibiotic intake. He had no history of smoking or alcohol. However, the patient recently traveled to Bangladesh. On examination, the patient was alert and oriented but looked dehydrated. His blood pressure was 85/56 mmHg with tachycardia. The lungs were clear, with an oxygen saturation of 98% and a respiratory rate of 17 breaths/minute. The abdomen was soft and distended with normal bowel sounds.
Initial laboratory investigations revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis (neutrophil count 40 x 103/mcL), hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 18.8 g/dL, hematocrit level 54.3%), metabolic acidosis (pH of 7.1), low bicarbonate (8.9 mmol/L), hyponatremia (sodium 124 mmol/L), hypokalemia (potassium 2.9 mmol/L), elevated serum creatinine (438 micromol/L) and urea (16.2 mmol/L), reduced eGFR (15.6 mL/min), and rhabdomyolysis (creatinine kinase 6,094 IU/L, alanine transaminase (ALT) 83 IU/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 153 IU/L). Furthermore, other biomarkers, C - reactive protein (174.5 mg/L) and procalcitonin (20.5 microg/L), were elevated. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (urine protein of 4+) and hematuria (red blood cells of 8-10/high power field and hemoglobin of 3+). Chest radiograph and ultrasound abdomen were unremarkable (Figure 1). Ultrasound revealed that both left and right kidneys were of normal shapes and sizes with no calculi or back-pressure changes. 
Aggressive intravenous hydration was initiated with normal saline along with potassium chloride. Sodium chloride 0.9% was given at a variable rate according to the patient's response. Intravenous fluid rates ranged from 500 ml/h at first presentation with severe dehydration status to 83 ml/h during recovery. Intravenous potassium chloride supplementation was added to sodium chloride to correct mild hypokalemia. Additionally, the patient was given ceftriaxone and doxycycline. A urinary catheter was inserted, but no urine output was obtained. Renal function deteriorated further with worsening azotemia and persistent metabolic acidosis. Pre-renal acute kidney injury secondary to severe volume depletion was suspected. On day 3 of admission (26th March 2022), a femoral catheter was inserted, and the patient was initiated on intermittent hemodialysis with no ultrafiltration using K2 dialysate fluid and a dialyzer size of 1.8 m2.
Consequently, the patient received five dialysis sessions, and laboratory investigations showed a decrease in serum creatinine and urea levels with normal electrolytes. The patient was stable after each session of hemodialysis. In the meantime, stool culture was positive for Vibrio cholerae on 28th March 2022. On 9th April 2022, after 17 days of hospitalization, the patient's symptoms were entirely resolved, and he was discharged.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presenting with acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and multiple episodes of watery diarrhea for 24 hours.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the hospital in Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, on March 24, 2022, with a 24-hour history of abdominal pain, nausea, recurrent vomiting, and multiple episodes of voluminous watery diarrhea. He denied hematochezia, melena, or antecedent antibiotic or drug intake. He reported no history of smoking or alcohol. He had recently returned from travel to Bangladesh.

subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, copious watery diarrhea; denies hematochezia, fever, or chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and oriented, but visibly severely dehydrated. Blood pressure 85/56 mmHg with tachycardia. Lungs clear to auscultation, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdomen: soft, distended, with normal bowel sounds. Urinary catheter placed with zero urine output obtained (anuria).
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: neutrophilic leukocytosis (neutrophil count 40 x 10^3/mcL), severe hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 18.8 g/dL, hematocrit 54.3%). Arterial blood gas and serum chemistries: metabolic acidosis (pH 7.1, bicarbonate 8.9 mmol/L), hyponatremia (sodium 124 mmol/L), hypokalemia (potassium 2.9 mmol/L), severe acute kidney injury (creatinine 438 micromol/L, blood urea 16.2 mmol/L, eGFR 15.6 mL/min). Muscle enzymes and LFTs: rhabdomyolysis with creatine kinase 6,094 IU/L, ALT 83 IU/L, AST 153 IU/L. Inflammatory biomarkers: C-reactive protein 174.5 mg/L, procalcitonin 20.5 microg/L. Urinalysis: proteinuria (4+), hematuria (RBCs 8-10/high power field, hemoglobin 3+). Plain chest radiograph: unremarkable. Abdominal and renal ultrasound: unremarkable; bilateral kidneys showed normal dimensions and parenchymal architecture without nephrolithiasis or hydronephrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae, complicated by severe prerenal acute kidney injury with anuria, severe metabolic acidosis, and secondary rhabdomyolysis: Stool culture confirmed growth of Vibrio cholerae on March 28, 2022. Resuscitation and intensive care: Aggressive intravenous hydration with 0.9% normal saline (titrated from 500 mL/h during initial severe dehydration down to 83 mL/h during recovery) supplemented with intravenous potassium chloride. Intermittent hemodialysis initiated on hospital day 3 via femoral venous catheter (5 sessions total without ultrafiltration using K2 dialysate fluid and 1.8 m^2 dialyzer) for refractory azotemia, anuria, and persistent metabolic acidosis. Antimicrobial therapy: Intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline. Renal function, muscle enzymes, and electrolytes completely normalized; symptoms resolved fully, and the patient was discharged in stable condition after 17 days of hospitalization on April 9, 2022.

raw_case_text: Male, 24-years-old, Caucasian, unemployed, from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted to the University Hospital, in January 2012, presenting diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria 399 mg/day (reference value >150mg/day). He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). The starting dose for MMF was 0.5 g per day and it was increased up to 1 g per day intravenously. In 2014, two years after SLE diagnosis, he was hospitalized, presenting with ulcerated-painless-skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, upper and lower limbs. Oral examination evidenced crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status and amelogenesis imperfecta ( Figure 1a and 1b). He developed secondary infection associated with fever, and antibiotic therapy with cephalexin was initiated (1g/day) and a maintenance dose of prednisone (5 mg/day intravenously). On the third day, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on the right lower limb lesions. The diagnosis of disseminated leishmaniasis was confirmed (positive PCR and Montenegro intradermal test). Liposomal amphotericin B was introduced on the fourth day of hospitalization at a dose of 150 mg/day up to a maximum dose of 2,400 mg. The patient treatment was followed-up for six months, and lesions were observed to have healed. One month later, during the follow-up for SLE, we observed new development of ulcerated skin lesions on the face and on the upper and lower right limbs. Blisters and fever were absent and the recurrence of disseminated leishmaniasis was confirmed. Few weeks later, the patient was admitted for treatment of new lesions, presenting with erythema, diffuse facial edema, lymphadenopathy and ulcerated and pustular lesions. Patient was treated with liposomal amphotericin B at a cumulative dose of 3,050 mg and followed-up until complete remission of the lesions. Currently, patient is under maintenance treatment for SLE.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus presented with extensive, painless ulcerated skin lesions on his face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 26-year-old male diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in 2012 (presenting with bullous lesions, osteoarthritis, and proteinuria, treated with mycophenolate mofetil). In 2014, he was hospitalized with painless ulcerated skin lesions distributed across his face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and upper and lower limbs. He developed secondary bacterial infection with fever, which was managed with cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintenance prednisone (5 mg/day). On hospital day 3, biopsies of the nasal mucosa and lower limb lesions were obtained. Following initial resolution on liposomal amphotericin B, he experienced a disease relapse 1 month later with new ulcerated lesions on his face and right limbs, followed weeks later by severe facial erythema, edema, lymphadenopathy, and pustular eruptions requiring readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) diagnosed in 2012, maintained on mycophenolate mofetil (titrated from 0.5 g/day to 1 g/day IV) and prednisone; amelogenesis imperfecta; poor oral health. Resident of Tancredo Neves, Bahia, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever associated with secondary bacterial superinfection; painless ulcerated skin lesions. Home medications: mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: painless ulcerated lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and upper and lower extremities. Oral: crusty upper lip lesions, amelogenesis imperfecta, poor dental status. Readmission examination: diffuse facial erythema, marked facial edema, regional lymphadenopathy, and ulcerated pustular lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Urinalysis: proteinuria 399 mg/day (reference value >150 mg/day at initial SLE presentation).
objective.advanced_workup: Biopsies: incisional biopsies performed on the left nasal mucosa and right lower limb lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated American tegumentary leishmaniasis in an immunosuppressed patient with systemic lupus erythematosus.
Diagnostic confirmation: Biopsies of nasal mucosa and lower limb lesions were confirmed by positive Leishmania polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and a positive Montenegro intradermal reaction (skin test).
Differentials ruled out: Bullous SLE flare, pemphigus vulgaris, disseminated fungal infection (paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis), cutaneous tuberculosis, and secondary bacterial ecthyma (treated with cephalexin).
Treatment and clinical course: Initially treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day up to a cumulative dose of 2,400 mg) alongside cephalexin and maintenance prednisone, achieving complete lesion healing at 6 months. For disease relapse, he received a second course of liposomal amphotericin B to a cumulative dose of 3,050 mg, resulting in complete lesion remission while remaining on maintenance therapy for SLE.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old man with no known chronic illnesses presented to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) in Kingston, Jamaica, with a history of back pain and fever beginning eight days prior to his presentation. The fever lasted for two days and settled with the use of paracetamol. He then started to experience severe arthralgia, myalgia, and generalized muscle weakness which lasted for the first few days of his illness. He was seen by his primary care physician three days after the onset of symptoms and was admitted to a private hospital with a diagnosis of dengue fever. He reported that his platelet count at that time was 44,000/muL but remained asymptomatic, with no signs of bleeding, and was therefore discharged with a plan for followup as an outpatient. Two days later he noticed dark-coloured, then red urine and therefore returned to the private hospital and was subsequently referred to the UHWI for further management.
At the time of presentation, there were no reports of mucosal bleeding, skin haemorrhages, or haematochezia. There was no history of retro-orbital pain, neck stiffness, or photophobia. There were no other urinary symptoms and no history of nausea or vomiting. Of note, he gave no history of exposure to rats and he had not travelled recently. However, he did recall a neighbour having a diagnosis of dengue fever 1-2 weeks prior to the onset of his symptoms. 
On physical examination, he had normal vital signs with a temperature of 36.3 C. His cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and central nervous systems were all normal. Examination of the skin did not reveal any petechiae, purpurae, ecchymoses, or rash. There were no wet purpurae in his mouth and fundoscopy was negative for retinal haemorrhages. A tourniquet test was performed and was negative. Urinalysis revealed a pH of 7.5 and tested positive for blood with no other abnormalities. 
Investigations from the private hospital revealed an initial leukopaenia, neutropaenia, and thrombocytopaenia, verified by peripheral blood film. By the time of his presentation to the UHWI, his white blood cell count had normalized but the platelet count remained low at 49,000/muL. However, manual review of the peripheral blood film revealed a higher count of 100,000/muL. His initial urea, creatinine, electrolytes, and coagulation studies were normal and remained normal for the duration of his admission. Creatinine level was 63 mumol/L on admission and 82 mumol/L at discharge. Admission aspartate transaminase was 1841 U/L (normal 7-32 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transferase was 159 U/L (normal 10-70 U/L), and lactate dehydrogenase was 5740 U/L (normal 105-200 U/L). These values declined steadily during the admission and eventually normalized by the time of discharge. His initial creatine phosphokinase (CPK) was 325,600 U/L (normal for a male 40-240 U/L). With early and aggressive treatment, this value decreased by about 30-50% every day until it was 2,463 U/L at the time of discharge (see Figure 1). Urine microscopy was negative for red blood cells, casts, or other abnormal urinary sediments, but urinary myoglobin was positive. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and leptospirosis were all negative. Laboratory tests for the dengue virus on day four of his illness revealed a positive test for the dengue virus antigen, non-structural protein 1 (NS1), and negative immunoglobulin M (IgM). Dengue IgM became positive on day eight and remained positive on day 14. 
In-hospital management included aggressive hydration with intravenous and oral fluids, strict input/output charting, daily urinalyses to monitor pH, and close monitoring of the urea, creatinine, electrolytes, CPK, and platelet count. Target urine output was 200 mL/hour as recommended by Bosch and colleagues. Urinary pH remained above 6.0 throughout and therefore alkalinization of the urine with sodium bicarbonate was not instituted. The patient's hospital course was uncomplicated, he remained clinically well and was discharged with instructions to return initially for review on the ward and then for followup in the out-patient clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with dark, then red-colored urine following an 8-day history of back pain, fever, severe arthralgia, myalgia, and muscle weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with back pain and fever that began 8 days prior, lasted for 2 days, and settled with paracetamol. He then developed severe arthralgia, myalgia, and generalized muscle weakness. He was evaluated at a primary care clinic and admitted to a local hospital on day 3 with thrombocytopenia (platelet count 44,000/muL), but remained asymptomatic without bleeding and was discharged. Two days later, he noted dark-colored, followed by red-colored urine, prompting re-presentation and referral to the tertiary university hospital. He denied mucosal bleeding, skin hemorrhages, hematochezia, retro-orbital pain, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, vomiting, or dysuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic illnesses. Denied recent travel or exposure to rats; noted an ill neighbor with an acute febrile illness 1-2 weeks prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dark/red urine, myalgias, arthralgias, back pain, and muscle weakness. Negative for mucosal bleeding, petechiae, hematochezia, retro-orbital pain, photophobia, neck stiffness, nausea, or vomiting. Home medications: paracetamol. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 36.3 C, vital signs normal. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, musculoskeletal, and central nervous system examinations were normal. Skin examination showed no petechiae, purpurae, ecchymoses, or rash. Oral cavity showed no wet purpurae. Fundoscopy negative for retinal hemorrhages. Tourniquet test was negative.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count on arrival showed normalized white blood cell count and thrombocytopenia with platelet count 49,000/muL (manual peripheral blood film review: 100,000/muL; initial counts at prior facility: leukopenia, neutropenia, and platelets 44,000/muL). Serum creatinine: 63 mumol/L on admission, 82 mumol/L at discharge; urea, electrolytes, and coagulation studies normal throughout. AST: 1,841 U/L (reference: 7-32 U/L), GGT: 159 U/L (reference: 10-70 U/L), LDH: 5,740 U/L (reference: 105-200 U/L), declining to normal by discharge. Initial creatine phosphokinase (CPK): 325,600 U/L (reference: 40-240 U/L), declining to 2,463 U/L at discharge. Urinalysis: pH 7.5, positive for blood, negative for red blood cells, casts, or abnormal sediments; urine myoglobin: positive. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and leptospirosis were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue fever complicated by severe rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria without acute renal failure. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen on illness day 4 (IgM negative), with subsequent seroconversion to positive dengue IgM on day 8 and day 14. Leptospirosis, viral hepatitis (B and C), and HIV were excluded by negative serologies.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with aggressive hydration using intravenous and oral fluids targeting a urine output of 200 mL/hour, strict input/output charting, daily urine pH monitoring, and serial tracking of electrolytes, renal function, CPK, and platelets. Urine pH remained above 6.0, obviating the need for urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate. CPK declined by 30-50% daily, liver enzymes normalized, and the patient made an uneventful recovery and was discharged home with scheduled outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old man presented with fever, headache, and myalgia for 7 days associated with vomiting and hematemesis of three episodes. He had reduced consciousness and suffered an episode of generalized tonic-clonic seizure on the day of the presentation. On initial assessment, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was E1V1M3 with unequal pupils of the right 3 mm and left 2 mm. The patient was hemodynamically stable with a pulse rate of 82, blood pressure of 148/87 mmHg and he was febrile with a temperature of 38.7 C. He was intubated and stabilized. Following that, his computed tomography (CT) brain revealed left thalamic bleed and right frontotemporoparietal acute subdural hemorrhage 30 mm in thickness with compression of adjacent brain parenchyma and the right lateral ventricle. There was midline shift of 20 mm to the left and effacement of basal cisterns [Figure 1].
The first blood tests on day 7 of fever recorded a total white cell count of 4.53 x 109/L, platelet count of 31 x 109/L, hematocrit 42.7%, and a lymphocyte count of 1.40 x 109/L. International normalized ratio (INR) was 2.63 with activated prothrombin time (APTT) 40.5 s. Nonstructural protein (NS1) antigen test was positive, dengue IgM negative and dengue IgG positive.
Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia were treated with transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and platelet concentrate. The patient was sedated for cerebral resuscitation. The platelet count improved to 56 x 109/L and the INR reduced to 1.2 with APTT of 34.5 s. Unfortunately, the pupils were both dilated (5 mm) and were nonreactive prior to operation.
An operation was attempted 8 h after admission. A right decompressive craniectomy, evacuation of blood clots, external ventricular drainage catheter insertion, and fascia duraplasty was done.
Postoperatively, pupils remained 5 mm and nonreactive with GCS of E1VTM1 without sedation. There was no cough or gag reflex present. A repeat CT brain postoperation showed generalized cerebral edema with loss of grey-white matter differentiation, effacement of sulci and basal cisterns, bilateral thalamic bleeds, and midline shift of 10 mm to the right. Soon after, the patient's hemodynamic status deteriorated and required inotropic support. The patient died on the 3rd day of admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old man presenting with a 7-day history of fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, three episodes of hematemesis, acute seizure, and coma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 47-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of fever, headache, and myalgia, complicated by recurrent vomiting and three episodes of hematemesis. On the day of admission, he experienced acute deterioration of consciousness and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, prompting emergent hospital presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, hematemesis, generalized seizure, and decreased consciousness. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.7 C, pulse rate: 82 beats/min, blood pressure: 148/87 mmHg. GCS on arrival E1V1M3 (5/15), unequal pupils (right 3 mm, left 2 mm). Following intubation and resuscitation, both pupils dilated to 5 mm and became nonreactive. Postoperatively: GCS E1VTM1 without sedation, absent cough and gag reflexes.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 4.53 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes: 1.40 x 10^9/L, platelet count: 31 x 10^9/L (improved to 56 x 10^9/L post-transfusion), hematocrit: 42.7%. Coagulation: INR 2.63 (reduced to 1.2 post-plasma), aPTT 40.5 sec (reduced to 34.5 sec).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (preoperative): Right frontotemporoparietal acute subdural hematoma 30 mm in thickness with marked compression of adjacent brain parenchyma and right lateral ventricle, midline shift of 20 mm to the left, effacement of basal cisterns, and a left thalamic bleed. Brain CT (postoperative): Generalized cerebral edema with loss of grey-white differentiation, effacement of sulci and basal cisterns, bilateral thalamic hemorrhages, and persistent 10 mm midline shift.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue hemorrhagic fever (secondary dengue) complicated by massive spontaneous acute subdural hematoma, bilateral thalamic hemorrhages, uncal herniation, and fatal cerebral edema. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) antigen; negative dengue IgM and positive dengue IgG, confirming acute secondary dengue infection.
Plan & Outcome: Emergent endotracheal intubation, cerebral resuscitation, and transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and platelet concentrates. Underwent emergency right decompressive craniectomy, clot evacuation, external ventricular drain insertion, and fascia duraplasty. Postoperatively, brainstem reflexes remained absent, hemodynamic collapse ensued requiring inotropic support, and the patient died on the 3rd hospital day.

raw_case_text: A 78-year-old man was admitted due to recurrent fever and fatigue for past one year. Two weeks prior to admission, his fatigue intensified, and the highest temperature reached 39.5C. He had lost 5kg over the past year and had a history of cerebral infarction and hypertension. On examination, the patient was febrile at 38C. His C-reactive protein (CRP) (62.49 mg/dl), procalcitonin (0.213ng/mL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (84 mm/h) were elevated. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed diffusely distributed nodules in both lungs, bilateral bronchiolitis, and tuberculosis could not be excluded. The aortic arch was thickened and the local calcified plaque moved inward, which indicated further aortic computed tomography angiography (CTA) examination (Figure 1). Echocardiography revealed no vegetation in the mitral and aortic valve areas. The chest CTA confirmed multiple atherosclerosis and ulcers, and intermural hematoma in the aortic arch and thoracic aorta. Combined with the medical history, the involvement of tuberculosis in the aorta should be highly suspected (Figure 2). Re-examination of lung CT revealed bronchiole lesions and multiple miliary foci in both lungs, which were larger than one week prior, with pleural effusion, and slightly thickened pleura, suggestive of miliary tuberculosis (Figure 3). The T cell spot test, sputum culture, and sputum GeneXpert test were positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and GeneXpert indicated sensitivity to rifampicin. Since disseminated tuberculosis was definite and the patient's disease potentially involved the major thoracic vessels, anti-tuberculosis and steroids were initiated immediately. Methylprednisolone was administered at 40mg/day for 3 days, 20mg/day for 3 days, 8mg/day for 3 days, 4mg/day for 7 days, and then discontinued. Due to liver dysfunction, with alanine aminotransferase of 161U/L and aspartate aminotransferase of 203U/L, a regimen consisting of meropenem 1 g every 8 h, linezolid 0.6 g once daily, amikacin 0.4 g once daily, and levofloxacin 0.5 g once daily was administered. Surgical consultation concluded that no immediate surgical intervention was needed because the aortic wall was not ruptured. On normalisation of liver function, the anti-tuberculosis regimen was changed to isoniazid 0.3 g once daily, rifapentine 0.45 g twice a week, linezolid 0.6 g once daily, ethambutol 0.75 g once daily, levofloxacin 0.5 g once daily. After two weeks of treatment, the patient's body temperature returned to normal, and a re-examination of the lung CT indicated that the lesion was partially absorbed (Figure 4). The patient was discharged and continued to receive oral medications. We planned the follow-up to be weekly initially, gradually transitioning to every two weeks, and then monthly after stabilisation. Routine blood, liver and kidney functions were examined at each follow-up visit. Sputum smears and cultures were performed monthly. Pulmonary CT was re-examined two months later, and aortic CTA was re-examined four months later. The patient tolerated and was compliant with anti-tuberculosis drugs.
