subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: Hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, levothyroxine, and clonazepam. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Oxygen saturation ~70% at rest on room air in severe respiratory distress. Clinical course notable for cardiopulmonary arrest requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation, critical illness deconditioning, and subsequent post-discharge residual exertional dyspnea and fatigue.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Acute renal dysfunction without dialysis requirement. Twelve weeks post-discharge fasting laboratory tests: Complete blood count, lipid profile, glucose metabolism, skeletal muscle damage markers, cardiac muscle damage markers, and systemic inflammatory markers.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission chest CT: Bilateral multifocal ground-glass opacities involving > 50% of lung parenchyma. Vascular imaging: Confirmed acute pulmonary thromboembolism. Follow-up functional evaluation (12 weeks post-discharge): Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET using modified Balke treadmill protocol), handgrip dynamometry, 30-second sit-to-stand (30-STS) test, and Timed Up and Go (TUG) test.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Critical SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia with ARDS) confirmed by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, complicated by acute pulmonary thromboembolism, acute renal dysfunction, in-hospital cardiopulmonary arrest, prolonged respiratory failure, and post-COVID-19 functional impairment / deconditioning.
Plan & Outcome: Acute management included 47 days of invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube transitioned to tracheostomy (decannulated 20 days post-procedure), cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intensive care support, and post-discharge nocturnal supplemental oxygen for 30 days. At 12 weeks post-discharge, she completed a 10-week semi-supervised home-based exercise training (HBET) program consisting of progressive aerobic walking, resistance exercises, and active stretching, resulting in marked improvement in physical fitness, endurance, and functional status.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old Iranian man with renal transplant and with two tumoral lesions was admitted to our dermatology ward on March 2008. The patient was suffering from chronic renal failure due to diabetes (non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, NIDDM) for several years before this admission.
The patient developed small popular lesion (2 x 5 millimeter) on his left wrist and right leg (shin) after traveling to an endemic leishmaniasis area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran) in April 2006. The diagnosis of CL was confirmed by a positive direct smear for leishman bodies. As the lesions were small, they remained untreated to obtain immunity for the patient.
Due to chronic renal failure, renal transplantation was performed on the patient in August 2007. After transplantation, he received prednisolone tablets 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). Several weeks after renal transplantation and immunosuppressive therapy, these small popular lesions became large cauliflower-like and tumoral lesions measured 3 x 4 x 5 cm on his left wrist and 4 x 5 x 6 cm on his right leg (shin) (Figures 1 and 2).
A slit-skin smear showed leishman bodies in Giemsa preparations. The leishmanin skin test (Montenegro) was positive with 5 mm induration.
Histopathological examination of the biopsy obtained specimens demonstrated ulcerative changes and irregular acanthosis in the epidermis, namely, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. In dermis infiltration of lymphocyte, plasma cell and histiocyte with multinucleated Giant cell were shown. Leishman bodies were seen in histiocytes, especially in the specimen obtained from the lower leg lesion (Figure 3). With regard to the clinical and histopathological findings, the diagnosis of reactivation of CL was made.
After admission to our dermatology department, he was treated with 800 mg/day IV sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam, pentavalent antimonials) for 3 weeks. In addition, his lesions were treated with local destructive cryotherapy; cryotherapy was applied by using the liquid nitrogen according to Asilian et al.. The patient responded favorably to the above treatment. Afterward, the patient was followed up for 5 years. At the latest visit on June 2013, the direct smear and polymerase chain reaction from the site of previous lesion were negative for leishman body.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male renal transplant recipient presented with two large, rapidly enlarging cauliflower-like tumoral skin lesions on his wrist and lower leg.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed small papules on his left wrist and right shin in April 2006 following travel to an endemic area, which had been intentionally left untreated. Following renal transplantation in August 2007 and initiation of high-dose immunosuppression, the quiescent lesions rapidly transformed over several weeks into massive cauliflower-like tumoral masses.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM); underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. Immunosuppressive therapy: oral prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg/day (600 mg daily). Prior untreated cutaneous leishmaniasis diagnosed in April 2006. Travel history: traveled to Natanz, Isfahan Province, Iran (an endemic area) in April 2006.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports rapidly enlarging exophytic masses; denies fevers, systemic pain, or graft dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 80 kg. Dermatologic examination revealed two large, exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one measuring 3 cm x 4 cm x 5 cm on the dorsal left wrist, and another measuring 4 cm x 5 cm x 6 cm on the right anterior lower leg (shin).
objective.advanced_workup: Cutaneous punch biopsy of leg lesion: epidermal ulceration with marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia; dermis exhibited dense infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes with multinucleated giant cells containing intracellular protozoa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Giemsa-stained slit-skin smear and biopsy demonstrated numerous intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman bodies) within dermal histiocytes. Leishmanin skin test (Montenegro) was reactive with 5 mm induration, confirming reactivation of cutaneous leishmaniasis induced by post-transplant immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma and deep fungal granulomas were excluded by biopsy. Management and Outcome: Treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) at 800 mg daily for 3 weeks, combined with serial liquid nitrogen cryotherapy sessions. The patient achieved complete clinical remission. Long-term follow-up over 5 years (through June 2013) demonstrated no recurrence, with negative repeat direct smears and negative Leishmania PCR.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old man in close contact with sheep presented with a one-month history of intermittent fever, fatigue, night sweats, and progressive low back pain. Physical examination revealed percussion pain in the L3 and L4 vertebrae. Laboratory data showed a white blood cell count of 5.6 x 109/L with 59.5% neutrophils and 27.8% lymphocytes. Inflammatory marker levels were elevated with erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 107 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 65 mg/L. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed apparent destruction at the anterior superior corner of the L4 vertebra, known as Pedro Pons' sign, accompanied by osteophyte formation (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging showed bone destruction in the L3 and L4 vertebrae accompanied by paravertebral abscesses (Figure 2). The patient underwent CT-guided percutaneous catheter drainage. Brucella ovis (B. ovis) was isolated from the pus. Furthermore, the serum agglutination test was positive for Brucella at a titer of 1:800. With a diagnosis of brucellar spondylitis, the patient received three months of antibiotic therapy and had a satisfactory response to the medical treatment.
Pedro Pons' sign was first described by Pedro-Pons and Farreras in 1944 as a destructive appearance at the anterosuperior angle of the vertebra accompanied by osteosclerosis and osteophytes, which are characteristic radiological findings of brucellar spondylitis  .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presented with a one-month history of intermittent fever, fatigue, night sweats, and progressive lower back pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-month history of intermittent fever, severe fatigue, drenching night sweats, and progressively worsening lower back pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous medical conditions documented. Epidemiological exposure: close contact with sheep.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, night sweats, low back pain, fever. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vertebral percussion tenderness elicited over the L3 and L4 lumbar vertebrae. Vitals and other physical examination details not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 5.6 x 109/L (59.5% neutrophils, 27.8% lymphocytes), ESR 107 mm/h, CRP 65 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar CT scan: pronounced destructive lesion at the anterior superior corner of the L4 vertebra (Pedro Pons' sign) with adjacent osteosclerosis and osteophyte formation. Lumbar spine MRI: bone destruction involving L3 and L4 vertebral bodies accompanied by bilateral paravertebral abscesses. Procedure: CT-guided percutaneous catheter drainage of the paravertebral abscess.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar spondylodiscitis (L3-L4 spondylitis) with bilateral paravertebral abscesses and Pedro Pons' sign. Confirmed by isolation of Brucella ovis from aspirated paravertebral pus and a positive Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) at a titer of 1 : 800. Pyogenic bacterial and tuberculous spondylitis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Underwent CT-guided percutaneous catheter abscess drainage and received a 3-month course of targeted antimicrobial therapy, achieving a satisfactory clinical response and symptomatic resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old, Nigerian college student presented to Sunway Medical Centre, Selangor, Malaysia with a 4-day history of fever associated with chills, rigors and body ache. Prior to onset of symptoms, he had gone back to Nigeria for 10 days during semester break and became unwell 5 days after returning to Malaysia. He was febrile upon admission with body temperature of 39.8  C, pulse rate of 126 beats per minute and blood pressure of 128/87 mm Hg. There were no other significant physical findings noted. He recalled to have had three episodes of malaria during childhood, but was uncertain about the causative Plasmodium species. Blood investigation showed thrombocytopaenia with a platelet count of 71,000 per microlitre (normal: 150,000-400,000 per microlitre) and raised C-reactive protein (97 mg/L; normal: <5 mg/L). White blood cell count, haemoglobin and albumin levels were within the normal range. Dengue NS-1Ag, dengue IgM and IgG, Leptospira IgM, Mycoplasma antibody test and Widal-Weil-Felix test were all negative. Blood cultures did not yield any result.
After three attempts using BinaxNOW  Malaria Test (USA), a T2 Line appeared, while no T1 Line (specific for P. falciparum infection) was observed, suggesting vivax, malariae or ovale malaria or a mix of these. Microscopy on thick and thin blood films detected the presence of malaria parasites suggesting P. ovale or P. vivax (Fig. 1), with 0.27 % parasitaemia.
DNA was extracted from whole blood collected in EDTA tube using the DNeasy  Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germany). Four microlitres of the purified DNA was used in the primary PCR reaction, followed by a secondary PCR amplification using standard nested PCR method (Table 1). The PCR result was negative for all reactions except the reaction using genus-specific primers, rPLU3 and rPLU4. Gel electrophoresis showed a band of 240 bp, corresponding to the product of the genus-specific nest 2 PCR (Fig. 2). At the same time, NM-PCR, a nested multiplex malaria PCR and NG-PCR, a nested PCR for Plasmodium genus amplification were performed (Table 1), as previously described. NG-PCR also successfully amplified a positive product. The positive products of both PCRs were gel purified using QIAquick  Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Germany) and cloned into pGEM -T vector (Promega, USA). For each PCR product, ten clones were screened and three positive clones were randomly selected for plasmid sequencing. Plasmids were extracted using QIAprep  Spin Miniprep Kit (Qiagen, Germany) and sequenced using BigDye  Terminator v3.1 in ABI PRISM  3730xl DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). No definitive result was obtained from NM-PCR due to non-specific bands observed on the gel.
Sequencing data between clones were similar except for a few nucleotide differences. A consensus sequence was generated from the plasmid sequences of the clones for each PCR product and analysed using NCBI BLAST. The result showed a 99 % identity to the ssrRNA gene of P. ovale wallikeri (GenBank accession number: AB182492.1, KF696360.1, KF018654.1). Subsequently, the full nucleotide sequence (746 bp) of the product from NG-PCR (herein named UM00134; GenBank accession number: KU255080) was compared to those found in the GenBank in a phylogenetic analysis using the MEGA 6.06 program. Sequences were trimmed and aligned using Clustal W. A phylogenetic tree was constructed using the neighbour-joining methods and Jukes-Cantor model, with a Bootstrap value of 1000 (Fig. 3). Sequence analyses confirmed that the infecting Plasmodium species was P. ovale wallikeri.
In light of this finding, primers rOVA1v and rOVA2v which are specific for P. ovale wallikeri, were used in the Nest 2 PCR reaction under the same condition as mentioned in Table 1. Primers rOVA1 and rOVA2 were included to exclude P. ovale curtisi infection. Parallel to that, a mixture of primer sets rOVA1/rOVA2 and rOVA1v/rOVA2v, besides primer set rOVA1WC/rOVA2WC which are able to detect both P. ovale forms were also employed. Positive products were obtained from the PCR. The mixture of these primer sets in a single Nest 2 PCR reaction and primer set rOVA1WC/rOVA2WC were able to detect P. ovale wallikeri (Fig. 4).
The patient was immediately treated with a course of Riamet  (artemether/lumefantrine) following detection of malaria parasites. His symptoms improved within 24 h of treatment but blood film for malaria became negative only after 36 h of treatment. However his platelet count seems to be slow to recover while C-reactive protein, which is known as a marker for severity in malaria, improved steadily following treatment. Primaquine 30 mg base daily was added 2 days after Riamet. He requested for discharge and agreed to complete the two-week course of primaquine at home. He continued to improve clinically post-discharge but could not afford to repeat his blood tests and dropped out from subsequent out-patient follow up visit.
The study was approved by the University of Malaya Medical Centre Medical Ethics Committee (MEC Ref. No: 817.18).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of high fever of 39.8 C, shaking chills, rigors, and generalized body aches following recent travel to West Africa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient traveled to Nigeria for a 10-day vacation during semester break and developed high fever, shaking chills, rigors, and generalized body aches 5 days after returning to Malaysia. Symptoms persisted over 4 days, prompting admission to a tertiary medical center. Physical examination revealed tachycardia and high fever with laboratory evidence of acute thrombocytopenia and markedly elevated inflammatory markers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born in Nigeria, university student in Malaysia. History of three episodes of febrile parasitic illness during childhood (specific species unconfirmed). No other chronic medical illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, shaking chills, rigors, and generalized arthralgias/myalgias. Negative for headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, cough, or rash. Medications: null. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.8 C, heart rate: 126 beats/min, blood pressure: 128/87 mmHg. Awake, alert; cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological physical examinations were completely unremarkable without hepatosplenomegaly or petechiae.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 71,000/muL (reference: 150,000-400,000/muL), C-reactive protein (CRP): 97 mg/L (reference: <5 mg/L). White blood cell count, hemoglobin, and serum albumin: Within normal reference ranges. Dengue diagnostic panel (NS1 antigen, IgM, IgG): Negative. Leptospira IgM serology: Negative. Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibody test: Negative. Widal and Weil-Felix febrile agglutination tests: Negative. Bacterial blood cultures: Sterile.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute imported Plasmodium ovale wallikeri (variant type) malaria with moderate thrombocytopenia.
Diagnostic confirmation: BinaxNOW Malaria rapid diagnostic test demonstrated a reactive T2 band (pan-Plasmodium aldolase) with negative T1 band (PfHRP-2). Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films showed intraerythrocytic Plasmodium parasites compatible with P. ovale or P. vivax with 0.27% parasitemia. Genus-specific nested PCR (rPLU3/rPLU4) and NG-PCR yielded diagnostic amplicons; plasmid cloning and sequencing of the 746-bp product (GenBank accession number: KU255080) revealed 99% nucleotide identity to the ssrRNA gene of Plasmodium ovale wallikeri. P. ovale wallikeri-specific nested PCR (rOVA1v/rOVA2v) confirmed P. ovale wallikeri and excluded P. ovale curtisi and P. vivax.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with an oral course of artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet). Clinical symptoms improved within 24 hours, and blood films cleared of parasites within 36 hours. C-reactive protein showed steady decline. Oral primaquine (30 mg base once daily for 14 days) was initiated 2 days post-Riamet to eradicate latent hypnozoites, and the patient was discharged in good condition to complete therapy at home.

raw_case_text: In February 2001, a 39-year-old man was hospitalized in Marseilles, France, with fever and disorientation. This truck driver lived in Portugal and had been driving in Spain for 2 weeks before entering France. He arrived in France 3 days before admission. The day of admission, his co-workers found him confused and febrile after sleeping in his truck. He had no previous relevant medical history. On admission, his temperature was 40 C with tachycardia, and his blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg. Clinical examination showed a drowsy, confused man with a bilateral headache, provoked myalgia of the legs, hepatalgia, and conjunctivitis. Neurologic examination showed signs of meningeal irritation, including cervical rigidity, Brudzinski's sign, hyperesthesia, and photophobia. There was no rash, and the rest of the physical examination was normal. Results of biochemical investigation included increased alanine aminotransferase (61 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase (78 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (781 IU/L), fibrinogen level (6.44 g/L), and C-reactive protein (273 mg/L), associated with hypoglycemia (2.9 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (26 g/L), hypoproteinemia (54 g/L), and hypocholesterolemia (2.3 mmol/L). The leukocyte count was 11,000/mm3 with 69% polymorphonuclear forms. Thrombocytopenia (110 G/L) was also observed. The kaolin cephalin time was 58 s (control 34 s), and the prothrombin rate was 42%. Blood smears showed no parasites. Cerebral scanning was normal. Analysis of the CSF on day 1 showed 4 leukocytes/mm3, 50,000 erythrocytes/mm3, and elevated protein levels (1.48 g/L). On day 2, another CSF analysis showed 75 leukocytes/mm3, with 70% polymorphonuclear forms, 5,500 erythrocytes/mm3, and increased protein (0.64 g/L). Direct examination by dark-field microscopy of the CSF from day 2 was performed and controlled by two experimental investigators, who observed many spirochetes. The patient received a 10-day treatment with 12 g/day intravenous amoxicillin. The fever decreased to 38 C on day 4 and resolved on day 7. The patient was discharged from the hospital and remained well. No occupational or recreational risks for leptospirosis could be established. The patient had been traveling recently in Spain and Portugal but had no apparent exposure to sources of leptospires.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old male presenting with acute high fever, headache, myalgias, and disorientation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A truck driver residing in Portugal had been driving through Spain for 2 weeks before arriving in France 3 days prior to admission. On the day of admission, co-workers discovered him drowsy, febrile, and confused inside his truck cabin. He complained of severe bilateral headache, provoked calf and leg myalgias, and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness (hepatalgia).
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous relevant medical history. Occupation: long-haul truck driver. Recent travel: traveled through Spain and Portugal over preceding two weeks; no specific recreational or occupational exposure to rodents, livestock, or freshwater could be established.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high fever, disorientation, bilateral headache, severe provoked leg myalgias, hepatalgia, and photophobia. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: drowsy, confused, and febrile with a body temperature of 40 °C, tachycardia, and blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. HEENT: bilateral conjunctivitis. Abdomen: hepatalgia (right upper quadrant liver tenderness). Neurological: pronounced signs of meningeal irritation including cervical rigidity, positive Brudzinski's sign, cutaneous hyperesthesia, and photophobia. Skin: no rash. Rest of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: leukocyte count 11,000/mm^3 (69% polymorphonuclear forms), thrombocytopenia with platelet count of 110 G/L. Biochemistry: ALT 61 IU/L, AST 78 IU/L, LDH 781 IU/L, fibrinogen 6.44 g/L, CRP 273 mg/L, blood glucose 2.9 mmol/L (hypoglycemia), serum albumin 26 g/L, total protein 54 g/L, cholesterol 2.3 mmol/L. Coagulation: kaolin cephalin time (APTT) 58 s (control 34 s), prothrombin rate 42%. Peripheral blood smears: negative for hemoparasites (malaria excluded).
objective.advanced_workup: Cerebral CT scan: normal without intracranial abnormalities. Lumbar puncture (Day 1): CSF leukocyte count 4/mm^3, erythrocyte count 50,000/mm^3, protein 1.48 g/L. Lumbar puncture (Day 2): CSF leukocyte count 75/mm^3 (70% polymorphonuclear forms), erythrocyte count 5,500/mm^3, protein 0.64 g/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute leptospirosis presenting as acute spirochetal meningitis/meningoencephalitis with meningism, conjunctivitis, hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy, and thrombocytopenia. Definitively confirmed by direct dark-field microscopic visualization of numerous motile spirochetes in the cerebrospinal fluid (controlled by two expert investigators). Malaria ruled out by negative peripheral blood smears.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous amoxicillin 12 g/day for a 10-day course; supportive care for hypoglycemia and hepatic dysfunction.
Outcome: Rapid clinical response with body temperature decreasing to 38 °C on day 4 and complete defervescence by day 7; discharged in good health with full recovery and no residual sequelae.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 20-30-year-old multiparous pregnant woman from sub-Saharan Africa who came to an emergency department at Providence Portland Medical Center, Portland, Oregon, USA, during her third trimester; she had inadequate prenatal care and a 2-week history of loose stools and abdominal pain before defecation. She reported chills and night sweats without fevers. She denied nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, runny nose, cough, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, dysuria, or vaginal discharge. The patient was tachycardic; fetal heart rate (FHR) tracing showed a normal FHR, moderate variability, accelerations, and late and variable decelerations. Initial laboratory evaluation on the woman showed microcytic anemia, leukocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, and an increased level of bilirubin (Table).
Testing results were negative for HIV, SARS-CoV-2, influenza, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, rubella, and syphilis. The result of a rapid point-of-care BinaxNOW malaria test (Abbott Laboratories, https://www.globalpointofcare.abbott) was positive for P. falciparum. Thick and thin malaria blood smears showed P. falciparum (Figure 1). Initial parasitemia was 0.2%. We submitted blood smears to the Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria diagnostic laboratory, Center for Global Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and P. falciparum morphologic identification was confirmed. A pretreatment blood sample was not available for molecular speciation or whole-genome sequencing.
We initiated a 3-day course of artemether/lumefantrine, and percentage parasitemia decreased to 0.1% within 24 hours. No parasites were observed by day 3 of therapy. The patient received intravenous fluids and 1 unit of packed red blood cells. Maternal tachycardia resolved, and FHR tracing displayed normal FHR with moderate variability, accelerations, and resolution of decelerations. The patient's anemia and thrombocytopenia improved, and her leukocyte count normalized. The patient gave birth to a healthy postterm infant without evidence of placental insufficiency. Placental pathologic analysis showed sickled maternal erythrocytes, pigment in perivillous fibrin, and mild lymphocytic deciduitis without immunohistochemical evidence of parasites.
The patient immigrated to the United States with her family 11 years before she sought care. She had lived in a metropolitan area of Oregon during the 5 years before she sought care and denied any history of foreign or domestic travel. The patient reported a history of malaria during childhood 19 years earlier, for which treatment was received while living in sub-Saharan Africa. She denied any history of blood transfusions or recent insect bites. The most recent visit to the patient's home by a person from sub-Saharan Africa occurred 2 years before her illness. She had a history of anemia during previous pregnancies, and her first pregnancy was complicated by thrombocytopenia and preeclampsia. She had a history of sickle cell trait diagnosed by hemoglobin fractionation.
We explored the plausibility of local malaria transmission by evaluating current mosquito surveillance data and conducting case finding with temporospatial proximity to the case. The investigation was anchored to month of symptom onset (September 2022). We used mapping to visualize spatial associations between mosquito surveillance, malaria case reports, syndromic surveillance, and death surveillance (Figure 2).
Anopheles freeborni and An. punctipennis mosquitoes were identified during Washington County Public Health's 2022 Mosquito Control trapping season, May-September 2022. However, during the period of our investigation, temperatures had decreased, and Anopheles mosquitos were not active in the area. P. falciparum case finding within the statewide reportable disease database showed 1 travel-associated malaria case with an onset 2 months before this patient and  4 miles away. There was no epidemiologic link between the cases; whole blood was not available to identify microsatellite parasite signatures. A search of Oregon's Electronic Surveillance System for the Early Notification of Community-Based Epidemics for emergency department encounters with a discharge diagnosis of fever of unknown origin (FUO) showed greater than expected activity in the week of the patient's onset of symptoms. However, the trend was not isolated to the proximity of the case-patient, and many encounters noted manifestations consistent with viral infections.
An Early Notification of Community-Based Epidemics query for mosquito bites and arboviral diseases did not show greater than expected activity. A vital records query for deaths with an associated diagnosis of FUO showed 1 death temporospatially related to the case. Medical record review by the Malaria Branch, Center for Global Health, Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, ruled out the death as related to malaria due to clinical and laboratory incompatibility. Thus, there was no evidence to support local mosquitoborne transmission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-30-year-old pregnant female presenting in the third trimester with loose stools, pre-defecation abdominal cramping, chills, and night sweats of two weeks' duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 20-30-year-old multiparous pregnant woman in her third trimester with inadequate prenatal care presented with a two-week history of loose stools, lower abdominal cramping prior to defecation, chills, and drenching night sweats. She denied subjective or measured fevers at home. On evaluation, she had persistent maternal tachycardia and non-reassuring fetal heart tracings, necessitating immediate hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immigrated to the United States from sub-Saharan Africa 11 years prior; lived in Oregon for past 5 years without domestic or international travel. Childhood malaria episode 19 years earlier treated in sub-Saharan Africa. Sickle cell trait (diagnosed by hemoglobin electrophoresis/fractionation). History of gestational anemia in prior pregnancies; first pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia and thrombocytopenia. Denied blood transfusions, recent insect bites, or contact with recent travelers (last visitor from Africa was 2 years prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for loose stools, pre-defecatory abdominal pain, chills, and night sweats. Negative for fevers, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, rhinorrhea, cough, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, dysuria, and vaginal discharge. Medications: prenatal vitamins. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Maternal tachycardia. Fetal heart rate (FHR) tracing demonstrated normal baseline FHR with moderate variability and accelerations, but with recurrent late and variable decelerations. Physical examination otherwise showed no signs of peritonitis, petechiae, or lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial laboratory evaluation: microcytic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated serum bilirubin. Negative infectious workup: HIV, SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, rubella, and syphilis. Thick and thin peripheral blood smears performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Placental histopathology: sickled maternal erythrocytes, pigment in perivillous fibrin, and mild lymphocytic deciduitis without immunohistochemical evidence of diagnostic abnormalities. Epidemiological surveillance: local mosquito trapping (identified Anopheles freeborni and An. punctipennis inactive during autumn) and statewide syndromic/death surveillance ruled out local mosquitoborne transmission.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Delayed-presentation / recrudescent Plasmodium falciparum malaria in pregnancy (third trimester) in a patient with sickle cell trait, complicated by maternal anemia, thrombocytopenia, and non-reassuring fetal heart rate decelerations.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid point-of-care BinaxNOW malaria test positive for Plasmodium falciparum; thick and thin peripheral blood smears showing Plasmodium falciparum with 0.2% parasitemia, confirmed by the CDC Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral artemether/lumefantrine for 3 days, intravenous fluid hydration, and 1 unit of packed red blood cell transfusion. Parasitemia fell to 0.1% within 24 hours and completely cleared by day 3. Maternal tachycardia and fetal decelerations resolved, cytopenias normalized, and the patient subsequently delivered a healthy postterm infant without placental insufficiency.

raw_case_text:
In February 2015, a 12-year-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with fever, vomiting and diarrhea. The patient was given IV fluids, tests were performed and he was sent home. Blood culture turned out to be positive for gram positive cocci in pairs and chains and the patient was called back for admission. The patient prior to these symptoms went to the desert for the school vacations, where he had contact with animals. On admission, he was given IV ceftriaxone; later on, doxycycline and rifampin were added to his treatment. The patient improved his fever subsided. After one week of hospitalization, ceftriaxone was discontinued and the patient was discharged on doxycycline and rifampin.
Three sets of aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures were collected. After four days, all three aerobic blood culture vials were flagged positive-by Bactec FX  system. Pleomorphic Gram-positive bacteria were isolated from the blood culture, ranging in shape from round cocci to short, thin rods bacilli Fig. (1). Coryneform species, usually interpreted as contaminants of unknown clinical importance, were suspected and a preliminary report of "Gram-positive bacilli" was generated and reported. After 24 hour- incubation on blood agar plates, tiny growth was observed on the primary streaking, further suggesting Coryneform isolates as many Coryneform species are characterized by slow growth. By 48 hrs, good growth was observed on a blood agar plate. Catalase test was positive, a characteristic commonly exhibited by both Coryneform species and Brucella species. Coryneform species are usually considered contaminants, however the presence of this organism in three consecutive vials prompted further identification by VITEK-2 Compact 60 (AES software) (bioMerieux, Inc., USA) automated system using the VITEK Anaerobe Identification (ANI) card. This was done to rule out Corynebacterium urealyticum, C. jeikeium, and C. striatum, which can be pathogenic in vulnerable individuals. After 18 hrs, the blood culture isolate remained unidentified on ANI by 2 different VITEK 2 system machines. Gram staining was repeated from the blood agar plate; pleomorphic Gram-variable bacteria were identified. The oxidase test using Remel BactiDrop  Oxidase ampules (Thermo Scientific) was performed and found to be strongly positive, allowing Coryneform species to be excluded and Brucella to be suspected. The urease test was performed using Urea Agar slant tubes (Saudi Prepared Media Laboratory Co. Ltd) and found to be strongly positive after 3 hour- incubation, further suggesting Brucella.
PCR confirmation of Brucella identification was done by using real-time PCR method. Briefly, DNA was extracted using the MagNA-Pure-Compact-System  (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany), based on the manufacturer's instructions. A total of 400 mul of blood was drawn from the blood culture positive bottle, poured into MagNa pure sample tube and DNA was extracted using the MagNA Pure LC DNA Isolation Kit I according to the manufacturer's instructions. The DNA material was eluted in 50 mul total volume and Brucella detected by real-time PCR using the proprietary Brucella Real Time PCR Kit (Shanghai ZJ Bio-Tech Co., Ltd). The PCR thermal conditions were followed as described by the manufacturer. After the activation of the enzyme at 37 C for 2 min, 1 cycle and 94 C for 2 min, 1 cycle, and amplification of PCR target was done at 93 C for 5 sec for denaturation, 60 C for 30 sec for annealing for a total of 40 cycles. The amplification signal was measured at 60 C using 530 detection fluorescent channel in LightCycler 2.0 instrument.
Identification of pleomorphic Gram-positive bacilli after initial Gram staining from blood culture should be done by careful interpretation as both Corynebacterium and Brucella species have similar slow growth patterns. Not only the Gram staining result might be misinterpreted, but also the final identification; hence inappropriate treatment may be prescribed due to such misinterpretations. It is recommended that oxidase test from the plate and urease test from the culture vial be performed after apparent identification of pleomorphic Gram-positive bacilli, once tiny growth is observed, in order to distinguish Brucella from Corynebacterium species. Brucella infection is of particular concern in Saudi Arabia, given the high volume of livestock importation. Misidentification due to misleading initial Gram-staining results can also lead to inadvertent exposure of laboratory staff to Brucella. Earlier detection would be helpful in ensuring subsequent appropriate handling of the relevant samples in the laboratory for example, in procedures that can result in aerosolization and protect other laboratory staff from exposure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old boy presented with acute fever, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department in February 2015 with acute fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. He was initially administered intravenous fluids and discharged home after preliminary testing. He was subsequently recalled and admitted after initial blood cultures flagged positive. Symptoms followed a school vacation trip to the desert where he had animal contact.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior illnesses documented. Received intravenous fluids in the emergency room. Epidemiological history: traveled to the desert for school vacation with direct animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting and diarrhea. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile on presentation. General physical exam details and vitals not further documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood cultures collected on presentation; initial preliminary report described Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and Gram-positive bacilli / pleomorphic bacteria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis bacteremia with gastrointestinal presentation, initially misidentified morphologically as coryneform bacteria/Gram-positive bacilli. Confirmed by 3 sets of aerobic blood cultures flagging positive at 4 days on Bactec FX, exhibiting positive catalase, strongly positive oxidase, strongly positive urease (at 3 hours), and definitive confirmation of Brucella by real-time PCR from blood culture broth (LightCycler 2.0). Differential diagnoses of Corynebacterium species (C. urealyticum, C. jeikeium, C. striatum) were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on IV ceftriaxone, followed by the addition of oral doxycycline and rifampin. Fever resolved and clinical symptoms improved. Ceftriaxone was discontinued after 1 week, and the patient was discharged on oral doxycycline and rifampicin to complete treatment.

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man was referred to us for a symptomatology of 2-week duration. Past medical history was unremarkable. The patient reported unprotected receptive oral sex one month earlier with a male whose status for HIV was unknown. The patient complained from abdominal pain, arthralgia of ankles and wrists, and purpura of legs.
On examination, an extensive vascular purpura of the legs was present without other abnormalities. Biopsy of the skin revealed signs of vasculitis. Standard biological exams were normal, except for a mild proteinuria (0.5 g/L). Creatinemia was normal (0.9 mg/dL). Complement was normal. Anti-DNA antibodies were negative. A mixed cryoglobulinemia was detected in the serum. HCV and HBV serology were negative. HCV serology was done one year later and remained negative.
HIV testing was positive on ELISA while an incomplete profile was found on western blot (gp120 +/-, gp41++++, p31-, p24+). p24 antigenemia was positive (28 pg/mL). HIV viral load (VL) was 4.7 log copies/mL. CD4 cells count was 213/mm3. Antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, and r/atazanavir) was given. After 3 months of treatment, VL was <50 copies/mL and CD4 cells count was 924/mm3. Western blot was repeated and was subsequently positive for all bands tested. During this period, symptoms progressively decreased with a complete resolution after 3 months. Cryoglobulinemia became negative after 1 year of treatment. After a followup of 3 years, the patient remained asymptomatic with CD4 cells count always above 500/mm3 and VL <50 copies/mL.
Prevalence of cryoglobulinemia is high in HIV-infected patients. Scotto et al. found a prevalence of 6% for HIV-monoinfected patients and 14.2% for HIV-HCV-coinfected patients. In spite of this high prevalence, cryoglobulinemia is rarely symptomatic even if rare neurological, dermatological, renal, or rheumatological complications have been described. These complications occurred usually during chronic phase of HIV infection. To our knowledge, it has been not reported during acute primary infection. At presentation, our patient clearly suffered from symptomatic cryoglobulinemia. Clinical and anatomopathological findings were consistent with this hypothesis ruling out an incidental discovery of a cryoglobulinemia during HIV infection. The simultaneous occurrence of symptomatic cryoglobulinemia and HIV primary infection argued in favour of a role of HIV in the appearance of cryoglobulinemia. The impact of HAART on disappearance of cryoglobulinemia in our observation is difficult to establish.
Nevertheless, we cannot rule out a positive effect given that, in epidemiologic studies, prevalence of cryoglobulinemia in HIV-infected patients has decreased in HAART era.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presenting with a 2-week history of abdominal pain, ankle and wrist arthralgias, and purpura of the lower extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed diffuse abdominal pain, bilateral ankle and wrist arthralgias, and extensive lower extremity purpura over a 2-week period. He reported an episode of unprotected receptive oral sex one month prior with a male partner of unknown health status.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; no prior hospitalizations, chronic medical conditions, or drug allergies. Epidemiological history: unprotected receptive oral intercourse with a male partner of unknown health status one month prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for abdominal pain, bilateral wrist and ankle arthralgia, and cutaneous purpura; negative for macroscopic hematuria, fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. Home medications: none. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Extensive palpable vascular purpura on both lower extremities without other cutaneous or systemic physical examination abnormalities. Vital signs normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL; urinalysis: mild proteinuria (0.5 g/L); serum complement: normal; anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) autoantibodies: negative; viral hepatitis serologies: HBV and HCV serologies negative (repeat HCV serology negative at 1 year). Serum mixed cryoglobulinemia: detected.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy: histopathologic signs of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Symptomatic mixed cryoglobulinemic leukocytoclastic vasculitis secondary to acute primary human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection. Autoimmune vasculitides ruled out by normal complement and negative anti-dsDNA; chronic viral hepatitis B and C ruled out by repeatedly negative serologies. HIV-1 confirmation: ELISA positive with evolving Western blot pattern (gp120+/-, gp41++++, p31-, p24+), positive p24 antigenemia (28 pg/mL), plasma HIV RNA viral load 4.7 log10 copies/mL, and CD4 cell count 213/mm3. Management & Outcome: Initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir). Symptoms progressively subsided with complete clinical resolution within 3 months, accompanied by viral suppression (<50 copies/mL), CD4 count rising to 924/mm3, complete Western blot seroconversion, and disappearance of serum cryoglobulinemia at 1 year, maintaining clinical and virological remission at 3-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
On his return from Cameroon, Africa, a 36-year-old man with no previous exposure to malaria was admitted to the hospital with a fever. He had spent two months traveling across the country. He experienced a high-grade fever (39.8 C), chill, and headache two days after returning. Oral aspirin treatment showed no improvement after 2 days. He went to the hospital on the third day of his illness. Pallor, a fever of 39.3 C, and splenomegaly were discovered during the physical examination.
A normal leukocyte count, hemoglobin (Hb) 8.6 g/dl, thrombocytopenia (platelet 32 x 109/l), C-reactive protein (CRP) 45.5 mg/l, procalcitonin (PCT) 6.62 ng/ml, erythrocyte sedimentation (ESR) 93 mm/h, D-Dimer 1.58 mg/l and total/direct serum bilirubin of 34.2/24.5 mumol/L were discovered in the laboratory. Renal function and blood sugar levels were both within normal limits. The electrocardiogram (ECG) and chest radiography both came back normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no hepatosplenomegaly (Figure 1). A blood smear investigation confirmed the Plasmodium falciparum diagnosis. Artesunate tablets were given to the patient, and the first dose was 100 mg orally, 50 mg once from the 2nd day, twice a day. For 2 days, the fever subsided. A full course (5 days) of artesunate tablets was continued. On the fourth day of treatment, the patient complained of pain in his left upper abdomen and a fever of 38.9 C. Plasmodium falciparum is not seen in peripheral blood smears. The spleen was bigger (5 cm) and sensitive on inspection. D-Dimer was found to be 5.24 mg/l in a lab test. Splenomegaly with several rounded, focused, low-density spots in various places (biggest 35 mm x 29 mm) suggested splenic infarct on abdominal CT (Figure 2). His hemodynamic condition was stable. For treatment, Nadroparin-calcium 0.4 mg was injected subcutaneously once a day for 5 days, and acetaminophen oxycodone tablets three times a day for pain relief. On day 3, after analgesic and anticoagulant treatment, abdominal pain was relieved, the fever subsided, and D-Dimer decreased (2.46 mg/l) on day 5. Thus emergent surgery was not required. Six months later, abdominal CT showed that the spleen infarction had recovered (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, chills, and headache for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 36-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of high fever (up to 39.8 °C), chills, and headache starting 2 days after returning from a 2-month trip to Cameroon. Self-treatment with oral aspirin for 2 days provided no relief. Antimalarial therapy was commenced upon admission, resulting in defervescence for 2 days. However, on day 4 of treatment, he acutely developed left upper quadrant abdominal pain and recrudescent fever of 38.9 °C.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous malaria exposure. Travel history: Two-month travel across Cameroon, returning 2 days before symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, chills, left upper abdominal pain; denies nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Febrile (39.3 °C), pale, palpable splenomegaly. Day 4: Febrile (38.9 °C), hemodynamically stable, spleen palpably enlarged to 5 cm and exquisitely tender.
objective.routine_investigations: Normal WBC, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelet count 32 x 10^9/L, CRP 45.5 mg/L, procalcitonin 6.62 ng/mL, ESR 93 mm/h, D-dimer 1.58 mg/L, total bilirubin 34.2 μmol/L, direct bilirubin 24.5 μmol/L. Blood glucose and renal function tests normal. ECG and chest radiograph unremarkable. Day 4: D-dimer increased to 5.24 mg/L, decreasing to 2.46 mg/L on day 5.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT on admission showed no hepatosplenomegaly. Repeat abdominal CT on day 4: Splenomegaly with multiple rounded focal hypodense areas (largest 35 x 29 mm) diagnostic of acute splenic infarction. Follow-up CT at 6 months confirmed complete resolution of the splenic infarction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Imported Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by severe thrombocytopenia and delayed acute splenic infarction. Confirmed by peripheral blood smear demonstrating Plasmodium falciparum on admission. Repeat blood smears on day 4 were negative for parasites. Surgical abdomen ruled out by hemodynamic stability and non-operative management.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral artesunate tablets (100 mg initially, then 50 mg twice daily for a 5-day course). For splenic infarction, treated conservatively with subcutaneous nadroparin calcium (0.4 mg daily for 5 days) and oral acetaminophen-oxycodone. Abdominal pain resolved, fever subsided, D-dimer normalized, and surgery was averted. Six-month follow-up CT documented full structural healing of the spleen.

raw_case_text:
A 50 years-old male born in Morocco was admitted to the Hospital for detection of visceral PET positive lymph nodes. He was a former smoker (quit 5 years before admission; 31 pack years) and his occupation was working with plastic. He had been treated for his HIV infection for 5 years. Recently, he had been submitted to surgery and radiotherapy for rectal cancer. He had antibodies against surface Hepatitis B virus and was therefore also treated with Tenofovir, Lamivudine and Efavirenz.
Radiographic and Nuclear Investigations were previously carried out for a low-grade fever of unknown origin. Physical examination documented hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged lymph nodes in the inguinal area.
Altered routine blood tests results are reported in Table 1. Computed tomography scan of the thorax and abdomen mainly showed disseminated enlarged lymph nodes (mediastinum, abdomen) and an enlarged liver and spleen with splenic and portal veins showing enlarged diameters. (Figure 1)
The clinical reasoning was based on three pillars: 1; clinical profile characterized by low grade fever in an HIV patient already under retroviral treatment, 2; laboratory findings characterized by moderate white cells cytopenia (2.45 x 109/L), hypergammaglobulinemia (38.7%), an increase of erythrosedimentation rate (85 mm/h) and a mild increase of beta2-microglobulinemia (5.5 mg/L) and 3; imaging features, mainly represented by enlarged visceral PET positive lymph nodes. Therefore, the most probable diagnosis is included in the following differential diagnosis list: lymphoproliferative disorders, infections (fungal or parasite infections) and metastatic epithelial tumors. PET positive reachable lymph nodes are mainly sited in the mediastinum. Because the lymphoproliferative disorders in HIV positive patients are usually of the large B cell subtypes and a diagnosis is possible using cytological material and infections manifesting with visceral enlarged lymph nodes are more frequently due to intracellular microscopically or microbiologically easy to identify agents (i.e. Cryptococcus, mycobacteria) and because inguinal lymph nodes are frequently not specifically inflamed, a transesophageal ultrasound (EUS) approach was scheduled with fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB, 22 G needle) of lymph nodes in station 4L.
Smears and cell block preps stained by May Grunwald Giemsa, Papanicolaou, Hematoxylin-Eosin and Giemsa were analyzed. Histiocytes laden by amastigotes were identified; amastigotes were also found outside the cells (Figure 2). Amastigotes is one of the transformation stages (the intracellular phase) of the Leishmania parasites life cycle. It is the form the Leishmania parasite takes in the vertebrate host and it is diagnostic when found. A final diagnosis of Lehismaniasis was therefore done. A molecular test on peripheral blood confirmed the morphologic diagnosis. Leishmania donovani DNA copies were present (1,700 genome copies/mL). Other microbiological investigations (bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex type I and II viruses) were negative. The patient was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg iv for 5 days).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male with HIV infection presented for evaluation of visceral PET-positive lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever of unknown origin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 50-year-old male with HIV on antiretroviral therapy who underwent radiographic and nuclear investigations for investigation of persistent low-grade fever of unknown origin. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (PET) revealed hypermetabolic visceral lymph nodes, prompting admission for diagnostic evaluation of suspected lymphoproliferative disorder, opportunistic infection, or metastatic recurrence.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 5 years prior; history of rectal adenocarcinoma treated with surgical resection and radiotherapy; presence of antibodies against surface hepatitis B virus. Former smoker (quit 5 years prior, 31 pack-years). Occupation: plastic manufacturing. Epidemiological background: born in Morocco.
subjective.review_of_systems: Low-grade fever of unknown origin. Home medications: tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination documented hepatosplenomegaly. Lymphatic examination revealed enlarged lymph nodes in the inguinal region.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count: 2.45 x 109/L (moderate leukopenia); Hypergammaglobulinemia: 38.7%; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 85 mm/h; Beta-2-microglobulin: 5.5 mg/L. Microbiological investigations: negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and herpes simplex virus (HSV) types I and II.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) of thorax and abdomen: disseminated enlarged lymph nodes involving mediastinum and abdomen; hepatosplenomegaly with dilated diameters of splenic and portal veins. Positron emission tomography (PET): visceral PET-positive hypermetabolic lymph nodes, predominantly in the mediastinum. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB, 22G needle) of station 4L mediastinal lymph nodes: smears and cell blocks stained with May-Grunwald-Giemsa, Papanicolaou, H&E, and Giemsa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani) presenting as hypermetabolic mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy in an HIV-coinfected individual.
Diagnostic confirmation: Cytological examination of station 4L lymph node FNAB smears and cell block preps demonstrated histiocytes laden with amastigotes as well as extracellular amastigotes. Peripheral blood molecular PCR confirmed Leishmania donovani DNA with 1,700 genome copies/mL.
Differentials ruled out: Large B-cell lymphoma / lymphoproliferative disorders, metastatic recurrence of rectal adenocarcinoma, mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis), cryptococcal / fungal infection, CMV, and HSV.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg IV daily for 5 days).

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old woman with a background of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma was re-admitted 2 weeks after being discharged with COVID-19. She had known follicular lymphoma stage 4A diagnosed in May 2018. She was treated with rituximab, last receiving a dose 3 months before her first admission. At the time of her first admission, she presented with a few weeks' history of fever, myalgia and a sore throat. She had been given co-amoxiclav and azithromycin in the community, 1 week before admission. Her shortness of breath on exertion was worsening, and she was found to have a saturation of 89%. NPS confirmed SARS-CoV-2, and her CXR was consistent with the diagnosis. She was managed on the ward with oxygen and i.v. antibiotics and was discharged 3 weeks later, having had a CT pulmonary angiogram, confirming no pulmonary emboli, and a PET scan, which showed no advancement of her non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
She was re-admitted 21 days later with profound hypoxia, requiring intubation on arrival in hospital. A CT pulmonary angiogram at the time showed extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli, with evidence of right heart strain. There were severe COVID-related changes, with widespread ground glass opacification throughout both lung fields. On admission, ferritin was 29 784 microg/l, CRP 78 mg/l and procalcitonin 2.04 mug/l. She was anaemic (haemoglobin 100 g/l), but not cytopenic, with platelets of 199 x 109/l and a neurophilia of 15.9 x 109/l. NPS and EDTA blood samples were positive for SARS-CoV-2.
She was admitted to the ICU, initiated on tazocin i.v. and underwent thrombolysis for her pulmonary emboli. The following day, ferritin rose to 40 069 microg/l, CRP was 109 mg/l, and procalcitonin increased to 9.85 mug/l. Anakinra i.v. was initiated (Table 1). She was initially started on 100 mg four times a day, but owing to pressures on the nursing staff this was changed to 200 mg twice a day. Within 24 h of commencing anakinra i.v., the ferritin improved to 20 479 mug/l (Fig. 1), and 3 days later continued to fall to 5118 mug/l. A BioFire film was positive for Streptococcus pneumonia. Her ICU stay was complicated by worsening consolidation on her CXRs, necessitating a prolonged course of meropenem. She commenced ambisome on day mug/l2 of admission, which was continued after a positive galactomannan test on her sputum and strongly positive betaD-glucan (341.5 pg/ml), 2 weeks into her admission. It took 24 days from admission for the SARS-CoV-2 viraemia to disappear on both EDTA blood and NPS. She remains in the ICU and is currently weaning off the ventilator, with a tracheostomy in situ and on minimal inotropic support.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old female with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma presenting with profound acute hypoxemia and respiratory failure 3 weeks after prior hospitalization for viral pneumonia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 68-year-old female with stage IV follicular lymphoma recently treated with rituximab had been hospitalized for hypoxemic pneumonia with confirmed viral infection, receiving supplemental oxygen and antibiotics for 3 weeks before discharge. Twenty-one days following discharge, she presented with acute, profound hypoxia and severe respiratory failure requiring immediate emergency endotracheal intubation upon arrival.
subjective.past_medical_history: Stage 4A follicular non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (diagnosed May 2018), treated with rituximab (most recent dose 3 months prior to initial illness). Prior antibiotics included outpatient co-amoxiclav and azithromycin.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for profound dyspnea, history of fever, sore throat, and myalgias. Home medications: rituximab (recent). Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon arrival: acute respiratory failure with profound hypoxemia requiring immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation; hemodynamic instability requiring inotropic support.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 100 g/L; platelet count: 199 x 10^9/L; absolute neutrophil count: 15.9 x 10^9/L; C-reactive protein (CRP): 78 mg/L (rose to 109 mg/L next day); serum ferritin: 29,784 mcg/L (rose to 40,069 mcg/L; declining to 20,479 mcg/L and 5,118 mcg/L after anakinra); procalcitonin: 2.04 mcg/L (rose to 9.85 mcg/L). Sputum BioFire PCR: positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae. Fungal serology: serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan strongly positive at 341.5 pg/mL; sputum Aspergillus galactomannan positive. Serial chest radiographs: progressive severe bilateral airspace consolidation.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial readmission CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA): extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli with signs of acute right ventricular strain, alongside severe bilateral widespread ground-glass opacities throughout both lung fields. Tracheostomy placed during ICU stay for prolonged mechanical ventilation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe persistent COVID-19 with persistent SARS-CoV-2 viremia (positive on EDTA blood and nasopharyngeal swab for 24 days) in a B-cell depleted lymphoma patient, complicated by massive bilateral pulmonary embolism with acute right heart strain, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)/hyperferritinemic storm (peak ferritin 40,069 mcg/L), Streptococcus pneumoniae bacterial superinfection, and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Management & Outcome: Emergent systemic thrombolysis for pulmonary embolism, intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam transitioned to meropenem, liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) for invasive fungal disease, and intravenous anakinra (initially 100 mg four times daily, transitioned to 200 mg twice daily). Anakinra resulted in prompt down-regulation of ferritin and inflammatory parameters. After 24 days, viral clearance from blood and nasopharynx was achieved, and the patient was successfully stabilized on minimal inotropic support with tracheostomy-assisted ventilator weaning.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old male Guatemalan soldier presented to the facilities of the Military Hospital on June 29, 2012, to confirm suspected P. vivax malaria. Three months previously he had returned from a 9-month deployment in Africa, as part of a Guatemalan Army operation to aid the UN Organization Stabilization Mission in DRC.
The soldier reported that during his time in DRC he stayed in the towns of Dungu, Bangadi and Bunia. He travelled for a short period of time to Entebbe and Kampala (Uganda) and Mombasa (Kenya) as part of his rest and recuperation time. During the entire mission, he used an untreated bed net and received mefloquine prophylaxis (250 mg base/week). He reported high compliance with the drug, although he admitted to skipping some doses during his period in Uganda and Kenya. Upon his return to Guatemala, he and all deployed personnel were screened by malaria microscopy and P.vivax/P.falciparum PCR. Microscopic and molecular results were negative for the entire contingent.
Two months after his return to Guatemala, the patient travelled to Puerto de San Jose, Escuintla (a coastal zone in the southern Guatemala) and then returned to his residence in Jalpatagua, Jutiapa (eastern region). Malaria is endemic in both of these regions. He reported fatigue and fever, and malaria was clinically diagnosed by a private physician without any laboratory confirmation. He was given chloroquine diphosphate injections (no available dosage data) because the standard treatment in P. falciparum/P. vivax (the two endemic malaria parasites of the country) includes chloroquine.
The patient reported an improvement and returned to military duties. Three weeks later, he again presented with fever and fatigue. Malaria microscopy conducted at the Jutiapa Malaria Vector Control Program erroneously diagnosed a P. vivax infection. The patient was transferred to Guatemala City to be evaluated in the Military Medical Center.
Venous and capillary blood was taken for laboratory testing. A thin blood film identified P. vivax, although concerns about the morphology of some of the observed parasites were raised by the hospital microbiologist. A complete blood count at admission revealed thrombocytopenia (71,000 platelets/mul) and anemia (haemoglobin 12 g/dl). A rapid dengue diagnostic assay showed a current or recent infection. Other laboratory tests results were within reference values.
Based on the travel history of the patient and the doubts arisen as to its species identity, molecular testing was conducted to confirm the Plasmodium species. A P. ovale mono-infection was identified on both the blood film and whole blood of the patient using a Plasmodium genus-specific nested PCR (Figure 1) and a SYBR Green-based quantitative real-time PCR. The blood film was re-examined to identify the morphological features of this parasite (Figure 2). Sequence analysis was conducted to discriminate between the classic or variant P. ovale. Basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) analysis revealed 95% similarity with P. ovale ssrRNA gene. The strain was classified as the classic type, P. ovale curtisi, based on its nucleotide polymorphisms. The Genetics and Immunology Laboratory, Malaria Branch at Centers for Disease Control (Atlanta, US) confirmed these findings.
For malaria treatment he was prescribed 1,500 mg of chloroquine base given over 3 days and 15 mg of primaquine base over 14 days, following national guidelines for the treatment of P. vivax infections, as the results of the molecular analyses were not available at the time of treatment initiation. The patient was discharged after his clinical condition and hematological results improved. Follow up specimens were taken at day 1, one and two months after treatment completion, confirming parasite clearance. Also, all family members in the household and one neighbor provided blood samples, with negative results for Plasmodium spp. As a control measure, the household was sprayed with deltamethrin.
Here we present the first imported Plasmodium ovale case in Guatemala. Based on the patient's travel history, he could have acquired the infection in any of the African countries he stayed in, as P. ovale is present in all of them. Lack of strict compliance with both chemoprophylaxis and personal protective measures has been cited as a cause of imported malaria in deployed military personnel. The patient's late onset of symptoms corresponds to previous observations that anti-malarial prophylaxis delays, but does not prevent, the primary attack.
This report highlights the need to consider P. ovale as a cause of imported malaria and to include its detection, as well as P. malariae, in imported malaria screening programs. This patient presented particular diagnostic challenges that resulted in a failure of early detection and diagnosis of P. ovale infection. Distinguishing P. ovale from P. vivax by microscopy, already difficult due to the species' morphologic similarity, was further confounded in this case by P. ovale's non-indigenous status. Since this event, all returning military contingents are being tested with a pan-Plasmodium real time PCR assay. In addition to malaria screening programs, clinical diagnoses should not automatically exclude consideration of non-endemic species of malaria. Regular training of microscopists for the accurate identification of all malaria parasites, including non-indigenous species, should be mandatory.
In addition to mitigating the diagnostic challenges of imported malaria, monitoring imported cases into an already malaria-endemic area is important because the presence of viable vectors could lead to secondary autochthonous cases and the spread of drug-resistant strains, thus hampering malaria control and elimination efforts in regions, such as Central America that remains one of the few areas of the world where no antimalarial drug resistance has been reported. An observed change in the number of imported cases or species of malaria could help re-direct prevention efforts both internationally and within Guatemala. Moreover, the combined use of molecular methods and microscopy will have the added benefit of possibly increasing detection of asymptomatic infections, allowing us to determine the true burden of infection and potential interactions among Plasmodium species.
Considering the long latency of these infections, further strategies should be considered to improve prevention. For instance, the use of presumptive anti-relapse therapy could be an effective approach to prevent relapses of P. vivax or P. ovale infections in long-term Army deployments which are significantly exposed to these parasites.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male soldier presenting with recurrent fevers, fatigue, and thrombocytopenia 3 months after returning from a peacekeeping deployment to Central and East Africa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months after returning from a 9-month United Nations peacekeeping deployment to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (with brief visits to Uganda and Kenya), the patient developed fatigue and fever. He received empiric chloroquine injections from a local practitioner with temporary relief. Three weeks later, he suffered recurrent fever spikes and fatigue. Initial local peripheral blood microscopy suggested a benign tertian parasitic infection, prompting transfer to the central military medical center for species verification and definitive management.
subjective.past_medical_history: Deployed for 9 months to DRC (Dungu, Bangadi, Bunia) with travel to Uganda and Kenya; utilized untreated bed nets and took weekly mefloquine chemoprophylaxis (250 mg base/week) with self-reported missed doses. Routine port-of-entry microscopic and molecular screening upon return was negative. Travel within Guatemala to Escuintla and Jutiapa 2 months post-return.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fevers, chills, and fatigue. Negative for headache, vomiting, jaundice, or bleeding manifestations. Medications: chloroquine diphosphate injections 3 weeks prior. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile during paroxysms; cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological physical examinations were completely normal without organomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 12.0 g/dL, platelet count: 71,000/muL (thrombocytopenia). Rapid dengue diagnostic assay: Positive for current or recent dengue infection. Routine serum biochemistry and organ function tests: Within normal reference values.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: First documented imported Plasmodium ovale curtisi (classic type) infection in Guatemala, accompanied by serologic evidence of recent dengue virus infection.
Diagnostic confirmation: Genus- and species-specific nested PCR and SYBR Green-based real-time PCR from whole blood confirmed Plasmodium ovale monoinfection (ruling out P. vivax and P. falciparum). Nucleotide sequence analysis of the small subunit ribosomal RNA (ssrRNA) gene confirmed 95% homology to P. ovale curtisi, independently validated by the CDC Malaria Branch (Atlanta, USA).
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral chloroquine (1,500 mg base divided over 3 days) and oral primaquine (15 mg base daily for 14 days) for eradication of hepatic hypnozoites. Thrombocytopenia normalized, fever resolved, and serial blood smears and PCR assays at day 1, 1 month, and 2 months confirmed complete parasite clearance. Vector control (indoor residual spraying with deltamethrin) and negative contact tracing were conducted for household members.

raw_case_text:
A 9-year-old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1-day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He also has been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for a month prior to his presentation. A week before his admission, there was a noticeable increase in his pallor. Upon presentation, he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced. He was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. System examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly small palpable lymph node in the supraclavicular and inguinal region. The remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable.
His initial Laboratory tests at admission showed a picture of bi-cytopenia in the form of anemia and thrombocytopenia. Platelet 11 x 109/L (normal range: 150-400 x 109/L); hemoglobin 97 mg/L (normal range: 113-150 mg/J); white blood cells 10.2 x 109/L (normal range: 4-12 x 109/L); and reticulocyte counts 2.45% (normal range: 0.5%-1.5%). Peripheral blood smear showed red blood cell fragmentation (Schistocytes) at 1.45%, and white blood cells, mainly neutrophilia, displayed reactive changes in forms of toxic granulation.
Lactate dehydrogenase was 1,021 U/L (normal range: 125-220 U/L); aspartate aminotransferase 46 IU/L (normal range: 5-34 U/L); alkaline phosphatase 143 IU/L (normal range: 156-369 U/L); total bilirubin 41.3 micromol/L (normal range: ~20.5 micromol/L); and direct bilirubin 12.7 micromol/L (normal range: ~8.6 micromol/L). Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine were within normal limits. Urinalysis showed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation screening tests were within the normal range; fibrinogen level was decreased to 1.72 g/L (normal range: 1.5-4.1 g/L); Coombs test was negative.
Initially, the patient was diagnosed with atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg. He received two doses of IVIG without response, and his Hgb and platelet counts declined further.
In order to rule out bone marrow infiltration, bone marrow aspirations (BMA) and biopsy were performed. The preliminary report of the BMA did not suggest malignancy; however, it showed megakaryocytes which is suggestive of immune destruction. Therefore the patient was started on a six days trial of pulse steroid therapy (intravenous methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day divided twice a day), with no improvement in Hgb or platelet count. The final result of BMA revealed peripheral destruction of blood cells, indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), likely TTP, congenital or acquired due to an immune reaction to ADAMTS-13; this diagnosis was supported by repeated peripheral blood smear showing Schistocytes fragments of red blood cells >2.5% (Normal range <1.5%), accordingly a five days trial of fresh frozen plasma transfusion was initiated, in which the patient showed improvement in LDH and platelet levels.
In addition, bone marrow biopsy results showed morphologic evidence of frequent small epithelioid non-necrotizing granuloma. Considering that this is a nonspecific finding that could be attributed to various etiologies, including infections (viral, bacterial, and tuberculosis), infiltrating diseases such as sarcoidosis, and malignancies, further investigation has been pursued. Viral surveillance, including EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and computerized chest and abdominal tomography (CT) scan showed splenomegaly with no significant lymph node enlargement. Since Brucella is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, brucella titers were sent, and the result showed Brucella abortus 1:5,120 (normal range: <1:160), and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480 (normal range: <1:160).
A combination of Doxycycline (5 mg/kg/day orally twice a day) and Rifampin (20 mg/kg/day orally twice a day) antimicrobial therapy was commenced for a total of 6 weeks (42 days) to treat brucellosis. Once starting the anti-brucellosis management, the patient did not require further FFP transfusion. The ADAMTS-13 essay result showed: extremely low ADAMTS-13 activity, which was found at 0.02 IU/ml (normal range: 0.40-1.30 IU/ml), with an antigen assay below the detection level of 0.01 IU/ml (normal range: 0.41-1.41 IU/ml); and anti-ADAMTS-13 antibodies were detected at high concentrations of >95 IU/ml (>15 IU/ml is considered positive). All these findings, along with the presentation of thrombocytopenia and hemolysis, are specific to acquired TTP.
Several days following the commencement of antibiotic therapy, the platelets count and hemoglobin levels recovered to the normal range (Figure 1), while the lactate dehydrogenase levels decreased substantially to a normal level.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old previously healthy Syrian boy presented with a 1-day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain, along with a 1-month history of pallor, decreased activity, poor appetite, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 9-year-old boy presented with acute bleeding manifestations including epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena for 1 day, associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. Over the preceding month, he exhibited pallor, decreased activity, poor appetite, and weight loss, with noticeably worsening pallor during the week before admission. Under an initial diagnosis of atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), he received two doses of IVIG (1 g/kg) without response, followed by a 6-day trial of pulse IV methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day divided BID) with continued decline in hemoglobin and platelet counts. Upon identification of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, a 5-day course of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) transfusions was initiated, resulting in improvement in LDH and platelets.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Epidemiological exposure: recent consumption of a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese in Saudi Arabia. No other past medical conditions, hospitalizations, or allergies documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Hypoactivity, pallor, jaundice, decreased appetite, and weight loss. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced. Normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Abdomen: hepatosplenomegaly. Lymphatic: small palpable lymph nodes in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions. Remainder of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelets: 11 x 109/L (normal range: 150-400 x 109/L); Hemoglobin: 97 mg/L (normal range: 113-150 mg/J); WBC: 10.2 x 109/L (normal range: 4-12 x 109/L); Reticulocyte count: 2.45% (normal range: 0.5%-1.5%). Peripheral blood smear: schistocytes 1.45% with reactive toxic granulation in neutrophils; repeat smear showed schistocyte fragments >2.5% (normal range <1.5%). LDH: 1,021 U/L (normal range: 125-220 U/L); AST: 46 IU/L (normal range: 5-34 U/L); ALP: 143 IU/L (normal range: 156-369 U/L); Total bilirubin: 41.3 micromol/L (normal range: ~20.5 micromol/L); Direct bilirubin: 12.7 micromol/L (normal range: ~8.6 micromol/L). BUN and creatinine: normal. Urinalysis: hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation screen: normal; Fibrinogen: 1.72 g/L (normal range: 1.5-4.1 g/L); Coombs test: negative. Viral serologies (EBV, CMV, HIV): negative. QuantiFERON-TB Gold: negative. Abdominal ultrasound: splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest and abdominal CT scan: splenomegaly with no significant lymph node enlargement. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy: presence of megakaryocytes indicating peripheral immune destruction (ruling out leukemia/malignant infiltration); evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; morphologic evidence of frequent small epithelioid non-necrotizing granulomas. ADAMTS-13 assay: ADAMTS-13 activity 0.02 IU/ml (normal range: 0.40-1.30 IU/ml), antigen <0.01 IU/ml (normal range: 0.41-1.41 IU/ml), and anti-ADAMTS-13 antibodies >95 IU/ml (>15 IU/ml is considered positive).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis complicated by secondary acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
