The past medical history: 6 years ago, the patient was diagnosed with malaria in Africa and was treated with oral Quinine. Examination results after admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test: negative, blood cell analysis (five categories): Hb 83 g/L, Plt count 16 x 109/L, WBC count 2.82 x 109/L, NE percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture: methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The patient was hypersensitive to all quinolones, such as moxifloxacin. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Other tests such as hepatitis A virus and hepatitis B virus were also negative. Autoimmune liver, alpha fetoprotein (AFP), and carcinoembryonic antigen were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen (Figure 1). Chest and plain abdominal CT: cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The following diagnosis was considered: sepsis, fever of undetermined origin (FUO): infection? The tumor? Child-Pugh B stage of decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency mNGS blood test was performed to diagnose the fever with unknown cause. Even after being treated with moxifloxacin anti-infective therapy, the patient continued to suffer from recurrent fever. The blood mNGS test results on the 4th day of admission detected Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani (Figure 2). Suspected diagnosis: kala-azar. One day later, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention performed an rK39 antibody test and the result appeared positive; therefore, the clinical diagnosis of kala-azar was made, and the patient was subjected to sodium stibogluconate (SSG) treatment. According to the treatment standard of 90-130 mg/kg, a total of 9000 mg SSG was used (the maximum dose was given according to the weight of kg) and then stopped. The SSG was divided into 8 days, 600 mg on the first day and 1,200 mg/d after the first day. During the treatment, the patient persistently showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulation dysfunction, so repeated transfusion therapy was administered. After 3 days of the treatment, the patient's temperature decreased and the fever never returned. However, after 10 days of sodium stibogluconate treatment, the patient developed decreased blood pressure and multiple organ failure (progressive deterioration of coagulation, renal function, and liver function and continued thrombocytopenia). Septic shock was considered, and active anti-infection, fluid replenishment, and non-invasive ventilation were arranged. The patient's condition was not alleviated, and his family refused to adopt emergency treatment measures, such as endotracheal intubation, chest compressions, and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). The patient died 18 days after admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of recurrent high fever and a 1-month history of frequent watery diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to presentation, the patient developed abrupt afternoon fevers up to 39.9 °C accompanied by headache, diffuse myalgias, and nausea, which failed to respond to oral antipyretics and artemisinin. Following temporary defervescence in October 2020, persistent high fever up to 39.0 °C recurred 1 month prior to admission, accompanied by frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times daily).
subjective.past_medical_history: History of malaria diagnosed in Africa 6 years prior and treated with oral quinine. Allergy: reported hypersensitivity to quinolones.
subjective.review_of_systems: Afternoon fevers, headache, muscle pain, nausea, and severe watery diarrhea (>10 bowel movements per day).

objective.physical_examination: Febrile appearance. Abdominal examination revealed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and abdominal distension with signs of ascites.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 83 g/L, platelets: 16 x 10^9/L, WBC count: 2.82 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 84.0%, lymphocytes 8.0%), procalcitonin: 0.87 ng/mL. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. Negative testing: SARS-CoV-2 nucleic acid, Cryptococcus antigen, fungal (1,3)-beta-D-glucan (G test), galactomannan (GM test), Schistosoma japonicum IgG, Echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody, Plasmodium antigen and peripheral smear, hepatitis A and B serologies, autoimmune liver panel, AFP, and CEA. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen.
objective.advanced_workup: Plain computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen demonstrated liver cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion (Child-Pugh stage B).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) superimposed on decompensated cirrhosis and secondary methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteremia: blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) on hospital day 4 detected Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani; CDC rK39 antibody test was positive. The patient was treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG; 600 mg on day 1, then 1,200 mg/day for a cumulative 9,000 mg over 8 days), empirical moxifloxacin, fluid resuscitation, and blood product transfusions. Body temperature normalized within 3 days of initiating SSG. However, 10 days post-SSG, he developed refractory septic shock and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome with worsening coagulopathy, severe thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and liver failure. The family declined endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and CRRT, and the patient died 18 days after admission.

raw_case_text:
Of the 24 Leishmania strains typed at Inciensa and CLIOC, only one (internal code #108-19/CLIOC code IOCL3804) was positive after LRV1 examination, the same one typed as L. (V.) guyanensis, a not yet identified etiological agent of CL in Costa Rica. This strain was isolated from a male patient, 29 years of age, from one of the northernmost regions of the country, Cutris de San Carlos, of the Alajuela province. On the right side of the neck the patient had a 5 cm (Fig. 1A), 3 months old, deep ulcer, with pruritic and sanguine-purulent tissue. Below his right ear, and above this ulcer, he had a visibly swollen lymph node. No other symptom was reported. The diagnosis was confirmed locally at the Area de Salud de Santa Rosa de Pocosol, through light microscopy of a direct smear, and the stained slide, along with culture media seeded with lesion aspirate, were send to Inciensa for confirmation and species characterisation. This strain was identified as L. (V.) guyanensis by isoenzyme electrophoresis, routinely used for Leishmania typing by the CLIOC and confirmed by sequencing of a hsp70 fragment amplified by PCR. The obtained sequence (GenBank  accession ON075820) was aligned with 32 other Leishmania hsp70 sequences retrieved from GenBank and clearly clustered with L. (V.) guyanensis sequences (Fig. 1B).
One typical RT-PCR product gel is shown in Fig. 2, illustrating the confirmation of one, out of the 24 strains, as positive for the endosymbiont. Nested LRV RT-PCR and parasitic actin tests are not show herein. The amplified product chosen for sequencing was the longest one (corresponding to Fig. 2A), since this fragment displays approximately 850 base pairs (bp) corresponding to part of the orf1 region and the beginning of the orf2 region, including the portion responsible for encoding the viral capsid protein. 
Assessing the relationship between sample and reference strains we produced a tree (Fig. 2B) that shows two distinct groups separating the main Leishmania (Viannia) species harbouring virus: L. (V.) guyanensis and L. (V.) braziliensis. The #108-19 sample clustered with the LRV1 sequences from L. (V.) guyanensis strains, confirming the identification of this strain, which was previously characterise through isoenzyme electrophoresis and hsp70 sequence analysis. The #108-19 LRV1 sequence grouped with other LRV1 sequences from the Northeast of the Brazilian Amazon region and from the French Guiana (Fig. 2C). It was more distantly related to sequences from the Amazonas and Rondonia states of Brazil (northwest Amazonian region) and Bolivia, which could indicate a geographic association.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presented with a 3-month history of a deep ulcerated lesion on the right neck and an adjacent swollen cervical lymph node.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a slowly progressive, pruritic, deep ulcerative lesion on the right side of his neck over the course of 3 months, accompanied by sanguineous-purulent discharge and enlargement of an adjacent ipsilateral cervical lymph node.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Cutris de San Carlos, Alajuela Province, northern Costa Rica; no other medical history reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Lesional pruritus; denies fever, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed a 5-cm deep ulcerated lesion on the right lateral neck with a pruritic base and sanguine-purulent tissue. Directly superior to the ulcer below the right ear, an enlarged, visibly swollen lymph node was palpable. No other cutaneous lesions or physical abnormalities were detected.
objective.routine_investigations: Light microscopy of a direct smear from the lesion base was performed locally at the Area de Salud de Santa Rosa de Pocosol.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis harboring Leishmania RNA virus 1 (LRV1): direct light microscopy of the lesion smear confirmed Leishmania amastigotes; aspirate culture followed by multilocus isoenzyme electrophoresis at CLIOC and Sanger sequencing of an amplified Hsp70 gene fragment (GenBank ON075820) definitively identified Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis; nested RT-PCR and sequencing of an 850-bp fragment spanning orf1/orf2 confirmed infection with the viral endosymbiont LRV1.

raw_case_text:
In this case report we present a case of 54 years old male patient of Chinese descent who presented to the clinic with a complaint of mobility restriction on right lower extremity for 40 years. Upon investigation, the patient was found to have a history of right sided hip joint TB at the age of 14. The patient had increasing pain on his right lower extremity with restriction of movements especially abduction and external rotation. After seeking medical consultation, a battery of tests were conducted that led to the diagnosis. The Tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) test was conducted in the clinic which was positive as was demonstrated by the size of the induration formed at the site of infiltration. The patient had received anti- TB chemotherapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol along with prophylactic antibiotics to prevent the secondary infections. The patient was not clear about the exact duration of the therapy. A progressive restriction on the right hip joint had ensued after a short time post therapy. But further intervention however was not sought since there was a certain degree of alleviation in patient's condition. After a few years the movement restrictions had grown even more severe accompanied by pain while maneuvering the joint. On presentation, the patient had 0 degree abduction, internal and external rotation. Recent radiological findings showed right hip joint fusion along with deterioration of the articular surfaces [Figure 1]. The patient didn't suffer from any other systemic condition.
After admittance to the Qilu Hospital of Shandong University, all the required tests were carried out that included blood work, microbiological assessment, chest and spine X-rays, CT scans, in order to exclude the persistent tuberculosis lesions in any other organ thus ultimately omitting any contraindication for the total hip arthroplasty. Sputum and urine cultures were negative. The routine blood work showed an elevated Erythrocytic Sedimentation Rate (ESR 87 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (CRP 75 mg/L). The diagnosis was made from the patient's history, clinical symptoms, radiological data and the histopathological reports from the surgically extricated tissue that showed granulomatous inflammatory tissue with strains of acid-fast bacilli which was confirmed as M. tuberculosis bacilli by the microbiological testing. However a prior attempt to aspirate the synovial fluid for culture was unsuccessful. The patient was put on anti-tuberculous drug regimen including isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for a period of 3 months before arranging the surgical procedure.
Total hip arthroplasty was performed during which an excessive callus formation was observed around the femoral neck which was chiseled out from the intact bone cortex as far as possible. The inter-operative tissues were preserved for a histopathological analysis. An acetabular cup of optimal measurement was set along with a high cross linking polyethylene sleeve, then a metallic traditional femoral component was set. After reduction, the joint movements were evaluated where a flexion of 90 , abduction of 30  was attained. The X-rays taken post-surgery showed proper prosthetic alignment [Figure 2]. The postoperative recovery was unremarkable for any complication and the patient was discharged in 15 days after the surgery. Regular follow-ups were arranged to monitor the patient's condition and he was counseled to refrain from activities that put extra strain on the weight-bearing joints. No aberrant lesions were detected in lungs or bladder or genital organs. Chest [Figure 3] and spine X-rays were devoid of any lesions thus excluding the co-existence of a pulmonary or any other extrapulmonary TB. The same regimen of anti-TB drugs as mentioned earlier was continued for one year postoperatively. Timely follow-ups were conducted for a period of 24 months during which the patient presented with a normal gait and no complaint of pain at the affected side.
OATs are the most common forms of extrapulmonary TB (El Titi et al.). However; the obscurity of the symptoms puts many hurdles on the path to its early diagnosis. Most patients only present with joint swelling and pain. According to a recent case study presented by Mohammed J et al. only 38% of the patients reviewed showed some systemic symptoms of tuberculosis like low-grade fever and night sweats while there was no systemic signs in the rest of the cases thus there was an average of 2 years of delay in diagnosis (Al-Sayyad & Abumunaser). The delay in diagnosis in the forms of extrapulmonary TB involving sacroiliac joint might be caused by the examination traditionally carried out with patient in the supine position and also due to the physicians failure to perform the sacroiliac joint pain provocation maneuvers (Babhulkar & Pande; Laslett & Williams). OAT usually manifests as a monoarticular arthritic condition rather than affecting multiple joints (Grosskopf et al.). Frequently Mycobacterial infection of the sacroiliac joint may present as psoas abscess and may not be diagnosed till the spontaneous drainage into the groin (Feldmann et al.; Kim et al.; Richter et al.).
Total hip arthroplasty or total hip replacement has now emerged as one of the most common orthopedic procedures performed for debilitating lesions of the hip joint that lead to restriction of joint movement, pain and deteriorates the patient's living standards. The therapeutic outcome of THA has been substantial in the treatment of the osteoarthritis in comparison to the conventional techniques with obvious alleviation in pain symptoms, joint movements as well as the patient's living standards. THA is also the established method of treatment in cases of dormant TB of hips (Tulsi; Kim et al.). The implementation of THA in the cases of active tuberculous coxitis has been a debated concept. There are certain risks involved with THA on patients with tuberculous arthritis which can't be undermined. There is a potential risk of reactivation of the TB infection postoperatively. Many orthopedic surgeons argue that the risks outweigh the benefits thus they suggest that anti-TB drug therapy should be started preoperatively for an optimal duration (Babhulkar & Pande; Kim et al.; Sidhu & Singh; Xun-wu et al.). In a study presented by Sidhu AS et al., the recurrent case of tuberculous arthritis was attended with a three month course of preoperative drug therapy followed by total hip replacement after which an extended duration of drug therapy was continued postoperatively (Sidhu & Singh). There have been few reports which demonstrated various cases of peri-prosthetic tuberculous infection post surgery. M Kaya et al. presented a case of peri-prosthetic tuberculous infection in the patient with history of THA for osteoarthritis performed 9 years earlier (Kaya et al.). Walczak P et al. presented a case report of a patient with a history of tuberculous hip in 58 years earlier who underwent THA 9 years before (Walczak et al.). Thus proper prophylactic measures are crucial while undertaking this treatment method.
The limitation of our paper is its being a single patient case-report however we believe that there are very few case-reports on the recurrence of the TB of hip after a considerably long duration. Although detailed history was collected from the patient regarding compliance to the medication, it can however still be one of the fators for the recurrence of TB after a considerably long duration of time. TB is considered quiescent after 10 years of remission while some authors prolong the duration to 20 years (Kim et al.; Hardinge et al.). In our case the TB had relapsed after 40 years of purported remission. The therapeutic approach was extrapolated from the techniques chosen for an active TB infection of hip and there was no relapse of the disease for as long as 12 months after cessation of a year-long postoperative anti-tuberculous drug therapy although a longer follow up is still crucial.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male presented with restricted mobility and pain in his right lower extremity, especially upon abduction and external rotation, lasting 40 years.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 54-year-old male of Chinese descent presented with severe right hip movement restriction and pain. He had contracted right hip joint tuberculosis at age 14 and was treated medically. Following completion of therapy, he experienced progressive right hip restriction, which gradually intensified over four decades with increasing joint pain on maneuver.
subjective.past_medical_history: Right-sided hip joint tuberculosis at age 14 treated with antituberculous chemotherapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) and prophylactic antibiotics (exact duration unclear). No other systemic conditions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Increasing pain in right lower extremity and joint stiffness on maneuvering. Denies systemic symptoms such as fever or night sweats. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right hip joint: 0 degrees abduction, 0 degrees internal rotation, and 0 degrees external rotation. No aberrant lesions in lungs, bladder, or genital organs.
objective.routine_investigations: ESR 87 mm/hr, CRP 75 mg/L. Sputum and urine cultures negative. Tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test positive. Plain chest and spine radiographs negative for active pulmonary or extra-articular lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Radiographs and CT scans of right hip: joint fusion (ankylosis) with severe deterioration of articular surfaces. Attempted synovial fluid aspiration for culture was unsuccessful. Total hip arthroplasty performed with excision of extensive callus around femoral neck; intraoperative tissue histopathology revealed granulomatous inflammatory tissue.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Recurrent/reactivated right hip joint tuberculosis after 40-year remission resulting in bony ankylosis, confirmed by histopathology of surgically extricated tissue showing granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli and microbiological testing confirming Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Synovial fluid aspiration prior to surgery was non-diagnostic; chest and spine X-rays and sputum/urine cultures excluded active extra-articular disease. Management & Outcome: Treated preoperatively with a 3-month course of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by total hip arthroplasty (acetabular cup, high cross-linked polyethylene sleeve, metallic femoral component). Postoperative joint motion reached 90 degrees flexion and 30 degrees abduction with correct prosthetic alignment. Antituberculous therapy was continued for 1 year postoperatively. At 24-month follow-up, patient ambulated with normal gait and remained pain-free and recurrence-free.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male patient was referred to Mirriah District Hospital located at 20 km from Zinder, the regional capital, for a fever associated with vomiting and sudden onset of a consciousness disorder. A week earlier, he had received malaria rapid diagnostic tests (RDT), positive result reflecting the presence of Plasmodium falciparum antigen in the blood. This prompted the initiation of an antimalarial treatment based on quinine injection at a rate of 25 mg/kg/day, which was discontinued after 3 days. Treatment was resumed 4 days later after the reappearance of symptoms. On the third day after resumption of treatment, corresponding to 10 days after the onset of symptoms, the patient was referred to Zinder National Hospital following a clinical aggravation marked by impaired consciousness. On arrival, clinical examination revealed a fever at 39 C, impaired consciousness with a Glasgow score of 11, mucous membrane pallor, conjunctival jaundice (Figure 1(a)), tachypnea with 40 cycles/min, bronchial rales, and tachycardia at 120 beats/min.
The haemodynamic state was stable with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. Urine was Coca-Cola colored (Figure 2), which led to the diagnosis of BWF. Test strip urine examination revealed hemoglobinuria at 2 plus, bilirubinuria 3 plus, proteinuria 2 plus, and absence of urobilinogens, red blood cells, and leucocytes. The malaria RDT was positive, while the thick peripheral blood smear was negative. Biological examinations showed leucocytosis of 15000 elements/mm3, normochromic anaemia with a hemoglobin level of 4 g/dl, and a normal platelet count of 194,000/mm3. The direct Coombs test was negative. Urea: 74.9 mmol/L, serum creatinine: 559.6 mumol/L, proteinuria: 0.56 g/24 h, ASAT: 334 IU/L, ALAT: 185 IU/L, CRP: 92 mg/L, blood ionogram: 128 mEq/L of sodium and 5 mEq/L of potassium, TP: 100%, INR: 0.99, TCA: 29.5, TQ: 12 sec, and a blood bilirubin level of 200 mg/L predominantly unconjugated. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys, discrete renal dedifferentiation, and vesicular sludge. This presentation required dialysis for uremic syndrome. The patient received 3 hemodialysis sessions with transfusion of erythrocyte concentrates. The antimalarial treatment was continued with an intramuscular artemether derivative. Clinical status and renal function normalized after 7 days. The patient was discharged cured.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presenting with fever, vomiting, dark urine, and altered consciousness for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever and vomiting ten days prior to referral. One week earlier, he received an incomplete 3-day course of injectable quinine, which was interrupted and restarted four days later upon recrudescence of symptoms. On the third day of re-treatment, his condition deteriorated with impaired consciousness, tachypnea, and passage of black, cola-colored urine.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant chronic medical illnesses documented. Received intermittent intramuscular/intravenous quinine therapy over the preceding ten days.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 39.0 °C, pulse rate 120 beats/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Neurological: Impaired consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale 11/15. HEENT: Severe conjunctival jaundice and mucosal pallor. Respiratory: Bilateral bronchial rales. Urinary: Passage of dark 'Coca-Cola' colored urine.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 4 g/dL (severe normochromic anemia), white blood cell count 15,000/mm3, platelet count 194,000/mm3. Direct Coombs test: Negative. Biochemistry: Serum urea 74.9 mmol/L, serum creatinine 559.6 micromol/L, total bilirubin 200 mg/L (predominantly unconjugated), AST 334 IU/L, ALT 185 IU/L, C-reactive protein 92 mg/L, sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 5 mEq/L, TP 100%, INR 0.99, TCA 29.5 sec, TQ 12 sec. Urinalysis (dipstick): Hemoglobinuria 2+, bilirubinuria 3+, proteinuria 2+ (24-hour proteinuria 0.56 g/24h), with absence of intact red blood cells or leukocytes. Renal ultrasound: Normal-sized kidneys with discrete parenchymal dedifferentiation and gallbladder sludge.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Blackwater fever (BWF; severe quinine-induced intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuric acute kidney injury) triggered by Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) was positive for P. falciparum antigen, while thick peripheral blood smear was negative (parasite clearance following prior quinine administration). Immune hemolytic anemia was ruled out by negative direct Coombs test.
Plan & Outcome: Quinine was immediately discontinued. Antimalarial therapy was transitioned to intramuscular artemether. The patient was managed for acute uremic syndrome with three hemodialysis sessions, supportive fluid therapy, and packed red blood cell transfusions. Clinical condition and renal function normalized within 7 days, and he was discharged cured.

raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old female presented with painful swelling in the left lateral neck region for 15 days. There was no erythema or heating sensation on neck area, and she had no symptoms of fever. Ten months earlier, she had undergone total thyroidectomy with central neck lymph node dissection due to PTC (T3N1aM0 by American Joint Committee on Cancer/International Union against Cancer Staging System 7th Edition), followed by radioactive iodine therapy and maintenance treatment with levothyroxine.
Thyroid function tests showed mildly suppressed thyrotropin-stimulating hormone (TSH; 0.01 mIU/L; normal range, 0.27-4.2 mIU/L) and elevated free thyroxine (fT4; 2.12 ng/dL; normal range, 0.93-1.70 ng/dL) concentrations. Her white blood cell and neutrophil counts were normal. No pathogens were cultured from her blood, stool, urine, or sputum.
Neck ultrasonography revealed a large heterogeneous echoic (cystic) mass in the left lateral neck (Figure 1) and computed tomography revealed a 3.3 x 5.6 cm sized thick-walled cystic lesion along left levels II, III, and IV (Figure 2). Cytologic examination of the dark brown colored fluid collected from the lesion by fine-needle aspiration showed many neutrophils and macrophages in necrotic background, but there was no evidence of malignancy (Figure 3). However, the mass was suspected of being a metastatic lymph node and was resected.
Intraoperative examination showed that mass was encapsulated and very highly adhesive to the internal jugular vein and around the tissue. There were no other abnormally enlarged lymph nodes. The mass contained dark brown colored fluid and some debris. Microscopic examination of the lymph node mass showed massive necrosis and immunohistochemistry clearly showed that the mass was a metastatic papillary carcinoma (Figure 4). Culture of the fluid showed the presence of Salmonella Typhi.
No postoperative complications occurred. The patient was treated with intravenous cephalosporin for 6 days; following antibiotic sensitivity testing of the cultured Salmonella Typhi, she was switched to oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days. Regular follow-up examinations have shown no evidence of additional metastasis, recurrence of metastasis, or residual infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old female presented with painful swelling in the left lateral neck for 15 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a painful swelling in the left lateral neck region of 15 days' duration. There was no local erythema, warmth, or fever. Ten months prior to presentation, she underwent total thyroidectomy with central neck lymph node dissection for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC, stage T3N1aM0), followed by radioactive iodine therapy and maintenance levothyroxine therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (AJCC/UICC 7th edition stage T3N1aM0) treated 10 months prior with total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine ablation and maintenance levothyroxine suppression therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Painful lateral neck swelling. Denies fever, chills, local erythema, warmth, or gastrointestinal complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Painful swelling/mass in the left lateral neck without erythema or increased local temperature. Afebrile.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell and neutrophil counts were normal. TSH was mildly suppressed at 0.01 mIU/L (normal range 0.27-4.2 mIU/L), and free T4 was elevated at 2.12 ng/dL (normal range 0.93-1.70 ng/dL). Blood, stool, urine, and sputum cultures were negative for pathogens.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck ultrasonography showed a large heterogeneous echoic (cystic) mass in the left lateral neck. Contrast-enhanced neck CT revealed a 3.3 x 5.6 cm thick-walled cystic lesion along left cervical levels II, III, and IV. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) yielded dark brown fluid; cytological examination demonstrated abundant neutrophils and macrophages in a necrotic background without malignant cells. Surgical excision revealed an encapsulated mass densely adherent to the internal jugular vein and adjacent tissues containing necrotic debris and dark brown fluid; histopathological and immunohistochemical examination confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with massive necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi abscess / bacterial infection localized within a necrotic metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma cervical lymph node. Fluid culture from the resected mass yielded Salmonella Typhi. Blood, stool, sputum, and urine cultures were all sterile.
Plan & Outcome: Complete surgical excision of the infected metastatic nodal mass without postoperative complications. Treated with intravenous cephalosporin for 6 days, then transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days based on antibiotic susceptibility testing of the S. Typhi isolate. Regular follow-up examinations showed no evidence of residual infection, local recurrence, or distant metastases.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old Pakistani male presented to the hospital with diarrhea and progressively worsening fatigue for ten days. Diarrhea was watery and did not contain any blood. He also complained of decreased appetite, pain while passing urine, and a reduction in the amount of urine for five days. There was no history of fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cough, skin rashes, or altered sensorium. The patient had no sick contacts and no history of eating food from outside. The patient was a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus for two years, was stabilized on metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and was not taking any other medication. He had a recent history of travel to Pakistan, and his symptoms developed during his return flight to Qatar.
On physical examination, the patient was febrile (38  C) and tachycardiac (104 beats per minute) with normal blood pressure and respiratory rate. The rest of the physical examination was non-significant.
Initial laboratory workup revealed pancytopenia, raised C-reactive protein (CRP), deranged liver enzymes, and elevated creatinine (830) (Table 1). Urinalysis did not show any significant blood cells or casts. Further workup revealed raised creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin, giving an impression of rhabdomyolysis (Table 1). There was no proteinuria, making diabetic nephropathy unlikely. An ultrasound of the urinary tract revealed bulky kidneys with normal echogenicity, with no features of chronic kidney injury or obstruction. Fluid resuscitation was initiated considering pre-renal AKI. The patient was also empirically started on intravenous (IV) Ceftriaxone 2 g daily, given the possibility of an infectious trigger. The stool sample was negative for Clostridium Difficile toxin, ova, or parasites. There was no bacterial growth in urine and stool samples; however, blood cultures grew Salmonella Typhi. Given his recent travel to Pakistan, antimicrobial coverage was escalated to renal adjusted dose of Meropenem (0.5 g every 12 h), considering the possibility of a resistant strain. Subsequently, the sensitivity results revealed a multidrug-resistant Salmonella Typhi (including ceftriaxone and azithromycin).
Over the next days, the patient's creatinine kept rising (Fig. 1), and he became oliguric. His symptoms had mildly improved with a reduction in diarrhea frequency and improvement in his appetite. On day 3, hemodialysis (HD) was initiated due to persistent oliguria and worsening renal parameters despite fluid resuscitation. The patient underwent 4 HD sessions over the next ten days with remarkable creatinine improvement (Fig. 1). On day seven, the patient began to produce urine, which reached up to 2 L per day by day 10. Creatinine normalized by day ten, and repeated blood cultures came negative. The patient took antimicrobials for 14 days (including one day of ceftriaxone and 13 days of meropenem) and was subsequently discharged asymptomatic with normal renal function.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old Pakistani male presented with watery diarrhea and worsening fatigue for 10 days, accompanied by decreased appetite, dysuria, and oliguria for 5 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Watery nonbloody diarrhea and progressively worsening fatigue began 10 days prior during a return flight to Qatar from Pakistan. Over the preceding 5 days, he developed anorexia, dysuria, and marked reduction in urine volume. He denied fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cough, skin rashes, or altered mental status.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years, stabilized on metformin 1000 mg twice daily; no other medications. Travel history: Recent travel to Pakistan. Denied sick contacts and eating food from outside.
subjective.review_of_systems: Decreased appetite, dysuria, oliguria; denies fever, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, cough, rashes, or altered sensorium. Home medication: metformin 1000 mg twice daily.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (temperature 38 °C), tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats/min), normal blood pressure and respiratory rate. Rest of physical examination non-significant.
objective.routine_investigations: Pancytopenia; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP); deranged liver enzymes; elevated serum creatinine (830 umol/L). Elevated creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin, consistent with rhabdomyolysis. Urinalysis: no significant blood cells, casts, or proteinuria. Stool testing: negative for Clostridium difficile toxin, ova, parasites, and bacterial pathogens; urine culture negative. Renal ultrasound: bulky kidneys with normal echogenicity, without features of chronic kidney injury or obstruction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Multidrug-resistant Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) complicated by rhabdomyolysis and severe oliguric acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis. Blood cultures isolated Salmonella Typhi, with sensitivity testing demonstrating resistance to multiple drugs including ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Regimen: Initially received fluid resuscitation and empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily (1 day). Following blood culture growth and travel history, escalated to renal-adjusted IV meropenem (0.5 g every 12 h) for 13 days (total 14 days of antimicrobials). Due to progressive oliguria and rising creatinine, hemodialysis was initiated on day 3; he underwent 4 sessions over 10 days. Diarrhea and appetite improved; spontaneous urine production resumed on day 7 (2 L/day by day 10), and creatinine normalized by day 10. Repeat blood cultures were negative, and he was discharged asymptomatic with normal renal function.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old unmarried male presented with an 8-month history of tense fluid-filled lesions over the back of both hands leaving behind erosions and scars. There was history of photosensitivity, weight loss and high-risk behavior over the past 1 year. He reported moderate alcohol intake in the past, but denied drinking during the previous 1 year. There was no history suggestive of liver disease or of having similar complaints in the family. Physical examination revealed multiple erosions with crusts, scars over the dorsum of both hands [Figure 1] and face. Minimal hypertrichosis of the face was present [Figure 2].
Examination of oral mucosa and genitals were within the normal limits.
Blood investigations revealed: Hemoglobin level 13.4 g/L, total count 4,200 cells/cumm, iron 146 mcg/mL, ferritin 429.2 ng/mL. Except for the elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels of 128 U/L, the remaining parameters of liver function tests were within normal limits. On serological testing, patient was found to be HIV positive with a CD4 count of 32 cells/mm3. Serological screening for hepatitis-B and C were negative. No abnormality was detected on abdominal ultrasonography.
Examination of urine under Wood's light revealed a bright pink fluorescence consistent with the presence of porphyrins [Figure 3]. Histopathological examination revealed a subepidermal bulla with scanty lymphocytic infiltrate and hemorrhage. There was deposition of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stained material around the dermal capillary blood vessels [Figure 4].
Direct immunofluorescence study showed linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane. Urinary porphyrin levels were elevated.
Based on the clinical presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of PCT was made. The patient was treated with low-dose hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice weekly, antiretroviral drugs and was advised photo protective measures. Three months following the initiation of treatment, there was clinical remission of the skin lesions [Figure 5] with a CD4 count of 232 cells/mm3.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old male presenting with an 8-month history of tense fluid-filled bullae on the dorsal aspects of both hands, resulting in erosions, crusting, and scars.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed tense, fluid-filled bullous lesions over the dorsum of both hands over an 8-month period, which ruptured leaving erosions, crusts, and permanent scarring. He reported marked photosensitivity, progressive weight loss, and high-risk sexual behavior over the preceding year. He reported moderate alcohol consumption in the past, but completely abstained during the previous year.
subjective.past_medical_history: Denied history of chronic liver disease, previous medical illnesses, or family history of porphyria or photosensitive dermatoses. Past moderate alcohol consumption (none in prior 12 months). Epidemiological history: high-risk sexual behavior over the past year.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cutaneous photosensitivity, tense hand blisters, and unintentional weight loss; negative for abdominal pain, dark urine, or joint pain. Home medications: none. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: multiple tense bullae, erosions with crusts, and atrophic scars over the dorsum of both hands and face; minimal facial hypertrichosis; oral mucosa and external genitalia normal. General examination: afebrile, vital signs normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 13.4 g/dL (transcribed 13.4 g/L); total leukocyte count: 4,200 cells/cumm; serum iron: 146 mcg/dL (transcribed mcg/mL); serum ferritin: 429.2 ng/mL. Liver function tests: AST elevated at 128 U/L; other hepatic parameters normal. Viral hepatitis serologies: HBsAg and anti-HCV negative. Abdominal ultrasonography: normal, no hepatomegaly or focal liver lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Urine examination under Wood's lamp: bright pink fluorescence consistent with elevated urinary porphyrins. Skin punch biopsy: subepidermal bulla with festooning of dermal papillae, scanty lymphocytic infiltrate, hemorrhage, and PAS-positive material deposition around upper dermal blood vessels. Direct immunofluorescence: granular perivascular deposition of IgG and C3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) triggered by severe human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection / AIDS (CD4+ T-cell count 32 cells/mm3). Confirmed by reactive HIV serology, characteristic coral-pink urine Wood's lamp fluorescence, subepidermal blister with festooning and perivascular PAS deposition, and perivascular IgG/C3 direct immunofluorescence. Chronic hepatitis B and C ruled out by negative serologies; primary hepatic cirrhosis ruled out by ultrasound and LFTs. Management & Outcome: Advised strict photoprotection and broad-spectrum sunscreens. Initiated on repeated small-volume phlebotomies (350 mL every 2 weeks) and low-dose chloroquine (125 mg twice weekly). Following transaminase stabilization, HAART with tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz was started. Cutaneous blisters completely ceased, erosions healed with minimal scarring, and remission was maintained at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man with complaints of dry cough and breathlessness for 15 days was referred to the Radiology Department for Computed Tomography of the thorax. His chest X-ray showed cavitation and fibrosis with patchy consolidation in the right upper zone. Patient was a diagnosed case of sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and had received the complete course of antitubercular treatment 2 years earlier. On present Computed Tomography of the thorax (axial images), there were multiple thick-walled cavitary lesions in the posterior segment of right upper lobe with multiple parenchymal nodular opacities indicative of endobronchial spread of infection [Figure 1]. In addition to these findings, there was an air-filled tubular structure alongside the esophagus on the left side, beginning at the level of the T2 vertebra and communicating with the normal esophagus at the level of carina [Figure 2]. We considered a provisional diagnosis of pulsion diverticula or possibly proximal esophageal duplication as an incidental finding along with the findings of sequelae of post-primary pulmonary tuberculosis.
Barium swallow study [Figure 3] was done to rule out diverticulum. On barium study, a contrast-filled tubular structure was seen alongside the normal esophagus on the left side extending from the T2 to the T4 vertebral level and communicating with the esophagus both superiorly and inferiorly. Fluoroscopically, swallowing mechanism was normal with normal mucosa and presence of peristalsis in the duplicated segment. There was no evidence of any aspiration or gastroesophageal reflux. Gastroesophageal junction was normal. With these definitive findings, diagnosis of incomplete communicating tubular duplication of upper esophagus was considered.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with dry cough and breathlessness for 15 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 15-day history of persistent dry cough and exertional breathlessness. He was referred to the Radiology Department for computed tomography of the thorax after a routine chest radiograph demonstrated upper zone cavitary and fibrotic changes.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed case of sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years previously, having completed a full course of antitubercular treatment.
subjective.review_of_systems: Dry cough, breathlessness. Denies hemoptysis, fever, dysphagia, regurgitation, or chest pain.

objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiograph showed cavitation, fibrosis, and patchy consolidation in the right upper zone.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic computed tomography (axial images) demonstrated multiple thick-walled cavitary lesions in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe accompanied by multiple parenchymal nodular opacities indicative of endobronchial spread; an incidental air-filled tubular structure was visualized alongside the esophagus on the left side, arising at the T2 vertebral level and communicating with the esophagus at the carina. Barium swallow study confirmed a contrast-filled tubular structure adjacent to the left esophagus extending from T2 to T4 vertebral levels, communicating superiorly and inferiorly, with normal peristalsis and mucosal folds; no aspiration or gastroesophageal reflux was noted; gastroesophageal junction was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Cavitary sequelae of post-primary pulmonary tuberculosis with endobronchial spread, and an incidental congenital incomplete communicating tubular duplication of the upper esophagus.
Diagnostic confirmation: Thoracic CT and barium fluoroscopy demonstrated communicating tubular esophageal duplication from T2 to T4 with preserved mucosal architecture, excluding pulsion diverticulum, in conjunction with thick-walled right upper lobe tuberculous cavities.
Management and outcome: Radiographic and fluoroscopic confirmation completed; patient was evaluated for post-primary tuberculous reactivation and conservative follow-up of benign congenital esophageal duplication.

raw_case_text: Case 9: A 25 year old patient that reported exanthema and pruritus in the third trimester of gestation. Her IgM serology was positive for Zika and the PRNT90% was positive for neutralizing antibodies. At 37 weeks of gestation, her baby girl was born by cesarean with a cephalic circumference of 27 cm. The placenta weighed 565 g.

subjective.chief_complaint: 25-year-old pregnant female in the third trimester of gestation presenting with exanthema and pruritus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed an acute pruritic exanthema during the third trimester of gestation. At 37 weeks of gestation, she delivered a baby girl by cesarean section who was found to have severe microcephaly.
subjective.past_medical_history: Third trimester of pregnancy; no prior chronic medical conditions reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus; denies other acute complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Maternal: Cutaneous exanthema. Neonatal: Female infant delivered at 37 weeks gestation by cesarean section with a cephalic circumference of 27 cm (severe microcephaly). Placental weight was 565 g.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Congenital Zika syndrome with severe neonatal microcephaly following maternal third-trimester Zika virus infection. Maternal infection was confirmed by positive Zika IgM serology and positive PRNT90% neutralizing antibodies. The infant girl was delivered at 37 weeks gestation with severe microcephaly (head circumference 27 cm; placental weight 565 g).

raw_case_text: The male patient was born on June 26, 1986, in Paulistana municipality, Piaui State. He was hospitalized at the Natan Portella Institute of Tropical Diseases (IDTNP) on seven occasions between the years 2009 and 2011, with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar confirmed by laboratory examination and tests including the finding of parasite amastigotes in bone marrow smears. The patient received all the recommended treatments, including the pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at a dose of 3 mg/kg/d, in three subsequent hospitalizations) and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other d, for a total of 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During the other two hospitalizations, the patient presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After the all the possibilities of treatment with medications were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on the blood count due to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012, he was hospitalized for the surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2 + / 4 +), fever (38.5  C), dehydration (2 + / 4 +), distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation and splenomegaly (8 cm below the left costal margin). Laboratory tests detected anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia and high levels of ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein). On May 2, 2012 splenectomy was carried out and the patient was discharged 5 d after surgery. The first 24 h of the patient's postoperative period were held in the ICU (Intensive Care Unit) and due to bleeding during surgery, the patient received three packed red blood cell transfusions, evolving with stable hemoglobin and hematocrit values. The spleen measurements were 25 x 17 x 9 cm, weighing 1860 g. The histopathological study confirmed the presence of Leishmania parasites in the surgical specimen. The patient was referred to the IDTNP, where he underwent a new course of amphotericin B and was discharged on the 8th day of hospitalization. He remained asymptomatic, with improvement observed in laboratory parameters no further relapse of leishmaniasis and has been followed-up at the outpatient clinic for more than seven years after the surgery. Unfortunately we have no images of this patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male with recurrent visceral leishmaniasis and persistent hypersplenism presented for elective splenectomy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 25-year-old male with a history of recurrent visceral leishmaniasis who had been hospitalized seven times between 2009 and 2011 at the Natan Portella Institute of Tropical Diseases (IDTNP). He received standard courses of pentavalent antimonials, liposomal amphotericin B, and pentamidine, yet consistently experienced transient symptomatic improvement followed by clinical relapse. Due to refractory hypersplenism and persistent severe pancytopenia despite exhausting all pharmacotherapies, he was admitted in January 2012 for scheduled therapeutic splenectomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent visceral leishmaniasis (seven hospital admissions between 2009 and 2011; treated with glucantime 20 mg Sb5+/kg/day for 30 days, liposomal amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day for 14 days across three admissions, and pentamidine 4 mg/kg every other day for 15 doses); recurrent transfusion-dependent anemia requiring multiple packed red blood cell transfusions. Negative HIV serology. Origin: Paulistana municipality, Piaui State, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Recurrent fevers, severe fatigue, abdominal fullness and distension. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General: mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+). Abdomen: distended with mild tenderness on deep palpation, massive splenomegaly extending 8 cm below the left costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: severe anemia and leukopenia (pancytopenia profile). Inflammatory markers: elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). Serum protein electrophoresis: marked hypergammaglobulinemia. HIV serology: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Splenectomy surgical specimen: spleen measured 25 x 17 x 9 cm and weighed 1,860 g. Histopathological examination of splenic tissue: performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Drug-resistant, relapsing visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with severe secondary hypersplenism.
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological analysis of the resected spleen confirmed the presence of Leishmania parasites within the splenic tissue; prior episodes were microbiologically confirmed by parasite amastigotes in bone marrow smears.
Differentials ruled out: HIV co-infection (negative serology) and primary lymphoproliferative disorders.
Treatment and clinical course: Underwent therapeutic splenectomy on May 2, 2012. Managed in the intensive care unit for the first 24 hours postoperatively; received three packed red blood cell transfusions for intraoperative blood loss, stabilizing hemoglobin and hematocrit. Transferred to IDTNP for an additional consolidation course of amphotericin B and discharged on postoperative day 8. Laboratory parameters and blood counts completely normalized, with no further relapse observed over seven years of outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
The index patient, a 26-year-old woman, was admitted to the infectious disease ward of a university hospital with a temperature of 40 C and myalgias 3 days after she returned from a 3-week trip to Cambodia and Thailand. Dengue virus infection was subsequently diagnosed, and mild hepatitis and a rash developed. She was discharged in good condition after the fever subsided. On the day of admission of the index patient (day 0i), a nurse sustained a needlestick injury with a hollow needle that had been used for drawing blood from the index patient. The needlestick resulted in a bleeding puncture wound that was immediately treated with an antiseptic. The index patient did not report any high-risk activity for HIV or hepatitis B virus, and the nurse had been immunized against hepatitis B virus. Therefore, no specific postexposure prophylaxis was performed. The nurse had previously been in good health and had not traveled outside Germany in the preceding 12 months.
Four days after the needlestick, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias developed in the healthcare worker, for which she took ibuprofen. Seven days later, when she was experiencing an intense headache and noticed a macular rash on her trunk, she sought treatment from a local doctor (day 0n). Physical examination showed bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. On day 2n, she visited our service, where dengue virus infection was diagnosed by using a Light Cycler (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) method. Her symptoms lessened gradually over the course of 4 weeks, and she was on sick leave for 5 weeks. The time frame of the respective clinical presentation and the virologic results of the index patient and the nurse are shown in the Figure; laboratory data are presented in the Table.
Serologic studies were performed with the PanBio dengue immunoglobulin (Ig) M capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and PanBio dengue indirect IgG ELISA (PanBio Ltd., Brisbane, Australia); arbitrary units relative to a simultaneously measured calibrator >11 were considered positive. For detecting virus RNA, RNA was prepared from 140 microL of serum by using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer's instructions. To detect specific dengue virus RNA, we adapted a TaqMan-reverse transcription (RT)-PCR to detect any of the four serotypes by using the following: degenerated forward primer (DEN FP), reverse primer (DEN RP); and probe (DEN P): DEN FP 5 AAggACTAgAggTTAKAggAgACCC3 , DEN RP 5 ggCCYTCTgTgCCTggAWTgATg3  and the probe DEN P 5  FAM-AACAgCATATTgACgCTgggARAgACC-TAMRA-3 . RT-PCR conditions for the Light Cycler (Roche Diagnostics) were: RT at 61 C for 20 min, activation at 95 C for 5 min, and 40 cycles of PCR at 95 C for 15 s, 60 C for 60 s. We used the RNA Master Hybridization Probes Kit (Roche Diagnostics) with 500-nM primers and 200-nM probes. The kit includes an aptamer-blocked Thermus thermophilus DNA polymerase, which performs RT and, once the aptamer drops out at activation, hotstarts PCR amplification.

subjective.chief_complaint: A female healthcare worker presented with fever, intense headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and a macular rash 11 days after an occupational hollow-bore needlestick exposure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A nurse sustained a deep bleeding needlestick puncture injury from a hollow needle while drawing blood from a febrile traveler returning from Southeast Asia. Four days post-exposure, she developed headache, generalized myalgias, and arthralgias, managed symptomatically with ibuprofen. Seven days after initial symptom onset, she experienced an intense headache and noticed a macular exanthem spreading across her trunk, prompting clinical evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy healthcare worker in Germany without foreign travel in the preceding 12 months. Documented immunization against hepatitis B virus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported intense headache, generalized myalgias, arthralgias, fatigue, and cutaneous rash. Denied nausea, vomiting, or mucosal bleeding. Home medication included ibuprofen.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature elevation was noted. Dermatologic examination revealed a macular rash across the trunk. Head and neck examination revealed bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was otherwise normal without focal deficits or hemorrhagic lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematologic and biochemical profiles: Serial laboratory evaluations demonstrated leukopenia, mild thrombocytopenia, and transaminitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Nosocomially acquired Dengue virus infection via percutaneous hollow-bore needlestick transmission, confirmed by positive Dengue virus RT-PCR (TaqMan LightCycler assay) and subsequent seroconversion with positive Dengue IgM and IgG capture ELISA. Ruled out hepatitis B and HIV transmission based on negative source screening and post-exposure monitoring.
Treatment and outcome: Managed conservatively and supportively with oral analgesics and rest. Symptoms resolved gradually over 4 weeks with complete recovery, and she resumed work following 5 weeks of medical leave.

raw_case_text: The patient was a 37-year-old Japanese man without a significant medical history. Two weeks prior to admission, he had returned to Japan from Nigeria after a 6-month business visit. He had taken no chemoprophylaxis for malaria. He had not used any repellent and was sometimes bitten by mosquitoes. Six days prior to admission, he experienced general malaise, fever, and headache. Five days prior to admission, he visited a clinic nearby and was diagnosed with common cold. Loxoprofen and cefaclor were prescribed. Three days prior to admission, he visited another clinic and was again diagnosed with common cold. His symptoms had not improved, and his mental state appeared altered. He was transferred to the Japanese Red Cross Narita Hospital by ambulance. On admission, his mental status was E4V4M6. His vital signs were as follows: blood pressure of 138/87 mm Hg, heart rate of 126 beats/min, body temperature of 38.5 C, respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation on room air of 98%. His physical examination results revealed slight jaundice on the conjunctiva. Laboratory test results revealed anemia with a hemoglobin level of 12.5 g/dL, thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 17 000 /muL, high bilirubinemia with a total bilirubin level of 5.1 mg/dL, and elevated inflammatory markers, with elevated C-reactive protein levels of 23.14 mg/dL. The examination of his peripheral blood smear showed P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes with a parasitemia index of 5.4% (Figure 1). A rapid immunographic test (Binax NOW Malaria Test; Binax, Portland, OR) result for P. falciparum was positive. P. falciparum infection was later confirmed by performing polymerase chain reaction. We administered intravenous quinine. After an initial increase in his parasitemia index to 8.6%, it decreased to <0.1% on hospital day 3. Intravenous quinine was replaced with artemether/lumefantrine and was continued for 3 days. He recovered fully and was discharged on hospital day 10.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presenting with fever, headache, malaise for six days, and altered mental status.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed general malaise, fever, and headache six days prior to admission. He visited two outpatient clinics five and three days prior to presentation, where he was diagnosed with a common cold and treated with loxoprofen and cefaclor without improvement. His mental state deteriorated progressively, prompting emergency ambulance transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history. Epidemiological exposure: Returned to Japan from Nigeria two weeks prior to admission following a 6-month business visit; took no antimalarial chemoprophylaxis, used no repellent, and reported mosquito bites.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological: Mental status Glasgow Coma Scale E4V4M6 (confused, altered). Vital signs: Blood pressure 138/87 mmHg, heart rate 126 beats/min, body temperature 38.5 °C, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, SpO2 98% on room air. General: Scleral/conjunctival icterus noted on examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; platelet count 17,000/microL; total bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL; C-reactive protein 23.14 mg/dL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe cerebral Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Peripheral blood smear examination demonstrated P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes with an initial parasitemia index of 5.4%, rapid immunochromatographic test (BinaxNOW) was positive for P. falciparum, and infection was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous quinine, during which parasitemia peaked at 8.6% before decreasing to <0.1% on hospital day 3. Intravenous quinine was then transitioned to oral artemether/lumefantrine for 3 days. The patient made a full recovery and was discharged home on hospital day 10.

raw_case_text: The patient is a 50-year-old Chinese male. He was admitted to the local hospital in November 2019 due to progressive right hip pain with left hip pain for five months. X-ray revealed that the right femoral head collapsed significantly, the joint space became narrow, and there were multiple areas of low density in the right femoral head; the left femoral head shape was regular, joint space was normal, and low-density area was visible in the left femoral head (Figure 5A and B). CT showed severe bilateral hip dysplasia, uneven bone density in the left femoral head, and a huge cavity in the right femoral head (Figure 5C). MRI of the hip joint showed bilateral effusion and bilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral head, particularly on the right side (Figure 5D). Blood tests revealed a WBC level of 4.70x109/L with neutrophils comprising 58.30%, CRP36.0mg/L, ESR52.00mm/hr. SAT was positive at a titer of 1:800. The patient was diagnosed with bilateral brucellar hip arthritis and bilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral head in the local hospital. Despite receiving anti-brucellosis medications for one month, his symptoms did not improve, and he was admitted to our orthopedics department for surgical treatment in December 2019. The patient had previously worked in a dairy factory for more than five years, and many of his colleagues suffered from brucellosis; he had no history of trauma, drinking, or hormone use. Physical examination revealed that both hips were tender, axial percussion was positive, active and passive hip movement was limited, especially on the right side, and a shortening deformity of the right lower limb is evident. In addition to hip joint puncture and irrigation, triple anti-infective therapy was administered after admission: rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals), doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals), and levofloxacin (0.2g ivgtt bid; Yangtze River Pharmaceuticals). Real-time PCR analysis of an effusion in the right hip joint revealed the presence of B. melitensis. We can confirm that Brucella is responsible for the necrosis of the right femoral head. Following three weeks of anti-brucellosis medications, inflammatory indexes returned to normal, and right total hip arthroplasty was performed (Figure 5E); the left femoral head was not treated since it has a regular shape. After being discharged from the hospital four weeks after the surgery, both hips were significantly less painful. The antibiotic regimen was adjusted to rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals) and doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals) after discharge; the total duration of the anti-brucellosis treatment is six months. This patient was hospitalized again in September 2020 due to progressive pain in the left hip, and all right hip symptoms had disappeared. Both the infection index and the SAT of the patients were standard; an X-ray of the hip joint indicated that the left femoral head collapsed and the joint space narrowed (Figure 5F and G). A left total hip arthroplasty was performed on the patient successfully. The patient's symptoms disappeared entirely at the follow-up in January 2022; there were also no abnormalities in blood tests and X-ray of the hip (Figure 5H). The clinical characteristics of three patients are summarized in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presented with progressive bilateral hip pain and right lower extremity shortening for five months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 5-month history of bilateral hip pain, predominantly affecting the right hip. Despite receiving one month of antimicrobial therapy at a local hospital, his hip pain and ambulatory dysfunction progressed. He was admitted to orthopedics in December 2019 for surgical intervention. Following preoperative medical stabilization and right total hip arthroplasty, he completed six months of oral antimicrobials. In September 2020, he presented with collapse of the contralateral femoral head and underwent successful left total hip arthroplasty.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bilateral developmental hip dysplasia; one month of prior antimicrobial therapy at a local hospital; denied history of trauma, alcohol use, or corticosteroid exposure. Epidemiological exposure/Occupation: Worked in a dairy factory for more than 5 years with occupational exposure to unpasteurized dairy products and livestock.

objective.physical_examination: Bilateral hip tenderness, positive axial percussion tenderness, and marked limitation of active and passive hip motion (right significantly worse than left). Obvious shortening deformity of the right lower extremity.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 4.70 x 10^9/L (58.30% neutrophils), CRP 36.0 mg/L, ESR 52.00 mm/hr. Following 3 weeks of medical therapy: Inflammatory indices normalized. Follow-up labs (September 2020 and January 2022): Completely normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvic X-rays (initial): Severe right femoral head collapse with marked joint space narrowing and multiple osteolytic areas; left femoral head regular in contour with focal osteopenia. Pelvic CT: Bilateral hip dysplasia, heterogenous bone density in left femoral head, and large cavitary osteonecrosis in right femoral head. Bilateral hip MRI: Bilateral hip effusions and bilateral femoral head osteonecrosis (severe on the right). Pelvic X-rays (September 2020): Subsequent secondary collapse and joint space loss of the left femoral head. Follow-up X-rays (January 2022): Well-seated bilateral total hip prostheses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Bilateral brucellar septic hip arthritis complicated by bilateral osteonecrosis of the femoral heads and underlying developmental dysplasia, confirmed by real-time PCR detection of Brucella melitensis in right hip joint effusion and positive Standard Tube Agglutination Test (SAT titer 1:800).
Plan & Clinical Course: Managed with right hip puncture/irrigation and triple antimicrobial therapy: oral rifampicin 0.6 g daily, oral doxycycline 0.1 g twice daily, and IV levofloxacin 0.2 g twice daily. After 3 weeks, inflammatory markers normalized, and a right total hip arthroplasty (THA) was performed. Discharged on oral rifampicin 0.6 g daily and doxycycline 0.1 g twice daily for 6 months. In September 2020, due to secondary collapse of the left femoral head (with negative infection markers and negative SAT), successful left THA was performed. At follow-up in January 2022, all symptoms had completely resolved with full functional mobility.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old woman was admitted for a 1-day history of diffuse myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and fever. The patient was pale, icteric, and tachycardic (108/min). The patient's blood pressure was normal. The liver and spleen were not palpable. Arterial oxygen saturation in the room air was normal (98%). The patient had sickle cell anemia (genotype SS) with irregular outpatient follow-up and no history of hydroxyurea intake. The average laboratory data from outpatient follow-up showed: Hb 8 g/dL, leukocyte count of 20.5 x 109/L, and platelet count of 612 x 109/L.
Upon admission, laboratory tests revealed findings (Table 1). Suspected classic dengue fever was confirmed by detection of the nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) antigen test (risk group C), and the diagnosis of sickle cell crisis associated with dengue fever was considered. The initial treatment consisted of vigorous hydration, analgesia, and intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g/day).
Two days after admission, there was clinical deterioration characterized by drowsiness, painful hepatomegaly (palpable liver 6 cm below the right costal border), and respiratory failure. Follow-up laboratory tests detected a drop in serum hemoglobin, reticulocytopenia, a marked drop in platelet count, an increase in LDH, and acute renal dysfunction (Table 1). Tests for renal function were normal. Serology for viral hepatitis (A, B, and C) was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatomegaly, suprahepatic vein ectasia, single calculus (1.8 cm) in the gallbladder with no inflammatory signs, and no dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Due to the marked clinical and laboratory deterioration, a probable diagnosis of SCIC was considered, and support with packed red blood cells (exchange transfusion until HbS reached 28%) and non-invasive ventilation was instituted. Subsequently, there was a progressive clinical improvement, and the patient recovered completely.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old female presenting with diffuse myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and fever for one day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old female with sickle cell anemia presented with a 1-day history of diffuse myalgias, arthralgias, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and fever. Initial evaluation showed tachycardia, pallor, and jaundice without organomegaly. Two days after admission, she suffered acute clinical deterioration characterized by drowsiness, severe painful hepatomegaly (liver palpable 6 cm below the right costal margin), and acute respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle cell anemia (genotype SS) with irregular outpatient follow-up; no history of hydroxyurea use; baseline outpatient labs: Hb 8 g/dL, WBC 20.5 x 10^9/L, platelet count 612 x 10^9/L.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting, diffuse myalgias, arthralgias, retro-orbital headache; no chest pain at onset.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Pale, icteric, heart rate 108 bpm (tachycardia), blood pressure normal, SpO2 98% on room air; liver and spleen not palpable. Day 2 of admission: Drowsy, acute respiratory failure, painful hepatomegaly with liver palpable 6 cm below the right costal border.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission and Day 2 labs: Acute drop in serum hemoglobin, reticulocytopenia, marked thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and acute renal dysfunction. Viral serologies: Hepatitis A, B, and C non-reactive. Abdominal ultrasonography: Hepatomegaly, suprahepatic vein ectasia, single 1.8 cm gallbladder calculus without cholecystitis, and no intra- or extrahepatic biliary dilatation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed acute Dengue virus infection (classic dengue fever, risk group C) precipitating acute sickle cell intrahepatic cholestasis (SCIC) and aplastic/hemolytic sickle cell crisis in homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS). Dengue confirmed by positive Dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen test upon admission. Viral hepatitis A, B, and C and acute cholecystitis/choledocholithiasis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initial treatment consisted of vigorous intravenous hydration, analgesia, and empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g/day). Upon clinical deterioration with SCIC and respiratory failure, management was escalated to non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and automated packed red blood cell exchange transfusions targeting HbS reduction (achieved HbS 28%). Following exchange transfusion, she achieved progressive clinical and biochemical improvement, resolution of encephalopathy and respiratory failure, and full recovery.

raw_case_text: More recently, we experienced the second case of disseminated-CL in Ecuador, which was clinically very similar to diffuse-CL. The patient was a 43-year-old male, as of February 22, 2006 (Fig. 2c, d), and came from a small community "Barrio 28 de Enero," Chimborazo province, a subtropical mountainous area at the beginning of Andean slopes, located at 500 m a.s.l. (Fig. 1 (3)). The lesion began with an insect bite-like papular lesion on the forearm. Then, the lesions appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions appeared on a wide range of the lower extremities, followed by multiple and confluent lesions on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh (photographs not shown). A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed as seen in Fig. 4a. At the time of examination in the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, the patient already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials Repodral  (20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center (Cumanda, Guayas province). After finishing several courses of the treatment, the patient received Glucantime  (10 mg/kg/day) during about 5 months and responded well to the treatment. Montenegro skin test showed positive with a 17-mm induration, and rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band, suggesting a higher level of functions of the humoral immune system(s). Smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for in vitro cultures, and materials on FTA  classic cards (Whatman ) were taken from the active lesions. The smear specimen revealed positive for the Leishmania amastigote with a scanty number. Promastigotes grown in vitro had a tendency to decrease gradually after several days of cultivation and then totally disappeared, probably because of the effect of previous treatment with Repodral  before the material aspiration for culture. The parasites from the biopsy and FTA  card materials were identified as L. (V.) guyanensis by PCR analysis (Fig. 3). Thus, the case was clinically very similar to diffuse-CL but showed the following marked differences: (1) the organisms isolated were identified as the subgenus Viannia, L. (V.) guyanensis, which is also known as one of the causative agents of disseminated-CL in different endemic countries of the New World; (2) the patient was sensitive against antimonials; and (3) the superficial involvement of mucosae was recognized as seen in Fig. 2c, such a mucosal sign is never seen in diffuse-CL cases. The patient was alcoholic, and complications of his liver cirrhosis led to the unexpected death after healing of disseminated-CL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with chronic widespread papulonodular skin lesions and superficial mucosal involvement of the nose and upper lip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 43-year-old male presented in February 2006 with widespread cutaneous eruptions. The illness began as an insect bite-like papule on the forearm, followed by papules on the right ear and nose. Over 2 years, lesions spread widely across the lower extremities, followed by multiple confluent plaques on the abdomen, thorax, flanks, and thighs, with superficial involvement of the mucosa of the nose and upper lip. He received 9 ampoules of trivalent antimonial (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center prior to presentation at the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic severe alcoholism and liver cirrhosis. Resident of Barrio 28 de Enero, Chimborazo province, Ecuador (subtropical mountainous area at 500 m a.s.l.). Pretreated with 9 ampoules of trivalent antimonial (Repodral).
subjective.review_of_systems: Widespread skin eruptions, nasal and lip mucosal irritation; denied sensory loss, motor weakness, or focal neurological symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Extensive, confluent papular and nodular lesions distributed across the right ear, nose, thorax, abdomen, flanks, thighs, and lower extremities. Superficial mucosal infiltration and erosions involving the nasal mucosa and upper lip. Neurological examination showed completely intact cutaneous sensation without peripheral nerve enlargement.
objective.routine_investigations: Stigmata and laboratory markers of chronic liver cirrhosis documented in context.
objective.advanced_workup: Smear specimens, skin punch biopsies, syringe aspirates, and FTA classic card samples obtained. Giemsa-stained smears showed intracellular microorganisms in scanty numbers. In vitro culture yielded promastigotes that gradually declined and cleared, attributed to prior antimonial therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (disseminated-CL) with mucosal involvement caused by Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis in a patient with alcoholic liver cirrhosis.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct smear specimens positive for Leishmania amastigotes. PCR analysis of skin biopsy and FTA card specimens identified Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis. Montenegro skin test was positive with 17 mm induration; rK39 rapid kit test showed a strongly positive band.
Differentials Ruled Out: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL; ruled out by positive Montenegro skin test, subgenus Viannia etiology, mucosal involvement, and response to antimonials) and lepromatous leprosy.
